title: Synthetic Data Generator
text:
NoteDeveloped at the Wasatch Front Regional Council (WFRC)



The application and its repository belong to WFRC; this page only summarizes my work.

title: Synthetic Data Generator
text:
Why it exists
AI coding agents are good at writing analysis code, but they work best when they can run that code and see what happens. The data WFRC analysts work with, such as household travel surveys and transit onboard surveys, holds respondent locations, demographics and identifiers that must not be shown to an agent.
The way around it is a mirror project. Make a fake copy of each table, let the agent write, run and debug code against the fakes, then swap in the real files (same names, same formats) and run the code locally. Final results always come from the real data, so the fake data does not need to reproduce real findings. It needs to be good enough that code written against it runs unchanged on the real file and produces output that looks plausible.
That sets an unusual bar. Statistics matter, but parsing details matter more: agents mostly break on a delimiter, a date format, a leading zero or a missing-value code, not on a mean.

title: Synthetic Data Generator
text:
What it does
The app works in three steps.

Ingest. Open a CSV, Excel, Parquet, JSON, SPSS, Stata or SAS file, or design a table from scratch. For a CSV the app detects the delimiter, encoding, quoting and header; for a workbook you pick the sheet, header position and range. It shows the row count and column names, never row values.
Review. One entry per column with its detected type and summary. You can override the type, confirm missing-value and “don’t know” codes, choose how numbers are generated, edit an ID pattern, add a codebook, set rules between columns, or exclude a column.
Generate. Set a seed, preview 50 fake rows, check that every summary was met, and download the fake file in the same format as the original (SAS files are read only and written as CSV or SAS transport files).

Next to the fake file you can download the spec, a JSON file of the summaries and settings used, and a README for the agent that says the data is not real and describes each column. The spec is the only thing derived from real data. It holds category labels, exact minimums and maximums, special codes, quantiles and ID patterns, and for names, emails, addresses and free text only counts, lengths and patterns. It never holds rows, ID lists, free text or personal values, so you can read it end to end and know exactly what was taken. A saved spec can generate the fake table again without the real file.

title: Synthetic Data Generator
text:
How fake values are made
Privacy comes from breaking the link between rows: columns are generated independently unless you add a rule, so no fake row describes a real person, even where individual values come from the real data.

Categories keep their exact label set and count per label, shuffled into new rows. Coded integers, such as a travel mode stored as 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 or 97, are treated as categories by default, because generating numbers between the minimum and maximum would create codes that do not exist in the codebook.
Numbers, dates and times always place the real minimum and maximum, then fill the rest in one of three ways: evenly between them, a beta distribution fitted to the real mean and standard deviation (the one common distribution that respects fixed bounds and hits both targets), or interpolation between stored percentiles to keep the shape, such as the morning and evening peaks in departure times.
Missing values and special codes like -9 or 998 are placed with their exact counts and left out of the statistics.
Survey IDs are never stored as lists. Each is described by a per-position pattern (digit, letter or fixed character) and how often each ID repeats, so a household ID that appears 2.4 times on average still does.
Names, emails, phone numbers and addresses are invented from word lists, with a choice of regions, and never copied. Free text keeps only its length distribution, and coordinates only their bounding box and decimal places.

Each column gets its own random sub-seed derived from the global seed and the column name, so changing one column’s settings does not change any other column’s output.

title: Synthetic Data Generator
section: Keeping the file identical to a parser
text:
Keeping the file identical to a parser
Much of the work went into making the fake file look the same as the real one to whatever code reads it. For CSV that means delimiter, quoting, encoding, line endings, header and byte-order mark; UTF-16 and Windows-1252 files needed their own transcoding path. For Excel it means the sheet name, header position, number formats, leading zeros kept as text, blank cells kept apart from empty text, and dates in either of Excel’s date systems. For Parquet it means the same logical types, down to integer width, decimal precision and timestamp time zone, with 64-bit values kept exact; the app writes Parquet with its own writer. For JSON it means the same keys in the same order, the same number of nulls and of absent keys, and the same indentation. SPSS and Stata files keep their variable and value labels.
All of this is read in the browser with DuckDB-WASM and its extensions, served from the site itself.

title: Synthetic Data Generator
text:
Proving the privacy promises
No backend, no uploads, no accounts. Everything runs in the browser tab. A strict Content-Security-Policy makes the browser refuse requests to any other origin, and a live counter in the header shows how many requests the page and its workers have made, counted as same-origin, cross-origin or blocked. Closing or reloading the page clears all real data.
The promises are tested, not just stated. Browser tests in Chrome, Edge, Firefox and WebKit check that no outside request is made, that nothing is stored, and that no real value of any column reaches the page, the spec, the preview, the output file or an error message. A robustness test runs the app on a collection of other people’s awkward CSV files; its first run found four bugs.
For machines that cannot reach the web page, each release includes an offline zip with a small launcher that serves the app from a local folder. The release workflow runs the real launcher on Linux, macOS and Windows with outside requests refused before attaching the zip, and the build is reproducible: the same commit gives the same file checksums. The hosted app also keeps working if the network drops after the page has loaded.

title: Synthetic Data Generator
text:
How it grew
The first design document set out a deliberately narrow version 1: one table at a time, every column independent, and CSV, Excel and Parquet only. Relationships across tables, rules within a row, and SPSS, Stata and JSON were listed as non-goals, along with their known costs: arrival times before departure times, and IDs that would not join across separately generated tables.
The app was then built in small, specified slices, each with its own spec, plan, tasks and tests. Later slices closed most of those gaps. Rules between columns now hold in every row and are checked on Generate. An ID column can take its values from another table, a count can follow how many rows another table has per ID, and values can be carried through a chain of tables. A test now generates four linked tables, households, persons, vehicles and trips, and checks that every ID, count and carried value joins.

title: Synthetic Data Generator
text:
What I worked on
The full application: the design document and slice specifications, a TypeScript front end with DuckDB-WASM for reading files, the profiling, generation and checking logic, the file writers, the offline release, and the privacy and browser tests.
My role: developer. I authored all the commits in the repository.

title: Proposal Evaluation Scoresheet
text:
NoteDeveloped at the Wasatch Front Regional Council (WFRC)



The application and its repository belong to WFRC; this page only summarizes my work.

title: Proposal Evaluation Scoresheet
text:
Why it exists
When WFRC selects a consultant through a request for proposals, a panel of reviewers scores each firm’s proposal against weighted criteria, and the scores are combined into a ranking. Before this tool, that happened in a spreadsheet: a setup sheet for the project, firms, reviewers, criteria and scale; one tab per reviewer; and a composite sheet that averaged the scores, applied the weights and ranked the firms.
The spreadsheet worked, but it had a weak spot. There are two kinds of reviewers: applicant reviewers (called “City” reviewers in the spreadsheet, “TLC Applicant” in the app), whose scores count toward both an overall total and a separate applicant-only total, and WFRC reviewers, whose scores count only toward the overall total. The sheet knew which was which only by column position, so adding or reordering a reviewer could quietly put scores in the wrong total. The number of firms, reviewers and criteria, and the 1/3/5 scale, were also built into its layout.
The goal was a tool that keeps everything that made the spreadsheet trustworthy (visible formulas, files people can open, nothing hidden), makes every one of those things configurable, and gives each reviewer an explicit type instead of a column position.

title: Proposal Evaluation Scoresheet
text:
What it does
The workflow has five steps.

Configure the project, the firms (invited and submitted, from a searchable list), the reviewers (TLC Applicant or WFRC, and whether each has signed the confidentiality form), the weighted criteria (as a decimal or a percent) and the scoring scale, either a set of discrete points or a continuous range such as 1.0 to 5.0.
Generate a real Excel workbook per reviewer, one at a time or all together as a zip. Reviewers fill it in Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice and never need to know the app exists.
Import the completed workbooks one at a time or in bulk, or enter scores by hand for anyone who reported back by phone or email.
Rank the firms on a dashboard with overall, applicant-only and WFRC-only weighted totals, each with its own rank, plus criterion breakdowns, radar charts, reviewer score-spread charts and reviewer comments tabbed by criterion.
Export a formatted PDF report for the official procurement record, a Calculations workbook, and a project.json that reopens the project later.

No backend, no database, no accounts. Everything stays in the browser. The only durable save is the project file the user chooses to download.

title: Proposal Evaluation Scoresheet
text:
How it’s built
The app is React and TypeScript, built with Vite and published as static files on GitHub Pages. State lives in a React context with a reducer, and the screens are a small state machine rather than a router. Charts use Recharts, workbooks use ExcelJS, and the PDF report uses @react-pdf/renderer. Colors, fonts and logos come from WFRC’s brand repository, adjusted where needed to meet WCAG 2.1 AA contrast in both light and dark mode.
I started from a written specification before writing any code: the business rules of the original spreadsheet, a set of non-negotiable principles (no server, one project at a time, nothing hard-coded, every number traceable), and file contracts for the project JSON and the reviewer workbook. The specification and contracts are in the repository alongside the code.

title: Proposal Evaluation Scoresheet
text:
The interesting parts
The Excel round trip. The reviewer workbook is the app’s only interface to reviewers, and the app both writes and reads it, so the two sides must agree on every detail. Each workbook has one “Scoring” sheet with a branded banner that states the scale, one row per firm and criterion, and only the Score and Comments cells unlocked. In discrete mode the Score cell is a dropdown of the allowed values; in continuous mode it is a decimal range. Hidden, locked columns carry the reviewer, firm and criterion IDs, so a returned file is matched by ID rather than by row order or firm name. The importer finds the header row by its content, skips blank trailing rows, and flags only scores or comments that actually changed when a file is imported twice. Sheet protection has no password on purpose: it is there to prevent accidental edits, and a lost password would lock staff out of their own files. Automated tests generate and parse workbooks, but opening a generated file in real Excel stayed a manual sign-off step, because a library reading its own output only proves it agrees with itself.
Formulas, not snapshots. The first version of the Calculations workbook wrote every average, weighted score and total as a number computed in JavaScript, so the exported file was a frozen picture with nothing to audit. Now every derived cell is a real Excel formula (averages, weighted values, firm totals, completion counts), cross-checked against the app’s own calculation functions, so changing a score or a weight in Excel updates everything downstream, the same way the original spreadsheet did.
A PDF fit for the record. The report started as the browser’s print dialog. Getting the charts to print in light colors while the screen stayed in dark mode took a separate off-screen chart copy, because Recharts writes colors directly into the SVG and flipping the whole page’s theme for an instant caused a visible flash. It was later replaced with a designed vector report: a cover, a results overview, the evaluation framework, a two-page profile per firm with its radar chart, criterion table, reviewer heatmap and comments, and data notes. The text is real and selectable, the charts are the app’s own Recharts charts converted to vector shapes, and the wording is neutral: the report supports a decision, it does not make one.
Privacy by having nothing to protect. Scores and comments are procurement-sensitive. Because the app has no server and calls no external service with project data, there is nothing to breach. The README records ideas raised internally for a version with sign-in, online scoring and notifications, and a draft design for a Google Workspace backend, and it is explicit that each one would mean giving up that property, with open questions about hosting, identity and data retention to answer first.

title: Proposal Evaluation Scoresheet
text:
Testing
The repository has three layers of tests: unit tests for the calculation engine, schema validation and color contrast; integration tests for the ExcelJS generate-and-parse round trip; and component tests that drive the full app with React Testing Library using real generated workbooks rather than mocks.

title: Proposal Evaluation Scoresheet
text:
What I worked on
The full application: the specification, the React and TypeScript front end, the calculation engine, the Excel workbook round trip and Calculations export, the PDF report, and the unit, integration and component tests around them.
My role: developer. I authored all the commits in the repository.

title: Housing Site Evaluator
text:
NoteDeveloped at the Wasatch Front Regional Council (WFRC)



The tool and its repository belong to WFRC; this page only summarizes my work. It is a complete rebuild of WFRC’s original Housing ATO Calculator. I did not create the original tool or its concept; my contribution was modernizing the scoring pipeline and the web apps.

title: Housing Site Evaluator
text:
Why it exists
Where new housing goes shapes how its residents live. A home near frequent transit, a grocery store and a school gives a household options that a home at the edge of the road network does not. The Housing ATO Calculator was made to put that idea on a map: a conversation starter and a data-informed guide for housing and land-use planning, where each community decides which kinds of access matter most to it.
The original tool was built by Bill Hereth at WFRC. Its data was prepared in a Jupyter notebook and served through an ArcGIS web app. The rebuild keeps the concept and the factors but replaces the machinery underneath: a reproducible R pipeline that scores the whole region, and two new interactive apps that read its output.

title: Housing Site Evaluator
text:
What it does
Users choose one or more communities, optionally filter by land use, and set a priority for each of eleven accessibility factors. The tool combines those priorities into a heat map from most to least accessible, which can be tilted into 3D, inspected cell by cell, saved as an image or downloaded as data.







Group
Factors




Employment
Auto access to jobs, transit access to jobs


Transportation
Transit stops, freeway exits, active transportation


Necessities
Childcare, healthcare, education, grocery stores, community centers, parks



Each factor is scored 0 to 1 per parcel and per H3 hexagon (resolution 10). Wasatch Choice center and Opportunity Zone layers are shown as context only; they are not part of the score.

title: Housing Site Evaluator
text:
How the scores are made
The pipeline runs as four Quarto steps, each writing GeoParquet that the next one reads.

Prepare. Download the ArcGIS layers (boundaries, transit stops and routes, bikeways, schools, healthcare, childcare, grocery stores, parks, job access by traffic analysis zone) and local parcel and building data from WFRC’s Real Estate Market Model (REMM), driven by a single source manifest.
Process. Generate travel-time isochrones with OpenRouteService at 5, 10, 15, 30 and about 60 minutes, using the travel mode that fits each amenity: walking for most daily needs, cycling for commuter rail and higher education, driving for healthcare and freeway exits. Bike facilities get straight-line distance bands instead. The H3 grid is built here too.
Join. Assign every parcel and hexagon the smallest time or distance band that reaches it, attach job access counts, and tag each with a land-use code.
Score. Normalize each measure to 0 to 1 and export the result for the apps and as a File Geodatabase.

Two rules do most of the scoring work. Travel time and distance are “cost” measures, so the regional minimum scores 1 and longer trips decay toward 0; job counts are “benefit” measures, scored against the regional maximum. And three factors combine several layers with a weighted maximum rather than an average: a hexagon next to a FrontRunner station is well served by transit even if it has no local bus stop, so the best-served sub-layer wins (commuter rail counts fully, rapid bus at 0.8, local bus at 0.5).
Land use needed its own logic, because neither building points nor parcel polygons cover every case. A hexagon takes the most common code among its buildings; gaps are filled by sampling the parcel underneath, then by a vote of the six neighboring hexagons when at least four agree, and anything still empty is marked “Other” rather than left blank. Ties are broken by building square footage and then alphabetically, so the same inputs always give the same answer.

title: Housing Site Evaluator
text:
Interesting problems
Moving off in-memory geometry. Instead of loading millions of geometries into R memory, the rebuild runs the spatial work in DuckDB over GeoParquet. That made the pipeline faster and easier to maintain, but it brought its own problems. Bulk updates across ten million rows built up DuckDB’s undo buffers until the R session crashed, and neither checkpointing nor vacuuming released them. The fix was to give binary columns a default value instead of filling nulls afterward, keep the working database in a file, and reconnect every couple of layers.
A join that could not use its index. Joining points to a dissolved isochrone band means testing them against a single polygon with tens of thousands of vertices, and a spatial index cannot help with one giant shape. Cutting each band into small pieces first made the matches identical and took the join step from about 13.6 minutes to 0.6. I first did this with hand-written tiling, then switched to DuckDB’s ST_Subdivide once a release added it.
Esri geometry and browser quirks. Some features in the parcel geodatabase are stored as curved geometry types that crashed DuckDB’s reader, so that loader falls back to sf to linearize them. On the web side, some browser extensions strip the MIME type from the DuckDB WebAssembly download; the app catches that and loads it another way.
Repeatable results. Several fixes were about making two runs agree: sorting outputs by key so row order is stable, deterministic tie-breaking for land use, and isochrone requests that retry, checkpoint each batch and only publish a complete layer, so a failed API call can never leave a partial layer cached as finished.

title: Housing Site Evaluator
text:
The apps
Both apps read the same scored data and let users weight the eleven factors.

A Shiny app in R with bslib and mapgl, with hover tooltips that show each factor’s contribution, pinnable tooltips, a screenshot control and data download.
A static Vue app with MapLibre GL and DuckDB-WASM that needs no server. Data is split into one file per community, so selecting a city loads only that city. Re-weighting is instant because the score and color are computed on the GPU from a map style expression, not by redrawing features. Hexagon outlines are built in a web worker from the H3 index. It uses UGRC’s Lite, Dark and Hybrid vector basemaps and UGRC’s address search. GitHub Actions builds and deploys it to GitHub Pages and WFRC’s web server.

title: Housing Site Evaluator
text:
What I worked on

The rebuilt scoring backend on R, DuckDB and GeoParquet, run as four sequential Quarto steps, with isochrone- and buffer-based proximity measures.
The land-use assignment, normalization and composite scoring.
Both interactive apps and their deployment.

My role: developer. I authored all the commits in the rebuilt repository. The app’s wording and icons were worked out with Bill Hereth, who is also listed with me as a contact for the project.

title: Utah Commuter Flow Patterns
text:
NoteDeveloped at the Wasatch Front Regional Council (WFRC)



The application and its repository belong to WFRC; this page only summarizes my work. It is a modernized version of WFRC’s earlier Regional Commuter Flows map. I did not create the original; my contribution was rebuilding it on open-source tools.

title: Utah Commuter Flow Patterns
text:
Why it exists
Where people live and where they work shapes almost every transportation question a regional council deals with: which corridors carry the most commuters, which cities export workers and which import them, and how far people travel to get to a job. As the map’s own introduction puts it, when roads and transit get more expensive to build, a better balance between housing and jobs is one way to reduce the need for long commutes, and that starts with seeing where commutes go today.
WFRC’s earlier Regional Commuter Flows map showed this, and I didn’t create it. My job was to rebuild it on open-source tools, as a map that runs entirely in the browser, with no server, no API key and no ArcGIS dependency, and that anyone can host as a set of static files.
The data is the Census Bureau’s LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics (LODES). It records, for every pair of Census blocks, how many people live in one and work in the other, built from employer wage records. A flow from Provo to Salt Lake City means workers live in Provo and their employer reports their workplace in Salt Lake City; it describes home and work locations, not daily routes, and the app says so.

title: Utah Commuter Flow Patterns
text:
What it does
Pick a city, county, Utah House district or Utah Senate district and see where its residents work, or where its workers live, as flow lines scaled by commuter volume. Zones on the map can be shown as cities or counties, and clicking a zone selects it.

LODES data from 2002 to the latest release, switchable from the header.
Six linked chart panels: commute balance (top destinations and origins side by side, with a trend over time), a flow diagram, means of transportation and travel time to work (ACS 5-year), commute distance, and industry mix. Every chart exports to PNG or CSV.
Statewide coverage: every county, city and legislative district in Utah, plus cities and counties within about 50 miles of the border in the six neighbouring states, which appear as points so cross-border commutes show up in the totals and charts.
Planning geographies: a Planning Boundaries mode, built from traffic analysis zones, alongside the civic boundaries.
Shareable views: the area, direction and zone level are kept in the URL.
Light and dark themes that carry through the map, charts and controls.

title: Utah Commuter Flow Patterns
text:
How it’s built
A Python pipeline does the heavy work once. It downloads the block-level LODES files for Utah and the Census geography crosswalk, labels blocks outside any city as “County Unincorporated”, assigns blocks to legislative districts by overlaying block centroids on the Census boundaries, and sums block pairs into city-to-city, county-to-county and district flows. Each year becomes a small set of Parquet files with commuter counts and their age, earnings and industry breakdowns. The processed files are committed to the repository.
The front end is plain JavaScript built with Vite. MapLibre draws the map on Carto vector tiles, Flowmap.gl draws the flows, and DuckDB-WASM queries the Parquet files in the browser whenever the area, year or direction changes. The charts are custom SVG and HTML rather than a charting library, which made it straightforward to match the map’s colours exactly. Every push builds the app twice, once for WFRC’s own web server and once for a GitHub Pages mirror.

title: Utah Commuter Flow Patterns
text:
Interesting problems
Matching the published totals. Early inflow and outflow totals didn’t agree with the Census Bureau’s own OnTheMap tool. Two things were missing: workers who live outside Utah but work in the state, which LODES publishes in a separate file, and flows between Wasatch Front counties and the rest of Utah, which a too-strict filter dropped. With both added, and with people who live and work in the same place counted separately from the cross-boundary flows, the totals reconcile.
Commute distance that holds at every level. Measuring distance between city centroids gives one number for every commute between two cities, however large they are. Instead, the pipeline computes the straight-line distance for every block pair before aggregating, and stores the sum of workers times miles alongside the worker count. Summing those two columns gives an exact weighted mean distance for any area, and the same pass fills the distance bands for the commute length chart.
Putting the point in the right place. Flow lines start and end at a point inside each area. Geometric centroids can fall outside an oddly shaped city, so the pipeline uses the Census Bureau’s internal points, which are guaranteed to be inside. One city still needed a hand override: Hooper’s Census boundary includes a large arm of the Great Salt Lake, which pulled its point about 15 miles west.
Places the Census doesn’t have yet. Ogden Valley City incorporated after the Census place geography that LODES uses, while the three census-designated places it replaced (Eden, Liberty and Wolf Creek) are still in the data. A small config file now adds and removes places on top of the Census geography. The change is applied to the crosswalk without dropping a single block, and the pipeline stops if an added boundary would take blocks from another real place, or if the names in the flows, metadata and boundaries disagree. Hill Air Force Base is drawn the same way as an information-only area, with a note that federal and military jobs are largely missing from LODES.
Travel mode and time for areas the Census doesn’t publish. The ACS publishes commute mode and travel time for places and counties only. For everything else (unincorporated areas, districts, planning areas, new places) the pipeline builds an estimate from block groups or tracts, weighted by how many of each unit’s resident workers live inside the area, and carries a margin of error with it. Estimates are shown, flagged as low reliability, or suppressed depending on how large the margin is relative to the estimate. The cutoffs come from a back-test that re-derives every place the Census does publish and compares the two. The same work fixed an older undercount in the district figures before 2020, where 2020 tract IDs had been matched against 2010 tracts.
Clicks that landed twice. A flow line drawn by deck.gl sits on top of city polygons drawn by MapLibre, and a click could reach both. Which handler won depended on timing, so the sidebar could show one city’s numbers under another city’s name. The fix replaced the timing check with a direct deck.gl pick at the click point, so the flow line always wins.
A year switch that silently did nothing. Switching years re-registered a file under the same name in DuckDB-WASM, which failed without an error, and the map stayed on the previous year. Each year’s files are now registered under their own names.

title: Utah Commuter Flow Patterns
text:
What I worked on

Rebuilding the application as a fully client-side web app: DuckDB-WASM queries pre-processed Parquet files directly in the browser, so there is no server, no API key and no ArcGIS dependency.
The data processing that prepares the LODES and ACS tables for the app, including the statewide and cross-border expansion, the planning boundaries, the custom places and the derived ACS estimates.
The map, chart panels, theming and export features.

My role: developer. I authored all the commits in the repository.

title: Demographic Profiles
text:
NoteForked from WFRC’s Community Profiles



A fork of Community Profiles, which I developed at the Wasatch Front Regional Council (WFRC), hosted in my own repository with WFRC’s permission. The original belongs to WFRC (details below). This app is still marked as a draft.
Utah’s population, housing, income, jobs and commuting figures come from several Census Bureau and Bureau of Labor Statistics sources (the American Community Survey, population estimates, LODES and QCEW), each with its own geographies and release schedule. Looking up “how has this county changed?” means piecing them together.
Demographic Profiles does that ahead of time and puts the result on a map, for the state, its counties and its cities and towns. A Python pipeline writes the data to Parquet files and the browser reads them directly, so there is no server behind it.

title: Demographic Profiles
text:
Try it


  
    Demographic Profiles
    Fullscreen
  
  
    
  



 Open app  GitHub

title: Demographic Profiles
text:
What it does
Facts and figures for Utah, its counties and its cities and towns, all in one dashboard with no backend. Census tracts can be drawn on the maps.

ACS 5-year indicators with trends from 2009 to 2024, annual population estimates, jobs, workers and commute flows from LODES, and employment and wages from QCEW.
Ten screens from Overview to Commute, with a year slider that drives every panel, side-by-side comparison of two areas, and a shareable URL for any view.
Honest numbers: every value carries a method label (published for exactly that area, or aggregated from whole Census blocks), so it is clear how a figure was produced.
A PDF report (a designed profile or a poster) generated in the browser for any area.


A profile is always “as of” one year
The screens are built around a single idea: pick an area, pick a year, and everything on screen describes that area in that year. The search box in the navbar is the area picker. The compare button adds a second area, suggesting areas of the same kind first (another county for a county, another city for a city) and then the state, so Salt Lake City against Salt Lake County, or a county against Utah, are one click away. The year slider has a Play button; moving it redraws the population pyramid and the distributions, and rings that year on every trend chart.
Each screen is laid out to fit on one desktop screen without scrolling, and the end-to-end tests check that it does. Every chart has a table view and a CSV download, which is also the accessible form of the data, and the tests run axe accessibility checks in light and dark mode.


A report you can print
The PDF report button builds a document from the view on screen: a cover with the methods, curated charts from every tab, tract maps of the area, the commute flow map, the indicator table, and a link and QR code back to the same dashboard view. The other format is a 24 by 36 inch poster of the key figures. Both are drawn as vector graphics with react-pdf, in the browser, from the same Parquet files and queries as the dashboard. The PDF code loads only on the first click.

title: Demographic Profiles
text:
How it’s built
There are two halves, and they meet at a folder of committed Parquet files.
The pipeline is a Python package run with uv, in stages: validate every configured ACS table against every vintage, download whole ACS tables for the state, counties, places and tracts, then population estimates, LODES jobs, workers and origin-destination flows, and QCEW employment and wages. A QA stage checks that county jobs add up to the state’s and compares LODES with QCEW, and an export stage writes simplified GeoJSON for the maps. Spatial work runs in DuckDB with its spatial extension. Output is deterministic, and a stage rewrites a tracked file only when its bytes change, so with the downloads cached the whole data folder rebuilds byte for byte and a rerun leaves no git diff.
The front end is Svelte 5 and TypeScript, built with Vite. DuckDB-WASM opens the Parquet files over HTTP and runs every query in the browser; it is set to work even on static servers that don’t support byte-range requests. Charts are Observable Plot, maps are MapLibre on an OpenFreeMap basemap, and the commute flow map is a Flowmap.gl layer that loads only when that screen opens.

Getting the numbers right
The part I spent the most care on is not the interface but whether each number means what its label says. Before the release I ran a full audit (recorded in the repository) and fixed what it found. A few examples:

The language card counted group totals together with their own sub-rows, which roughly doubled the Spanish share.
LODES reports educational attainment only for workers aged 30 and older, but the shares were divided by all jobs. Breakdowns LODES doesn’t publish for Utah, such as firm age and size, read as 0% bars; they now show as not published.
A filter on the QCEW state file matched no rows, leaving the Utah benchmark blank.

To keep these from coming back, a data-driven test checks every chart and indicator definition against Utah’s real values in every vintage. The source quirks that are in the data as published, such as one Millcreek block that holds thousands of jobs for some years and then doesn’t, are left as they are and documented on the in-app Methods page.


Where to draw a flow
A flow map needs a point for each area, and the middle of a polygon is often the wrong one. Each area is anchored at the job-weighted centre of its own Census blocks when that lies inside the area, otherwise at a point on its surface. Before this change, the original app’s flows for the whole WFRC region started out in the Tooele desert. Flows to the rest of the state go to a “Rest of Utah” point, placed at the weighted centre of the remaining blocks’ jobs and workers, with its outline drawn dashed so it’s clear what it stands for.

title: Demographic Profiles
text:
What I worked on
Everything in it. I developed the original at WFRC, both halves of it: the Python pipeline that downloads, validates and crosswalks the Census, LODES and QCEW data into committed Parquet files, and the Svelte and TypeScript front end that reads them in the browser with DuckDB-WASM, with MapLibre maps, Observable Plot charts and a Flowmap.gl commute layer. I authored all the commits in that repository.
This fork is mine to maintain. I reworked the geography from the WFRC region and its planning areas to the state, counties and cities and towns of Utah, and gave the app its own name and mark. Narrowing the scope removed a whole layer of the pipeline (the block crosswalk and the area aggregation described below); the remaining county, city and tract files were rebuilt from the cached downloads and came out unchanged.

title: Demographic Profiles
text:
The original: WFRC’s Community Profiles
Community Profiles is the WFRC app this one was derived from. It covers the WFRC region, its counties, cities and planning areas (AOG, MPO, RPO and workshop areas). It belongs to WFRC and is unchanged for now. WFRC allowed me to fork it and host this version in my own repository, with some adjustments, as a demographic profile. It will evolve to accommodate more diverse, strategic metrics for planning and regional development, such as population projections, land use characteristics, transit ridership and travel characteristics. Credit for the original, and for the Wasatch Front data work behind it, goes to the agency.
The planning areas are what made the original harder. They don’t follow Census geography, so the Census publishes no figures for them. The pipeline builds them from block groups: a block group that lies partly inside an area is split using Decennial Census counts for each block, by people for tables about people, by occupied homes for tables about households, and by housing units for tables about housing. Medians can’t be added across pieces, so they are interpolated from the allocated income, rent, home value and age brackets, with a margin of error built from the bracket margins and checked against published county figures. Every such value is labelled as a WFRC estimate rather than a Census figure.
