title: Fetch: a Wget Command Builder
text:
GNU Wget can download a file, a folder or a whole website, but only if you remember which of its many switches to combine. Fetch lets you build the command visually instead. It covers every option in wget --help for version 1.21 (155 settings), explains what each one does, and warns about risky choices. It runs entirely in your browser; nothing is uploaded.
Fetch started as a Wget companion to my Robocopy tool and was redesigned as part of Conduit, a pair of command builders that share one design system. Its sister app is Mirror, the Robocopy builder. This post covers what Fetch is for, what it does, and the parts of building it that were specific to Wget.

title: Fetch: a Wget Command Builder
text:
1 Try it


  
    Fetch
    Fullscreen
  
  
    
  



 Open app  GitHub

title: Fetch: a Wget Command Builder
text:
2 Why Wget needs a builder
Downloading one file with Wget is easy. Everything past that is a combination of options that only work well together. A usable offline copy of a documentation site, for example, needs Wget to follow links, stay below the starting folder, fetch the images and stylesheets each page uses, rewrite links so they point at the saved copies, give pages a proper extension, and slow down so the server is not hammered:
wget --mirror --no-parent --page-requisites --convert-links --adjust-extension \
     --wait=1 --random-wait --limit-rate=2m --tries=5 "https://docs.example.org/handbook/"
Leave out one of those and the copy is incomplete, or the crawl is much ruder to the server than it needs to be. Some options are also risky in ways that are not obvious from their names: --no-check-certificate accepts any certificate, even a fake one, and a password typed into the command ends up in your shell history. I wanted a form that knows these combinations, explains each flag in plain words, and says so when a choice is risky.

title: Fetch: a Wget Command Builder
text:
3 A quick tour

Pick a starting point. Choose a preset (One file, Offline site copy, Images only, Check for broken links, or Gentle crawl) or start from scratch.
Fill in the tabs. Target, What to download, Save layout, Filters, Performance, Requests, Security, Logging and Advanced. Rarely used options stay hidden until you turn on Show advanced.
Watch the command. It updates as you choose, with every flag explained and notes for risky choices such as skipping certificate checks, putting a password in the command, or crawling with no wait.
Add to queue. Build several downloads, reorder them, then download one .bat or .ps1 script. Stop on first failure is on by default.

The presets are where most of the Wget knowledge lives. Offline site copy is the command above. Images only follows links two levels deep and keeps only common image types. Check for broken links uses --spider to test every address without downloading anything and writes the results to a log. Gentle crawl waits three seconds between requests, limits the speed and skips large archives and installers.
The “What to download” tab starts with one choice that sets the shape of the whole command: one file, follow links to a chosen depth (-r), or mirror the site (--mirror). Mirror is flagged “Can be very large”, with a note to set a wait and a speed limit. Fetch also catches combinations that do not do what you might expect:

following links with no wait, which sends requests back to back;
saving as one file (-O) while following links, which puts every page into that one file;
“skip files you already have” (--no-clobber) together with “only download newer files” (--timestamping), which cannot be combined;
quiet output with a progress bar, which still shows the bar.


Other ways in

Find an option. Type a name or a flag, such as cookies or --limit-rate, to search every tab at once.
Paste a command. Paste an existing wget command and the form fills in. Flags the builder does not recognise are kept under Advanced.
Command palette. Ctrl+K jumps to any option, preset or page, and Ctrl+Enter adds the current command to the queue.
Profiles. Save a full set of options and load it later. Profiles, the queue and the form are remembered in your browser.

title: Fetch: a Wget Command Builder
text:
4 How it works
Fetch is generated from the same source as Mirror, so the engine is shared: each option is written once as a declarative entry (flag, label, explanation, tab, risk), and the form, the command, the explanations, search, the palette and the parser are all built from that list. The Mirror post explains that part and the build in more detail. The interesting differences come from Wget itself.
Long flags out, short flags in. Wget has a short and a long form for many options (-k and --convert-links). Fetch writes the long form for most options, so a saved script explains itself when you come back to it months later, but each option also lists its short aliases, so a pasted command using -k -p -E fills the form just as well.
Case matters. Robocopy’s switches are case-insensitive; Wget’s are not (-E and -e are different options). The parser matches Robocopy flags in upper case and Wget flags exactly as typed. It understands both --tries=5 and --tries 5, and treats the last address on the line as the URL. As in Mirror, anything it does not recognise is kept in the Extra flags field rather than dropped.
Secrets are flagged, not stored somewhere else. Fetch has fields for HTTP, FTP and proxy passwords because Wget does, and each one carries the same caution: a password typed here appears in the command text and in your shell history. There is no backend, so the URLs and credentials never leave the browser, but the script you download is plain text like any other.
A different idea of failure. In the exported scripts, a Robocopy job counts as failed only at exit code 8 or above, because Robocopy uses the lower codes to report success. Wget uses non-zero codes for errors, so Fetch’s scripts stop on any non-zero exit code when stop on first failure is on.
Like Mirror, Fetch is one self-contained index.html with no build step to run it. It is generated from the shared source in the Mirror repository, so the two apps keep identical design tokens and components, with an orange accent for Fetch where Mirror is green. Icons are from Lucide and the fonts are Bricolage Grotesque, Instrument Sans and JetBrains Mono. The code lives in the source repository.

title: Fetch: a Wget Command Builder
text:
5 How it got here
The first Fetch, in December 2025, was a Wget version of the Robocopy GUI in a Fluent-style design inspired by Windows 11, with toggles for flags, tooltips, and a queue exported as one .bat file. In November 2026 I rebuilt it alongside Mirror as part of Conduit, with Claude as a pair programmer. The rebuild added full coverage of wget --help, the tabs and presets, risk notes, search, the command palette, paste-to-fill, profiles and PowerShell export.

title: Fetch: a Wget Command Builder
text:
6 Who it is for

Digital archivists creating offline mirrors of websites before they go offline
Developers checking a site for broken links
Bulk downloaders working through long lists of files from a list file
Students learning Wget syntax by seeing what each option does


Feedback and contributions are welcome! Check out the project on GitHub: https://github.com/ar-puuk/wget-gui

title: Building a U.S. Census Data Explorer
text:
As a transportation planner, accessing and visualizing demographic and employment data is crucial for informed decision-making. The U.S. Census Bureau provides a wealth of information through various datasets, but navigating multiple APIs and data formats can be challenging. To streamline this process, I developed an interactive R Shiny dashboard that provides unified access to three major Census data sources:
This post walks through why I built it, what it does, how the pieces fit together, and where it could go next. The source code is on GitHub.

title: Building a U.S. Census Data Explorer
section: 1 The problem: three products, three ways in
text:
1 The problem: three products, three ways in
R already has excellent packages for each of these sources. tidycensus wraps the Census API for the ACS and the Decennial Census, lehdr downloads LEHD’s LODES files, and tigris fetches boundaries. But each one has its own arguments, its own variable codes and its own idea of geography, and every request starts with the same chores: look up the variable codes for the right year, remember which geographies a variable is published for, write the call, then convert the result to whatever format the next tool needs.
I wanted a single window for those chores. Pick a product, a year, a state and its counties, pick variables from a list, and download a CSV or a shapefile. The app is that window: a thin interface over tidycensus, lehdr and tigris, not a replacement for them.

title: Building a U.S. Census Data Explorer
text:
2 A quick tour



The ACS tab: a 2021 block group request for five Wasatch Front counties in Utah, with the selected counties shaded on the map and the returned table below it.


The app has one tab per product, and each tab follows the same pattern:

Paste a Census API key (the LEHD tab does not need one).
Pick a year and a state; the county list fills in for that state.
Choose a geographic level: counties, tracts or block groups for the ACS, plus blocks for the Decennial Census and LEHD.
Open the variable picker and select variables from a searchable table.
Choose whether to include geometry, press Submit, and download the result.

The map highlights the chosen state and shades the selected counties, and the returned data appears in a table under it. Downloads are CSV files, or zipped shapefiles when geometry is switched on.

title: Building a U.S. Census Data Explorer
text:
3 How it is put together

Core dependencies
The application leverages several specialized R packages for Census data access and geospatial processing:
# Census data access
library(tidycensus)   # ACS and Decennial Census API
library(lehdr)        # LEHD Origin-Destination data
library(tigris)       # Geographic boundaries

# Geospatial processing
library(sf)           # Simple features for spatial data
library(leaflet)      # Interactive mapping

# Shiny ecosystem
library(shiny)
library(shinydashboard)
library(shinyWidgets)
library(DT)          # Interactive data tables


Application structure
The whole app is a single app.R. Each product has its own UI object and its own block of server logic, and a navbarPage() ties the three together as tabs:
# One UI object per data source
acsUI <- fluidPage(...)      # American Community Survey interface
censusUI <- fluidPage(...)   # Decennial Census interface
lehdUI <- fluidPage(...)     # LEHD interface

# Unified navigation
ui <- navbarPage(...)
Keeping the tabs separate meant I could get the ACS tab working first and then adapt it for the other two. The cost of that shortcut shows up later in this post.

title: Building a U.S. Census Data Explorer
Building a U.S. Census Data Explorer
Building a U.S. Census Data Explorer
text:
6 Picking variables from thousands
The ACS publishes thousands of variables each year, which rules out a dropdown. The picker is a modal dialog holding a searchable, paged data table of the variable list. You can search by code, label or concept, select several rows, and confirm:
var_modal_acs <- modalDialog(
  title = h4("Select Variable(s) from the List"),
  DTOutput("var_table_acs"),
  size = "l",
  easyClose = TRUE,
  footer = actionButton("selectVarButton_acs", "Select Variable(s)")
)
The selected codes go into a reactiveVal(), which the data request reads when Submit is pressed. Keeping the list in a modal keeps the main screen to the controls, the map and the results.

title: Building a U.S. Census Data Explorer
Building a U.S. Census Data Explorer
text:
8 Small decisions that helped

Caching
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)  # Geographic boundaries
load_variables(..., cache = TRUE) # Variable metadata
Boundaries and variable lists rarely change, so both are cached on disk. lehdr’s downloads are cached as well (use_cache = TRUE). Repeat requests skip most of the waiting.


API keys






ImportantA Census API key is required



Request a free key from the Census Bureau and enter it in the app. It is never stored in the source code.


The key is typed into the app and passed straight to tidycensus, rather than hardcoded or installed in a user’s .Renviron. That keeps credentials out of the source code, leaves each user in control of their own API usage, and lets the same file run anywhere.


Waiting for complete input
API calls can take several seconds, so requests run only when Submit is pressed (eventReactive()), and only once every required input is present:
req(input$api_key_acs, input$year_acs, input$state_acs, input$county_acs, input$level_acs)
The download button appears only after the first request.

title: Building a U.S. Census Data Explorer
text:
9 What I would do differently
Looking back at the code, the main thing I would change is the structure. The three tabs are near-identical copies of the same UI and server logic with different input IDs (_acs, _census, _lehd). That made the app quick to write, but every fix has to be made three times. Rewriting each tab as a Shiny module would turn three copies into one function called with different settings.
A few things are also unfinished in the code:

The LEHD tab has a county selector and a geometry switch written but commented out, so LEHD requests are statewide and download as CSV only.
Code to disable the download button until data exists is also commented out.
The app runs locally (clone the repository, open app.R, run it); there is no hosted version.

title: Building a U.S. Census Data Explorer
text:
10 Ideas for later
Several features would make the app more useful:

Data visualization: built-in charts and maps of the returned data, not just the extent of the request
Comparison tools: side-by-side analysis across years or geographies
Custom geography: support for user-uploaded boundary files
Batch processing: several state and year combinations in a single request
API integration: direct connection to external GIS platforms
Shiny modules: one module shared by the three tabs, so a change lands in all of them at once

title: Building a U.S. Census Data Explorer
text:
11 Wrapping up
The app does one job: it turns the first hour of a Census data task (finding variable codes, writing the request, converting the output) into a few clicks. For transportation planning work in particular, having demographic characteristics, employment and commuting flows behind the same interface shortens the data-gathering step and leaves more time for analysis.
The code is on GitHub under the MIT license. Suggestions and contributions are welcome.

title: Building an Interactive Storymap using {mapgl}
text:
Interactive storymaps have become an increasingly popular tool for data visualization and storytelling, particularly in fields like urban planning, transportation analysis, and geographic data science. They allow us to combine spatial data with narrative elements, creating compelling visual stories that engage audiences while conveying complex information effectively.
In this post, I’ll walk you through creating an interactive storymap using the {mapgl} R package—a powerful tool that leverages MapLibre GL JS to create stunning, performant web maps. This particular storymap traces my personal journey across different locations where I’ve lived, studied, and worked, from Nepal to the United States.

text:
2 Why {mapgl} for Storymaps?
The {mapgl} package offers several advantages for transportation planners and data analysts:

Performance: Built on MapLibre GL JS, it handles large datasets and complex visualizations smoothly
Interactivity: Native support for user interactions, animations, and dynamic content
Customization: Extensive styling options and the ability to use custom map tiles
Integration: Seamless integration with Shiny for reactive web applications

Configuring the Map

server <- function(input, output, session) {
1  output$map <- mapgl::renderMaplibre({

2      style = mapgl::openfreemap_style("liberty"),

Implementing Section Behaviors

text:
6 Conclusion
The {mapgl} package provides a powerful platform for creating engaging, interactive storymaps that can effectively communicate spatial narratives. Whether you’re documenting personal journeys, presenting planning scenarios, or analyzing transportation patterns, this approach offers the flexibility and performance needed for professional applications.
The combination of R’s data processing capabilities with modern web mapping technology creates opportunities for innovative visualization approaches that can enhance public engagement and decision-making processes in transportation planning and urban analytics.

The package installation process incorporates essential libraries for comprehensive geospatial data analysis. The Python environment focuses on core data science libraries including {pandas} for data manipulation, {geopandas} for spatial analysis, and {pygris} for Census data queries. API authentication enables access to detailed demographic and economic datasets from the Census Bureau. The key configuration supports both R and Python environments for automated data retrieval workflows.






TipNeed a Census API key?



Get one for free at census.gov/developers


Put the key in a file named _environment.local at the project root. Quarto loads it for both the R and Python engines, and the repository’s .gitignore already excludes _*.local files, so the key is stored in one place and never committed:

text:
2.2 Load TAZ geometry
The TAZ shapefile provides the fundamental spatial framework for travel demand modeling. The geometry is loaded from the TDM exports geodatabase and filtered to include only zones within the six-county study area using FIPS code matching. Coordinate transformation converts the TAZ geometry to the project’s standard coordinate reference system (EPSG:3361) for accurate spatial calculations. The attribute selection retains essential fields including TAZ identifiers, area measurements, area type classifications, and county assignments.


 R
 Python




# Load TAZ Shapefile
# We assume the input TAZ file is in the data directory
taz_path <- file.path(data_dir, "SE_2019_AD_10_30_2023.gpkg")

lscog_taz <- sf::read_sf(
  taz_path,
  query = paste0(
    "SELECT * FROM \"SE_2019_AD_10_30_2023\" WHERE countyID IN (",
    paste0("'", fips_codes, "'", collapse = ", "),
    ")"
  )
) |>
  sf::st_transform(project_crs) |>
  dplyr::select(
    ID,
    Area,
    Acres,
    TAZ_ID = TAZ_IDs,
    AREA_TYPE,
    COUNTY,
    COUNTYID = countyID
  )

title: Base Year SE Data Development
text:
3.1 2020 Decennial census
The 2020 Decennial Census provides population and housing data at the census block level, offering the finest spatial resolution for demographic analysis. Population variables include total population, group quarters population, and household population derived by subtraction. Housing variables encompass total dwelling units and household counts by size categories. Household size distributions are consolidated into four categories: 1-person, 2-person, 3-person, and 4-or-more-person households. The 4-or-more category aggregates larger household sizes to simplify model implementation while maintaining essential demographic stratification for trip generation analysis. > For more information on the Decennial Census data, refer to the Decennial Census Technical Documentation.


 R
 Python




# Define variables to download
dec_variables <- c(
    TOTPOP = "P1_001N", # Total Population
    GQPOP = "P18_001N", # Population living in Group Quarters
    DU = "H1_001N", # Dwelling Units
    HH_1 = "H9_002N", # 1-person household
    HH_2 = "H9_003N", # 2-person household
    HH_3 = "H9_004N", # 3-person household
    # HH_4 = "H9_005N", # 4-person household
    # HH_5 = "H9_006N", # 5-person household
    # HH_6 = "H9_007N", # 6-person household
    # HH_7 = "H9_008N", # 7-or-more-person household
    HH = "H9_001N" # Total Number of Households
  )

# Load Population and Household Data
lscog_dec <- tidycensus::get_decennial(
  year = 2020,
  sumfile = "dhc",
  geography = "block",
  state = state_fips,
  county = county_fips,
  output = "wide",
  cb = FALSE,
  geometry = TRUE,
  keep_geo_vars = TRUE,
  key = Sys.getenv('CENSUS_API_KEY'),
  variables = dec_variables
) |>
  sf::st_transform(project_crs) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    HHPOP = TOTPOP - GQPOP,
    HH_4 = HH - (HH_1 + HH_2 + HH_3)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(GEOID, TOTPOP, GQPOP, HHPOP, HH, HH_1, HH_2, HH_3, HH_4, DU)

3.2 2020 ACS estimates
The American Community Survey 5-year estimates provide household income data at the block group level. Income categories are aggregated into three broad ranges: under $15,000, $15,000-$49,999, and $50,000 and above. This stratification aligns with travel behavior research indicating distinct mobility patterns across income levels. The block group geography represents the finest spatial resolution available for ACS income data, providing sufficient detail for socioeconomic modeling while maintaining statistical reliability through the 5-year aggregation period. > For more information on the ACS data, refer to the ACS Technical Documentation.

title: Base Year SE Data Development
text:
3.3 2019 LEHD data
The Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics Workplace Area Characteristics data provides employment counts by industry sector at the census block level. Employment categories follow the North American Industry Classification System and are aggregated into transportation-relevant sectors including retail, services, manufacturing, and public administration. The 2019 reference year represents pre-pandemic employment patterns, providing a stable baseline for long-term transportation planning. Employment data at the block level enables precise spatial allocation of work destinations within the travel demand model framework. > For more information on the LEHD data, refer to the LODES Technical Documentation.


 R
 Python




# Download LEHD WAC data at block level
lscog_emp <- lehdr::grab_lodes(
  version = "LODES8",
  state = tolower(state_abb),
  lodes_type = "wac",
  segment = "S000",
  job_type = "JT00",
  year = 2019,
  state_part = "",
  agg_geo = "block",
  use_cache = TRUE
) |>
  dplyr::filter(grepl(
    paste("^(", paste(fips_codes, collapse = "|"), ")", sep = ""),
    w_geocode
  )) |>
  # check the documentation at: https://lehd.ces.census.gov/data/lodes/LODES8/LODESTechDoc8.0.pdf
  dplyr::mutate(
    GEOID = as.character(w_geocode),
    TOTAL_EMP = C000, # Total Employment
    AGR_FOR_FI = CNS01, # Agricultural, forestry, and fishing employment
    MINING = CNS02, # Mining employment
    CONSTRUCTI = CNS04, # Construction employment
    MANUFACTUR = CNS05, # Manufacturing employment
    TRANSP_COM = CNS08 + CNS09, # Transportation, communication employment
    WHOLESALE = CNS06, # Wholesale employment
    RETAIL = CNS07, # Retail employment
    FIRE = CNS10 + CNS11, # Finance / Insurance / Real Estate employment
    SERVICES = CNS03 +
      CNS12 +

      CNS14 + # Service employment
      CNS15 +
      CNS16 +
      CNS17 +
      CNS18 +
      CNS19,
    PUBLIC_ADM = CNS20 # Public Administration employment
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    GEOID,
    TOTAL_EMP,
    AGR_FOR_FI,
    MINING,
    CONSTRUCTI,
    MANUFACTUR,
    TRANSP_COM,

3.4 2020 NCES school and college enrollment data
The National Center for Education Statistics provides comprehensive educational institution data including enrollment and staffing information for transportation planning analysis.
Public schools
Public school data is made available by National Center for Education Statistics through their Common Core of Data (CCD) program. For ease of processing, we retrieve the CCD from the ArcGIS REST service for the 2019-2020 academic year. The dataset includes total student enrollment and full-time equivalent teacher counts for each institution within the six-county region. Public schools represent major trip generation sources for both student and employee travel, requiring precise spatial location data for accurate modeling. > For more information on the NCES Public School data, refer to CCD Online Documentation.
To retrieve the data, we check if a local copy exists to ensure reproducibility and offline capability. If unavailable, we query the ArcGIS REST service and save a local copy.


 R
 Python




# Define local path for public schools
pub_sch_path <- file.path(data_dir, "lscog_pub_sch_enroll.gpkg")

if (file.exists(pub_sch_path)) {
  # Load from local if exists
  lscog_pub_sch_enroll <- sf::read_sf(pub_sch_path)
} else {
  # Public School Location data 2019-2020 via API
  lscog_pub_sch_enroll <- arcgislayers::arc_read(
    url = "https://nces.ed.gov/opengis/rest/services/K12_School_Locations/EDGE_ADMINDATA_PUBLICSCH_1920/MapServer/0",
    where = paste0(
      "LSTATE = '",
      state_abb,
      "' AND NMCNTY IN (",
      paste0("'", paste0(county_names, " County"), "'", collapse = ", "),
      ")"
    ),
    alias = "label",
    crs = project_crs
  ) |>
    dplyr::select(
      INSTITUTION_ID = NCESSCH,
      NAME = SCH_NAME,
      STATE = LSTATE,
      STUDENT_COUNT_PUB = TOTAL,
      TEACHER_COUNT_PUB = FTE
    )

  # Save locally for future use
  sf::write_sf(lscog_pub_sch_enroll, pub_sch_path)
}

Code# Create function to read ArcGIS FeatureLayer or Table
def arc_read(url, where="1=1", outFields="*", outSR=4326, **kwargs):
    """
    Read an ArcGIS FeatureLayer or Table to a GeoDataFrame.
    """

    # Ensure URL ends with /query
    if not url.endswith('/query'):
        url = url.rstrip('/') + '/query'

    # Build query parameters
    params = {
        'where': where,
        'outFields': outFields,
        'returnGeometry': 'true',
        # 'geometryType': 'esriGeometryPoint',
        'outSR': outSR,
        'f': 'geojson'
    }

    # Add any additional parameters
    params.update(kwargs)

    # Make request
    response = requests.get(url, params=params)

    # Read as GeoDataFrame
    return gpd.read_file(response.text)

Private schools
Private school enrollment data is accessed from the NCES Private School Universe Survey (PSS) archived dataset. The data is spatially enabled using latitude and longitude coordinates and filtered to include only institutions within the study area TAZ boundaries. Private schools contribute to the regional education trip matrix and must be incorporated alongside public institutions for comprehensive coverage. > For more information on the NCES Private Schools data, refer to PSS Online Documentation.

4.1 Household-weighted interpolation
The interpolation process transfers ACS block group data to individual census blocks using household counts as weights. This method ensures that socioeconomic characteristics are distributed proportionally based on residential density rather than simple geometric overlay. The tidycensus package provides robust interpolation functionality that preserves the extensive nature of count variables while maintaining spatial relationships. For Python, the interpolate_pw() function is implemented to achieve similar functionality using population-weighted interpolation.


 R
 Python




# Interpolate ACS data to Decennial Census blocks
lscog_acs_cb <- tidycensus::interpolate_pw(
  from = lscog_acs,
  to = lscog_dec,
  to_id = "GEOID",
  extensive = TRUE,
  weights = lscog_dec,
  crs = project_crs,
  weight_column = "HH"
)

Codedef interpolate_pw(from_gdf, to_gdf, weights_gdf, to_id=None, extensive=True,
                   weight_column=None, weight_placement='surface', crs=None):
    """
    Population-weighted areal interpolation between geometries.
    (Full function implementation hidden for brevity)
    """

    # Input validation
    if not all(isinstance(gdf, gpd.GeoDataFrame) for gdf in [from_gdf, to_gdf, weights_gdf]):
        raise ValueError("All inputs must be GeoDataFrames")

    # Make copies to avoid modifying originals
    from_gdf = from_gdf.copy()
    to_gdf = to_gdf.copy()
    weights_gdf = weights_gdf.copy()

    # Set CRS if provided
    if crs:
        from_gdf = from_gdf.to_crs(crs)
        to_gdf = to_gdf.to_crs(crs)
        weights_gdf = weights_gdf.to_crs(crs)

    # Check CRS consistency
    if not (from_gdf.crs == to_gdf.crs == weights_gdf.crs):
        raise ValueError("All inputs must have the same CRS")

    # Handle to_id
    if to_id is None:
        to_id = 'id'
        to_gdf[to_id] = to_gdf.index.astype(str)

    # Remove conflicting columns
    if to_id in from_gdf.columns:
        from_gdf = from_gdf.drop(columns=[to_id])

    # Create unique from_id
    from_id = 'from_id'
    from_gdf[from_id] = from_gdf.index.astype(str)

    # Handle weight column
    if weight_column is None:
        weight_column = 'interpolation_weight'
        weights_gdf[weight_column] = 1.0
    else:
        # Rename to avoid conflicts
        weights_gdf['interpolation_weight'] = weights_gdf[weight_column]
        weight_column = 'interpolation_weight'

    # Convert weights to points if needed
    if weights_gdf.geometry.geom_type.iloc[0] in ['Polygon', 'MultiPolygon']:
        if weight_placement == 'surface':
            weights_gdf = weights_gdf.copy()
            weights_gdf.geometry = weights_gdf.geometry.representative_point()
        elif weight_placement == 'centroid':
            weights_gdf = weights_gdf.copy()
            weights_gdf.geometry = weights_gdf.geometry.centroid
        else:
            raise ValueError("weight_placement must be 'surface' or 'centroid'")

    # Keep only weight column and geometry
    weight_points = weights_gdf[[weight_column, 'geometry']].copy()

    # Calculate denominators (total weights per source geometry)
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.filterwarnings('ignore', category=UserWarning)
        source_weights = gpd.sjoin(from_gdf, weight_points, how='left', predicate='contains')

    denominators = (source_weights.groupby(from_id)[weight_column]
                   .sum()
                   .reset_index()
                   .rename(columns={weight_column: 'weight_total'}))

    # Calculate intersections between from and to
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.filterwarnings('ignore', category=UserWarning)
        intersections = gpd.overlay(from_gdf, to_gdf, how='intersection')

    # Filter to keep only polygon intersections
    intersections = intersections[intersections.geometry.geom_type.isin(['Polygon', 'MultiPolygon', 'GeometryCollection'])]

    if len(intersections) == 0:
        raise ValueError("No valid polygon intersections found between source and target geometries")

    # Add intersection ID
    intersections['intersection_id'] = range(len(intersections))

    # Spatial join intersections with weight points to get weights within each intersection
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.filterwarnings('ignore', category=UserWarning)
        intersection_weights = gpd.sjoin(intersections, weight_points, how='left', predicate='contains')

    # Calculate intersection values (sum of weights per intersection)
    intersection_values = (intersection_weights.groupby('intersection_id')[weight_column]
                         .sum()
                         .reset_index()
                         .rename(columns={weight_column: 'intersection_value'}))

    # Merge back to intersections and keep only unique intersections
    intersections = intersections.merge(intersection_values, on='intersection_id', how='left')
    intersections['intersection_value'] = intersections['intersection_value'].fillna(0)

    # Remove duplicates created by the spatial join
    intersections = intersections.drop_duplicates(subset='intersection_id')

    # Merge with denominators to calculate weight coefficients
    intersections = intersections.merge(denominators, on=from_id, how='left')
    intersections['weight_total'] = intersections['weight_total'].fillna(1)

    # Calculate weight coefficients (intersection weight / total weight in source)
    intersections.loc[intersections['weight_total'] > 0, 'weight_coef'] = (
        intersections['intersection_value'] / intersections['weight_total']
    )
    intersections['weight_coef'] = intersections['weight_coef'].fillna(0)

    # Get numeric columns from source data
    numeric_cols = from_gdf.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns
    # Remove ID columns
    numeric_cols = [col for col in numeric_cols if col not in [from_id]]

    # Prepare intersection data for interpolation
    intersection_data = intersections[[from_id, to_id, 'weight_coef'] + numeric_cols].copy()

    if extensive:
        # For extensive variables: multiply by weight coefficient, then sum by target
        for col in numeric_cols:
            intersection_data[col] = intersection_data[col] * intersection_data['weight_coef']

        interpolated = (intersection_data.groupby(to_id)[numeric_cols]
                       .sum()
                       .reset_index())
    else:
        # For intensive variables: weighted average
        interpolated_data = []
        for target_id in intersection_data[to_id].unique():
            target_data = intersection_data[intersection_data[to_id] == target_id]
            if len(target_data) > 0 and target_data['weight_coef'].sum() > 0:
                weighted_vals = {}
                for col in numeric_cols:
                    weighted_vals[col] = (target_data[col] * target_data['weight_coef']).sum() / target_data['weight_coef'].sum()
                weighted_vals[to_id] = target_id
                interpolated_data.append(weighted_vals)

        interpolated = pd.DataFrame(interpolated_data)

    # Merge with target geometries
    result = to_gdf[[to_id, 'geometry']].merge(interpolated, on=to_id, how='left')

    # Fill NaN values with 0 for missing interpolations
    for col in numeric_cols:
        if col in result.columns:
            result[col] = result[col].fillna(0)

    return result



# Interpolate ACS data to Decennial Census blocks
lscog_acs_cb = interpolate_pw(
    from_gdf=lscog_acs,
    to_gdf=lscog_dec,
    weights_gdf=lscog_dec,
    to_id='GEOID',
    extensive=True,
    weight_column='HH',
    crs=project_crs
)

title: pukRhelpers: A Personal Toolbox of R Helpers
text:
I used to keep my reusable R functions in a separate repository and copy whatever I needed from it into each new project. pukRhelpers is where those small functions ended up. In February 2025 I moved them into a proper R package, so there is one copy, with documentation, that any project can install instead of a pasted file that drifts out of date.
It is a personal toolbox, not a polished library. Most of the functions exist because a project needed them, and I only update the package when my own work needs something. This post is a short tour of what is in it, the one function that turned into a bug report upstream, and a live demo you can run in your browser.

title: pukRhelpers: A Personal Toolbox of R Helpers
text:
2 What is in it
Most of my work is transportation and GIS data in Utah, so the package leans on two sources: ArcGIS REST services, where a lot of public agency data lives, and Utah’s State Geographic Information Database (SGID), maintained by the Utah Geospatial Resource Center (UGRC). The rest is spatial plumbing that kept coming up.







Function
What it does




load_esri()
Load and query an ESRI Feature Service layer


arc_read_encode()
arcgislayers::arc_read() with coded-value encoding built in, so no stray helper objects are left in the environment


load_ugrc_data(), load_ugrc_vars()
Load a dataset, or list the datasets, from Utah’s SGID


load_kml_sf()
Convert KML to an sf object with attributes preserved


st_aggregate()
Aggregate sf objects


geo_split_lines(), st_split_lines()
Split lines by a maximum length


convert_fgb_to_gdb()
Convert FlatGeobuf files to geodatabase layers


convert_xml_html(), extract_html_table()
XML to HTML via XSLT, and pull a table out of an HTML page by its anchor


load_packages()
Load, installing first if needed



Several of these build on other people’s gists and are credited to them in the function documentation and the README.

title: pukRhelpers: A Personal Toolbox of R Helpers
text:
3 A quick tour

Getting data out of ArcGIS and the SGID
load_esri() is a thin layer over arcgislayers. Give it the URL of a Feature Service and a layer id and it returns an sf object. Any other arguments go straight to arcgislayers::arc_select(), so you can filter on the server. If you leave the id out, it prints the service’s layers with their ids and asks which one you want, which is handy when exploring a service for the first time.
library(pukRhelpers)

# List the layers, then pick one at the prompt
layer <- load_esri("https://.../FeatureServer")

# Or ask for a layer directly and filter on the server
layer <- load_esri("https://.../FeatureServer", id = 0, where = "...")
load_ugrc_vars() and load_ugrc_data() do the same for the SGID. UGRC runs a public, read-only PostgreSQL copy of it called Open SGID, so instead of downloading a shapefile, these functions connect to that database, list its tables, or read one table as an sf object:
tables <- load_ugrc_vars()   # schema and table names
uta_stops <- load_ugrc_data("transportation.uta_stops_and_ridership")


File format chores
load_kml_sf() deals with KML files that keep their attributes as one block of text in the Description field, with lines like Owner: City separated by <br>. It reads the KML with sf, splits that field into label: value pairs, and turns each label into its own column. It builds on a gist by Michael Sumner.
convert_fgb_to_gdb() takes a folder of FlatGeobuf files and writes each one as a layer in a file geodatabase through GDAL’s OpenFileGDB driver, which is handy when the next person in the chain works in ArcGIS Pro. It skips layers that are already in the geodatabase unless you ask it to overwrite, and it replaces dots in column names with underscores on the way. convert_xml_html() and extract_html_table() handle the occasional XML metadata file and HTML report.


Two ways to split a line
Both line splitters come from a gist by David Blodgett and do the same job: break every line longer than max_length into equal-length pieces that are all under it. They differ in how they cut.

st_split_lines() works from the line’s own vertices. It measures the distance along the line at each vertex and cuts at the vertex closest to each ideal break point, so the pieces use only points that were already there.
geo_split_lines() uses lwgeom::st_linesubstring() to cut at exact fractions of the length, so the pieces really are equal, with new vertices at the cuts. It also warns you when max_length is under 50, since that usually means the units are not what you think.

title: pukRhelpers: A Personal Toolbox of R Helpers
text:
4 The function that went upstream
The newest function, arc_read_encode(), has a small story behind it. A lot of ArcGIS data stores categories as coded values. UGRC’s statewide roads layer, for example, has a cartographic code field (CARTOCODE) whose values are codes, with the meaning of each code kept in the layer’s domain. arcgislayers can translate those with encode_field_values(), but that needs the layer object as well as the data, so every read became several steps and left extra objects in my environment.
In February 2025 I asked on the arcgislayers discussion board how best to work with coded values, and while trying the answers I found that encode_field_values() failed with its default field = NULL on that same roads layer. That became issue #237. Meanwhile I wrote arc_read_encode(): a copy of arc_read() with two extra arguments, encode_field_values (TRUE for every field, or a vector of field names) and codes (replace the codes with their labels, or keep them and attach the labels). It opens the layer, selects the data and encodes it in one call:
roads <- arc_read_encode(
  "https://services1.arcgis.com/99lidPhWCzftIe9K/ArcGIS/rest/services/UtahRoads/FeatureServer/0",
  n_max = 100,
  encode_field_values = "CARTOCODE"
)
Like arc_read(), it also accepts tables and ImageServer URLs (an ImageServer returns a raster), and anything else gets a clear error.
Adding it in May 2025 is also when I set the package up properly: GitHub Actions now run R CMD check, rebuild the pkgdown site and report test coverage to Codecov.

title: pukRhelpers: A Personal Toolbox of R Helpers
text:
5 Try one in your browser
The package itself cannot run inside a web page: it talks to ArcGIS services and databases, and it needs system libraries that browsers do not have. st_aggregate() is different, because it is plain sf and base R. The code below is copied from the package and run on the North Carolina counties that ship with sf.
Edit anything and press Run code: the cells run in your browser.


st_aggregate() comes from a gist by rCarto, and the package credits it the same way.
First, load the counties and sort them into three zones:






Then define the function. It joins the geometries of each zone with st_union() and summarises the attributes you ask for:






Now aggregate: the mean and median births per zone, with the counties merged into three shapes. Try changing "BIR74" to "SID74", or "mean" to "max":

title: pukRhelpers: A Personal Toolbox of R Helpers
text:
6 What it doesn’t do
Because it grew out of my own scripts, the package has rough edges I have not needed to fix yet. load_esri() prompts for input when you leave out the layer id, so in a script or a Quarto document you should always pass one. The Open SGID functions need the database to be reachable on its PostgreSQL port, which some networks block. And the test suite is still a placeholder: CI checks that the package builds, installs and documents cleanly, not that each function gives the right answer.
When I catch myself copying a new function between projects, it will end up here. If one of them is useful to you, take it. The code is on GitHub under GPL-3, and the functions that came from other people’s gists say so in their documentation.

title: Building a Client-Side Geo/Parquet File Viewer
text:
Want a quick way to preview what is inside your Parquet file? Parquet Explorer is a browser-based, zero-backend viewer for Parquet and GeoParquet, built on DuckDB-WASM. Nothing is uploaded; everything runs locally in your tab.
Parquet and GeoParquet are compact, columnar binary formats, which is great for storage and analysis and less great when you just want to know what is in a file: you can’t double-click it and read it. Checking one usually means starting Python or R to print the schema and the first few rows, and plotting the geometry is a few more lines on top. I wanted to drop the file on a page and see its schema, its rows and, if it has geometry, a map. This post covers what the viewer does and the problems I ran into getting there, most of which were about geometry.
The live app is embedded below.

title: Building a Client-Side Geo/Parquet File Viewer
text:
1 A quick tour

Open it three ways: drop in a local file, paste an HTTP(S) URL, or paste an s3:// URL for a public bucket. DuckDB fetches only the row groups it needs via range requests, so a large remote file doesn’t have to be downloaded in full.
See the schema first: column names, types and nullability, plus row count, file size, row groups and (for spatial files) the geometry column, CRS and bounding box, all before any row data loads. Click a column for its min, max, null count and distinct count, sampled from up to 10,000 rows.
Query it: a CodeMirror SQL editor with column autocomplete and a short query history, or a point-and-click query builder for select, filter, sort, limit and group-by aggregates, whose generated SQL stays visible and editable. The table of results is virtualized and sortable.
Map it: GeoParquet and spatial files appear on a MapLibre map, synced with the table in both directions. Hover or click a row and the feature lights up on the map; click a feature and its row is selected and scrolled into view.

When a file opens, the viewer runs a default query, SELECT * EXCLUDE (blob_cols) FROM data LIMIT 1000, so there is something to look at right away. The LIMIT in your own SQL decides how many rows are loaded.

title: Building a Client-Side Geo/Parquet File Viewer
text:
2 How it works
The app is React, TypeScript and Vite, deployed to GitHub Pages. DuckDB-WASM does the heavy lifting: the file is registered with DuckDB’s virtual file system, a view called data points at it, and everything you see comes from SQL against that view. Schema, row count and file details come from DESCRIBE, COUNT(*) and DuckDB’s Parquet metadata functions, which only need the file’s footer, so they appear before any rows do. The map is MapLibre GL with an OpenFreeMap basemap, the table uses TanStack Virtual, and app state lives in a small Zustand store.

Query first
The first design was a classic data viewer: a table that paged through the whole file on its own, with the map loading geometry in its own batches. It didn’t hold up. Accumulating rows into one growing array hung the browser on big files, and fetching the geometry column with every page of table rows meant tens of megabytes per request for complex polygons.
I rewrote it so the SQL panel drives everything. One query runs, its result goes into the store, and both the table and the map read from that same result. The query runner wraps your SQL to add a zero-based __row_id, and the map’s features carry the same id, which is what makes the table-to-map sync a simple lookup rather than a join. Binary columns (WKB geometry and other blobs) are excluded from the table query and shown as [geometry] or [blob].


Finding the geometry
Spatial detection has two tiers. A proper GeoParquet file has a geo entry in its key-value metadata, which names the geometry column, its encoding, its CRS and its bounding box; the map can zoom to that box before a single row is read. Plenty of spatial Parquet files don’t have that metadata, so the fallback looks for columns with the usual names (geometry, geom, wkb_geometry, wkt, shape) and works out the encoding from the type: binary is WKB, text is WKT. DuckDB’s spatial extension is loaded only when a spatial file is detected, so plain tables don’t pay for it.

title: Building a Client-Side Geo/Parquet File Viewer
text:
3 The interesting problems

Geometry comes in more shapes than I expected
WKB and WKT were straightforward: DuckDB’s ST_GeomFromWKB or ST_GeomFromText, then ST_AsGeoJSON, then onto the map. Two other encodings were not.
GeoArrow structs. Some files store geometry as native coordinate structs (DuckDB types like POINT_2D and POLYGON_2D) rather than as WKB. DuckDB-WASM’s spatial extension had no cast from those types to GEOMETRY, so the usual functions didn’t apply. One attempt built WKT strings out of the coordinate lists with plain SQL list and string functions, choosing POINT, LINESTRING, POLYGON or MULTIPOLYGON from the nesting depth in the column’s type name. Another converted features through to_json(), which turned out to return null for these types and silently drop every feature. The latest approach selects the raw column and converts the nested {x, y} objects to GeoJSON in JavaScript. The README still lists this encoding as a known limitation: such files are detected, but their features may not render.
Esri JSON. Files exported from ArcGIS tools often store the shape column as Esri JSON ({"rings": [...], "spatialReference": {"wkid": 26912}}). Since that is a text column, the viewer took it for WKT and DuckDB rejected it with “Expected geometry type near ‘{’”. The viewer now samples a value to tell Esri JSON from WKT, converts rings, paths, points and x/y pairs to GeoJSON itself, and reads the CRS straight from spatialReference.wkid. One more wrinkle followed a few days later: some tools write these as a Python dictionary’s string form, with single quotes, which JSON.parse refuses. Detection now looks for the keys as text, and parsing normalizes the quotes first.


Projected coordinates
MapLibre wants longitude and latitude. A lot of planning data is in a projected system, such as UTM, and without GeoParquet metadata the file may not say which. The viewer samples a few coordinates, and if any have an absolute x over 180 or y over 90 it knows they can’t be degrees. A CRS panel then opens above the map: you can type an EPSG code, or click your study area on a small map to get a list of projections suggested for that location.
The obvious way to reproject, DuckDB’s ST_Transform, was unreliable in the browser build, so reprojection happens in JavaScript with proj4js after DuckDB returns GeoJSON. Until a CRS is set, the viewer deliberately pushes nothing to the map: feeding raw UTM eastings and northings to MapLibre could corrupt the map source so that later, correct data didn’t render either. Getting reprojected features to show up reliably also took fixing two race conditions in the map component, one where a “style loaded” event was awaited after it had already fired, and one where switching between light and dark styles wiped the layers and never refilled them.


Stale bytes from the previous file
One bug looked like a compression problem and wasn’t. After opening one file and then another, the second sometimes failed with a ZSTD error even though it wasn’t ZSTD-compressed. DuckDB-WASM caches data keyed by file name, and every file was being registered as data.parquet, so reads of the new file could be served pages from the old one. Dropping the old file first helped; the complete fix gives each load a unique name (data_1.parquet, data_2.parquet and so on) while the data view always points at the current one.


Column names that DuckDB doesn’t accept
The query builder at first generated explicit column lists from DESCRIBE, which reports names from the Parquet metadata. When a file has duplicate column names, DuckDB renames them (_1, _2) in queries but not in DESCRIBE, so the builder produced “column not found” errors. The schema now takes names from an empty SELECT * ... LIMIT 0, which returns exactly what DuckDB accepts, and the builder’s column picker hides columns in the table instead of rewriting the SQL.


Explaining failures
Many failures come from outside the app: a server that doesn’t allow cross-origin requests, a private file, a wrong URL, or a ZSTD-compressed file that the WebAssembly build can’t decompress. The raw DuckDB messages for these aren’t helpful, so one function classifies errors and explains them in plain words, including the commands to re-save a file with Snappy compression. It is applied both when loading a file and when running a query, because a ZSTD file can pass the schema step (the footer isn’t compressed) and fail only on the first SELECT.

title: Building a Client-Side Geo/Parquet File Viewer
text:
4 Limits and what’s next
The viewer reads public files only: no credentials, no private buckets. ZSTD-compressed files need to be re-saved with Snappy or Gzip, and GeoArrow struct geometry is the main encoding still listed as not rendering on the map. Those are the obvious places to improve.
The app was built in phases with Claude, which shows in the commit history: each phase and fix has a commit message explaining the cause. If you work with data and want a quick way to preview the contents of a .parquet file, give it a try. The code is on GitHub, and issues and PRs are welcome.

title: Building a Client-Side Open Matrix (OMX) File Viewer
text:
I spent way too long writing one-off Python scripts every time I had to check what’s inside an OMX (Open Matrix Format) file. There had to be a better way.
So I built a browser tool to preview OMX files directly: drop a file on the page and you can scroll through every matrix in it, look up any cell, summarize rows and columns, and do simple arithmetic between matrices, with nothing installed and nothing uploaded. This post covers why I wanted it, what it does, and the handful of problems that made “just show the numbers” harder than it sounds.
If you work with travel demand models and want to try it, the live app is embedded below.

title: Building a Client-Side Open Matrix (OMX) File Viewer
section: 1 What’s in an OMX file, and why it’s awkward to peek at
text:
1 What’s in an OMX file, and why it’s awkward to peek at
Travel demand models move a lot of zone-to-zone data around: trip tables by purpose and mode, travel time and cost skims, and so on. OMX is the common exchange format for these. It is a convention on top of HDF5: one file holds several named square matrices, all with the same zone dimensions, plus optional lookup tables of zone labels.
file.omx (HDF5)
├── /data/
│   ├── TAZ_AUTO      (float32 or float64, N × N)
│   ├── TAZ_TRANSIT
│   └── ...
├── /lookup/
│   └── zone_labels   (length N)
└── root attributes: OMX_VERSION, SHAPE
HDF5 is a binary format, so you can’t just open it in a text editor or a spreadsheet. The usual answer is a few lines of Python with openmatrix or h5py, which is fine once, and tedious the twentieth time you want to know “what matrices are in this skim file, and does zone 1,204 to 87 look sensible?” I wanted something closer to a file preview: open, look, close.

title: Building a Client-Side Open Matrix (OMX) File Viewer
text:
2 A quick tour

Matrix tabs: every matrix in the file gets its own tab.
A scrollable grid of the whole matrix, with zone labels in the headers when the file has them. Only the rows and columns on screen are ever rendered, so a 3,629 × 3,629 skim scrolls like a small table.
Go to cell: type a row and column (by the zone IDs shown in the headers) and the grid scrolls to centre that cell.
Cross-matrix inspector: click a cell to pin it, and a side panel shows that same origin-destination pair in every matrix in the file at once. Because all matrices in an OMX file share the same zones, this is a quick way to compare, say, auto and transit times for one pair.
Summaries: sum, min, max, mean, median, standard deviation or count of non-zero values, by row or by column, for the active matrix or for all matrices side by side, downloadable as CSV.
Arithmetic: add, subtract, multiply or divide two matrices element by element; the result opens as a temporary tab.
Number formatting with a choice of decimal places and compact notation (1.2M), and a light or dark theme.

title: Building a Client-Side Open Matrix (OMX) File Viewer
text:
3 How it works
It is a static site (Svelte 5, TypeScript and Vite) hosted on GitHub Pages, with no backend. The HDF5 parsing is done by h5wasm, which compiles the HDF5 C library to WebAssembly. When you drop a file, its bytes are written into h5wasm’s in-memory file system and opened as an HDF5 file; from then on the app reads slices of datasets rather than whole matrices.
Three pieces do most of the work:

Chunked reads with a cache. The grid asks for blocks of rows (200 by default, aligned to the dataset’s own HDF5 chunk shape when it has one) through h5wasm’s slice(). Each tab keeps a small least-recently-used cache of these blocks, so scrolling back and forth doesn’t re-read the file.
A two-way virtualized grid. TanStack Virtual virtualizes rows and columns independently, so only about 30 rows and 20 columns exist in the page at any moment, whatever the matrix size.
A worker for arithmetic. Element-wise operations run in a plain Web Worker. The two input matrices are handed over as transferable Float64Array buffers, so they move between threads without being copied.

h5wasm itself stays on the main thread. That sounds backwards, but every scroll event needs a slice, and sending each request to a worker and back would add serialization cost on exactly the path that has to feel instant.

title: Building a Client-Side Open Matrix (OMX) File Viewer
text:
4 The interesting problems

“No matrices found”
In the first deployed version, opening a real file failed with “No matrices found.” The parser was looking for matrices under /matrices/ with lowercase attributes, as the original OMX specification describes. Real-world files put them under /data/ with uppercase SHAPE and OMX_VERSION. The parser now looks the group up case-insensitively, accepts either name, and falls back to reading the shape from the first matrix if the SHAPE attribute is missing.


A grid that took two minutes to fill
My test file was a skim with 23 matrices of 3,629 × 3,629 float32 values, about 1.2 GB. The grid’s skeleton appeared immediately, but the numbers took one to two minutes to show up. There turned out to be two separate bugs, both about Svelte 5’s reactivity rather than about HDF5:

The function that schedules a row fetch (with a 50 ms debounce) was being called from inside the template, so every re-render reset the timer and the fetch kept getting postponed. It now runs from a plain onscroll handler that computes the visible rows from scrollTop directly.
Fetched blocks were stored in a Map, and Svelte 5 does not track Map.set(). The data was there, but nothing told the grid to redraw. A version counter that increments on every cache insert, and that the cell lookup reads, fixed it.

A third bug was hiding behind those: when the visible rows spanned two blocks (rows 180 to 210, say), only the first block was requested. After those fixes, values appear as soon as the grid does.


Summaries without running out of memory
The first version of the summary panel used DuckDB-WASM: register each matrix as a table, then run SQL aggregates. On the test file it failed with an out-of-memory error. DuckDB-WASM had a memory limit of about 512 MB, a single 3,629-column matrix took about 105 MB as a table, and “all matrices” meant 23 of them.
The replacement is much simpler. Aggregation streams through the matrix one 200-row block at a time (200 × 3,629 × 4 bytes is about 2.9 MB) and accumulates per-row or per-column results in a plain loop, one matrix at a time, yielding to the event loop between blocks so the page stays responsive. Peak memory is one block plus the results. Median by column is the expensive case, since it has to sort a full column. DuckDB is no longer used anywhere in the app, and it was removed when the code was restructured for the VS Code extension.


Go to cell, off by a column
Centering the grid on a cell sounds trivial, and took several commits. Cells were positioned as flex items and shifted with a CSS transform, so each column’s offset was applied twice and the effective column width doubled. Separately, the horizontal and vertical scrolls were two calls that raced each other. Absolute positioning and a single scrollTo({ top, left }) fixed both. Later, the navigator was changed to accept the zone IDs shown in the headers instead of raw zero-based indexes, which had been landing one row or column off.


Bringing it to VS Code
In July I restructured the repository into a shared engine with two apps on top: the web app and a VS Code extension. The parsing, aggregation, worker and the whole viewer UI are host-independent, since a VS Code webview is just a Chromium page. What differs is how the file arrives, how theme colours are resolved, and how worker scripts are located.
Getting the file into the webview had its own surprises. VS Code’s webview messaging turned out not to preserve typed arrays, so the extension sends base64 instead. For files above roughly 400 MB, a single base64 string exceeded V8’s maximum string length and failed before the webview received a byte; the extension now sends the file in 32 MB pieces that the webview reassembles into one preallocated buffer.
A smaller fix from the same release is worth mentioning: zone labels and matrix names come from the file, so they are now sanitized before going into exported CSVs, to stop a crafted file from injecting a spreadsheet formula.

title: Building a Client-Side Open Matrix (OMX) File Viewer
text:
5 Limits
The web app reads the whole file into the browser’s memory before opening it, so the README recommends files up to about 700 MB and warns above 750 MB. Arithmetic needs both matrices in memory, roughly twice the matrix size. Streaming summaries on a 10,000 × 10,000 matrix take seconds rather than milliseconds. The app needs cross-origin isolation for WebAssembly, which GitHub Pages can’t configure with headers, so a small service worker (coi-serviceworker) adds them in the browser.

title: Building a Client-Side Open Matrix (OMX) File Viewer
text:
6 What’s next
The plan for a second stage is geospatial: load a zone geometry file alongside the matrix, join it by zone ID, and show a row or column as a choropleth, or the largest flows as desire lines on a map. None of that is built yet.
The first working version was generated with Claude, and much of the later work was done the same way; the commit history and the design notes in the repository record what broke and why. If you work with travel demand models and want a quick way to preview the contents of an Open Matrix (OMX) file, give it a try. The code is on GitHub, and issues and PRs are welcome.

title: Nepal Electoral Constituency GeoJSON
text:
In this workflow, we tackle a common geospatial problem: extracting data from stylized news graphics (like election heatmaps) and converting them into GIS-ready formats.
Rather than just cleaning the rough edges of a scraped SVG, we will use a reconstruction technique. We will:

Scrape the electoral map to get rough constituency shapes (Section 3, Section 4).
Georeference the shapes to align them with real coordinates (Section 5).
Reconstruct the precise boundaries by grouping official administrative “Wards” based on which constituency shape they fall into (Section 6).








flowchart LR
  A["Scrape<br/>SVG"] --> B["Parse and<br/>georeference"]
  B --> C["Rough<br/>shapes"]
  W["Official<br/>wards"] --> D["Match each ward<br/>to a shape"]
  C --> D
  D --> E["Dissolve by<br/>constituency"]
  E --> F["Final<br/>GeoJSON"]




Figure 1: The workflow: rough shapes from the scraped map, precise boundaries from the wards.







The constituency map comes from the 2079 general election heatmap on ekantipur. Ward boundaries are the official administrative layer saved in this post’s data/ folder.

title: Nepal Electoral Constituency GeoJSON
text:
2 Setup and Libraries
We use sf for spatial operations and rvest for scraping. We also define paths for our inputs (official ward data) and outputs.


Show the setup code
library(sf)       # Spatial data handling
library(xml2)     # Parsing XML/SVG
library(rvest)    # Web scraping
library(httr2)    # HTTP requests
library(stringr)  # String manipulation
library(dplyr)    # Data manipulation
library(here)     # Robust project-relative paths

1post_dir <- here("posts", "nepal-election-geojson")

2wards_geojson_path    <- here::here(post_dir, "data", "nepal-wards.gpkg")
national_geojson_path <- here::here(post_dir, "data", "nepal-national.gpkg")

3output_svg_path       <- here::here(post_dir, "output", "nepal_electoral_map.svg")
rough_map_path <- here::here(post_dir, "output", "nepal_svg_rough.geojson")
output_geojson_path   <- here::here(post_dir, "output", "nepal_electoral_map.geojson")

4if (!dir.exists(dirname(output_svg_path))) dir.create(dirname(output_svg_path), recursive = TRUE)



1

The path to this post’s own folder, so the code runs from anywhere in the project.

2

Official ward and national boundaries, used as the reference.

3

Where the three outputs are written.

4

Create the output folder if it is missing.

title: Nepal Electoral Constituency GeoJSON
Nepal Electoral Constituency GeoJSON
text:
4 Parsing SVG Paths to Geometry
SVG paths are stored as strings in the d attribute. We need a robust parser to convert these strings into numerical coordinates. This function handles messy spacing and implicit commands often found in web SVGs.




Listing 1: Turning an SVG path string into polygon coordinates


parse_d_robust <- function(d) {
1  d_clean <- str_replace_all(d, "-", " -")
2  d_clean <- str_replace_all(d_clean, "[a-zA-Z]", " ")
  nums <- as.numeric(str_split(d_clean, "[\\s,]+")[[1]])
  nums <- nums[!is.na(nums)]

  if(length(nums) < 4) return(NULL)

3  mtx <- matrix(nums, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
4  if (!all(mtx[1,] == mtx[nrow(mtx),])) mtx <- rbind(mtx, mtx[1,])
  if (nrow(mtx) < 4) return(NULL)

  return(mtx)
}

path_nodes <- xml_find_all(svg_node, "//*[local-name()='path']")

polys_list <- list()
id_list <- character()

for (i in seq_along(path_nodes)) {
  d_attr <- xml_attr(path_nodes[i], "d")
  id_val <- xml_attr(path_nodes[i], "data-slug")

5  if (is.na(id_val) || id_val == "") next

  coords <- parse_d_robust(d_attr)
  if (!is.null(coords)) {
    polys_list[[length(polys_list) + 1]] <- st_polygon(list(coords))
    id_list <- c(id_list, id_val)
  }
}

if (length(polys_list) == 0) stop("No valid map districts found after filtering.")

6nepal_sf <- st_sf(constituency_id = id_list, geometry = st_sfc(polys_list))





1

Minified paths write negative numbers without a separator (100-100), so put a space before each minus sign.

2

Remove the path commands (M, L, C and so on) and keep only the numbers.

3

Pair the numbers up as x and y coordinates.

4

Close the ring if the path is open; a polygon must end where it starts.

5

Skip paths with no data-slug: they are buttons and background rectangles, not constituencies.

6

The result is still in raw SVG coordinates, which is why the next step georeferences it.




The parser in Listing 1 is deliberately forgiving, because the paths come straight from a web page.

title: Nepal Electoral Constituency GeoJSON
text:
5 Georeferencing (Affine Transformation)
The extracted SVG uses screen coordinates (pixels). To make this map useful, we must align it with the real world (Longitude/Latitude).
We do this by calculating the bounding box of a reference map (data/nepal-national.geojson) and scaling our SVG to fit those dimensions.

if (!file.exists(national_geojson_path)) stop("Reference map not found.")

nepal_ref <- st_read(national_geojson_path, quiet = TRUE)

1target_bbox <- st_bbox(st_transform(nepal_ref, 3857))

flip_matrix <- matrix(c(1, 0, 0, -1), ncol = 2)
2nepal_sf$geometry <- nepal_sf$geometry * flip_matrix

# Calculate Scale Factors
src_bbox <- st_bbox(nepal_sf)
src_w <- src_bbox$xmax - src_bbox$xmin
src_h <- src_bbox$ymax - src_bbox$ymin

tgt_w <- target_bbox$xmax - target_bbox$xmin
tgt_h <- target_bbox$ymax - target_bbox$ymin

3nepal_sf$geometry <- nepal_sf$geometry - c(src_bbox$xmin, src_bbox$ymin)

scale_matrix <- matrix(c(tgt_w / src_w, 0, 0, tgt_h / src_h), ncol = 2)
4nepal_sf$geometry <- nepal_sf$geometry * scale_matrix

5nepal_sf$geometry <- nepal_sf$geometry + c(target_bbox$xmin, target_bbox$ymin)

6st_crs(nepal_sf) <- 3857


1

The reference map, projected to Web Mercator (EPSG:3857), gives the target size and aspect ratio for a web map.

2

Flip the y-axis: SVG puts the origin at the top left, maps put it at the bottom left.

3

Shift the SVG so its lower-left corner sits at (0, 0).

4

Stretch it to the same width and height as the reference map.

5

Shift it onto the reference map’s position.

6

Declare the coordinate system, now that the numbers really are Web Mercator metres.





# Create interactive map
mapview::mapview(nepal_sf, map.types = "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas")






# Save the georeferenced SVG map before the ward dissolve
# We use 'delete_dsn = TRUE' to overwrite any old versions
st_write(
    nepal_sf,
    rough_map_path,
    driver = "GeoJSON",
    delete_dsn = TRUE,
    quiet = TRUE
)

message("Rough SVG map saved to: ", rough_map_path)

title: Nepal Electoral Constituency GeoJSON
text:
6 Reconstruction via Wards
The transformed SVG is roughly accurate but has “jagged” borders and low-quality topology. To fix this, we use the Wards method:

Convert high-quality Ward polygons to centroids.
Check which rough SVG shape each Ward centroid falls into.
Dissolve (merge) the Ward polygons based on that grouping.







TipThe result



This results in a map that perfectly matches official administrative boundaries.



message("Reconstructing boundaries using Wards...")

if (!file.exists(wards_geojson_path)) stop("Wards GeoJSON not found.")
wards <- st_read(wards_geojson_path, quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_make_valid()

1wards_utm <- st_transform(wards, 32645)
nepal_utm <- st_transform(nepal_sf, 32645) |> st_make_valid()

message("Matching wards to constituencies...")
2sf_use_s2(FALSE)
ward_centroids <- st_centroid(wards_utm)
3nearest_indices <- st_nearest_feature(ward_centroids, nepal_utm)
wards_utm$constituency_id <- nepal_utm$constituency_id[nearest_indices]

message("Dissolving geometries and removing slivers...")

final_map_utm <- wards_utm |>
  group_by(constituency_id) |>
4  summarise(geometry = st_union(geom)) |>
  st_make_valid() |>
5  st_buffer(dist = 1) |>
  st_buffer(dist = -1) |>
  st_make_valid()

6final_map <- st_transform(final_map_utm, 4326)


1

Work in metres: Nepal falls mostly in UTM zone 45N (EPSG:32645), which keeps the cleanup accurate.

2

Use the planar GEOS engine rather than spherical S2 for these joins.

3

Each ward centroid is matched to the nearest rough constituency shape.

4

Merge the wards that share a constituency into one polygon.

5

Remove slivers by growing the shapes 1 metre and shrinking them back.

6

Back to WGS84 (longitude and latitude) for the GeoJSON export.

# simplified copy (200 m tolerance). The exported GeoJSON below stays full resolution.
final_map_preview <- final_map_utm |>
  sf::st_simplify(preserveTopology = TRUE, dTolerance = 200) |>
  st_transform(4326)

mapview::mapview(final_map_preview, map.types = "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas")






# 6. Save Result
st_write(
    final_map,
    output_geojson_path,
    driver = "GeoJSON",
    layer_options = "COORDINATE_PRECISION=6",
    delete_dsn = TRUE,
    quiet = TRUE
)

message("Reconstruction Complete! Saved to: ", output_geojson_path)
