title: An Education Explorer for Public NCES Data
text:
The National Center for Education Statistics publishes a remarkable amount of open data on schools and colleges, but spread across separate surveys with different file layouts, identifiers and release schedules. Looking up “what has happened to enrollment near this school?” means stitching several of them together.
Education Explorer does that stitching ahead of time and puts the result on a map. It is a sibling of my freight explorer: same idea (a static site, a local data pipeline, DuckDB in the browser), different data. Education Explorer came first, and the freight project reused its conventions.
This post covers what the explorer shows, how it is built, and the parts of the pipeline that took the most work: finding the files, surviving forty years of changing layouts, and getting every school onto the map.

title: An Education Explorer for Public NCES Data
text:
1 Try it


  
    Education Explorer
    Fullscreen
  
  
    
  



 Open app  Data and methods  GitHub  DOI

title: An Education Explorer for Public NCES Data
section: 2 Why NCES data is hard to use
text:
2 Why NCES data is hard to use
There is no single “schools” dataset. NCES runs three separate collections, each with its own key:

the Common Core of Data (CCD) for public schools and districts, keyed on NCESSCH and LEAID;
the Private School Universe Survey (PSS), keyed on PPIN, collected every two years;
IPEDS for colleges and universities, keyed on UNITID.

Each one is distributed differently. The CCD file page is rendered by JavaScript from a JSON API, and the file names carry release dates and version codes, so the URLs cannot be guessed. The IPEDS file catalogue sits behind an ASP.NET postback form. Older CCD years exist only as SAS files (and the very oldest only as fixed-width text). The modern CCD membership file is a 2.3 GB national CSV, of which Utah is a small slice. And the CCD school directory, the obvious place to look for coordinates, has no latitude or longitude at all; those live in a separate NCES product (EDGE).
None of this is hidden. It is just a lot of plumbing between a question and an answer, and the plumbing changes every year.

title: An Education Explorer for Public NCES Data
text:
3 A quick tour








Layer
Source
Years




Public schools and districts
NCES Common Core of Data (CCD) + EDGE locations
1997-98 onward


Private schools
NCES Private School Universe Survey (PSS)
every survey, 1989-90 to 2023-24


Colleges
NCES IPEDS
1980 onward in the tables; map layer from 2000


School district boundaries
Census TIGER/Line
2010-11 onward



Each layer has its own shape and color, so the map stays readable with all three on. Beyond the map you get:

A year slider with play, a histogram of places per year, and markers for the biennial private-school survey years.
Detail panels with enrollment trends by race/ethnicity, sex and grade, free and reduced-price lunch, staff, finance, graduates, and IPEDS enrollment, awards and admissions. Colleges also get online course load, retention and graduation, tuition and net price, and revenue and spending.
A table explorer for every IPEDS and PSS table, with dictionary labels and CSV export.
Compare mode (up to four places), a table view with CSV export, and shareable URLs that carry the year, selection, filters, basemap and theme.
Optional marker coloring by school level, charter status or locale (the shape never changes, so color is never the only cue).
Light, dark and system themes, and five OpenFreeMap basemaps.







NoteWhat it does not do



It shows data and caveats only. It does not rank schools, compute quality scores or recommend anything, and a Data and methods page documents every source and release.


That rule shaped several small decisions. The admissions chart shows counts of applicants, admits and enrollees rather than a selectivity score. Where a school’s figures are shown against the state, the reference is the median and middle half of operating public schools, never a rank or percentile. Charts that could be read as quality (ratios, spending, graduation) carry a descriptive-only note.

title: An Education Explorer for Public NCES Data
text:
4 How it works






flowchart LR
  A["NCES / Census files"] --> B["Local pipeline<br>Python + DuckDB"]
  B --> C["Parquet in docs/data/"]
  C --> D["GitHub Pages"]
  D --> E["Browser: DuckDB-WASM<br>reads byte ranges"]






The first paint comes from small JSON “points” files; DuckDB-WASM loads afterwards and reads only the Parquet byte ranges a query needs. There is no backend, no GitHub Actions and no key-gated service, so the site costs nothing to run. Before writing any app code I checked that GitHub Pages answers range requests for Parquet (it returns 206 Partial Content with CORS headers), because the whole design depended on it.
Two details of shipping DuckDB to a static host:

GitHub Pages does not compress .wasm files, and the DuckDB engine is 36 MB raw. The site ships it gzipped (about 8 MB) and inflates it in the browser.
DuckDB-WASM normally downloads its Parquet extension from extensions.duckdb.org at runtime. The site hosts that extension itself, so the browser talks only to the site and to the OpenFreeMap tile server, and a smoke test asserts exactly that.

The front end is Vite, Svelte 5 and TypeScript, with MapLibre for the map and Observable Plot for the charts. The pipeline is Python run with uv, doing almost all of its work in DuckDB SQL.
Updating after NCES publishes a new release is two commands:
cd pipeline
1uv run python -m nces_pipeline fetch --check-only
2uv run python -m nces_pipeline update

1

List what is new without downloading anything.

2

Fetch, build, geocode, build boundaries and the dictionary, then validate. It prints a changelog of row-count changes.

title: An Education Explorer for Public NCES Data
text:
5 The hard parts

Finding the files
Because none of the three sources has a stable, guessable file list, each one needed its own discovery step. CCD files come from the NCES datatables JSON API, queried one school year at a time (asking for all years at once returns a server error). The IPEDS catalogue is scraped from its ASP.NET form, one postback per survey year, and the files come from the complete-data-files directory. Raw downloads stay on my machine; only a manifest with each file’s URL and SHA-256 hash is committed.
The API is not complete either. The district finance files (F-33) are missing from the CCD listing, so the pipeline reads a short list of extra files from config/ccd_extra_files.yml for exactly that case.


Forty years of changing layouts
NCES changes file layouts often: columns are added, dropped and renamed, and the older files use survey-year suffixes on column names. Every source therefore has a YAML column map. CCD has one map per topic and year; IPEDS and PSS have one map per table, with a year range on each column, which avoids writing roughly 850 near-identical files for IPEDS alone.
The build includes a schema-drift guard. When a release adds, drops or renames a column, the build stops and names the nearest known column:
+ NEWCOL not in the map (nearest known: OLDCOL)
The guard also checks types, and that is where the most instructive bug came from. Column types were first sniffed from Utah’s own rows. A smoke run for Colorado then failed: an IPEDS column that held only numbers in Utah held text codes in Colorado. Types are now sniffed from the national files, never the state subset, and any non-empty value that will not cast to its mapped type fails the build. (Integers are detected with a regular expression, because DuckDB’s TRY_CAST('40.76' AS BIGINT) quietly rounds instead of failing.) The same Colorado run showed that IPEDS uniqueness keys derived from one state’s rows do not hold for another, so keys are now widened against the national files too.
The legacy CCD years (1997-98 to 2013-14) are read from SAS files in 20,000-row chunks and written into the same tables as the modern years, with old codes recoded to the modern labels. The year suffixes are stripped only for files that use them, so a column like G10 (grade 10) is not mangled.


Missing is not zero
NCES marks missing, not-applicable and suppressed values with sentinel codes (-1, -2, -3, -9, or letters in some files). The pipeline turns these into NULL with a separate flag column that says why, so a suppressed count never shows up as zero on a chart. IPEDS is the exception: its negative codes are labelled categories in code columns, and finance values can legitimately be negative, so they are kept as published and documented in the caveats.
Sentinel handling has its own trap: Utah’s longitudes are negative. Coordinate columns are marked as signed in the maps after validation caught them being treated as missing.


Getting every school onto the map
Coordinates come from four places, in order of preference:

NCES EDGE files for public schools from 2014-15. The EDGE text files have no header row and their column order changes between years, so the pipeline reads the shapefile’s attribute table instead. A year that has a directory but no EDGE file yet carries each school’s latest coordinates forward.
CCD’s own coordinates in the legacy files, available from 1999-00.
PSS and IPEDS coordinates, where those surveys publish them (PSS from 2005-06, which is why the private-school layer starts there).
The Census Geocoder for whatever is left. Results are cached in a committed Parquet file so they are never requested twice. The first run matched 146 of 163 addresses; non-exact matches get a dotted marker outline so approximate locations look approximate.

Private schools add a timing problem: the survey is biennial. For any slider year, the map shows the latest survey that began in or before it and says so.


Deterministic output and a validation gate
Parquet output is written with explicit ordering, a single writer and fixed compression and row-group settings, so re-running update on unchanged inputs leaves git status clean. Every data change is a reviewable diff.
Validation also rejects row counts that fall more than 20% from the committed baseline, duplicate identifiers, files over 90 MB, columns without a dictionary entry and coordinates outside the state’s bounding box. That last check found a real exception: Navajo Mountain school sits just across the border in Arizona but is run by a Utah district. Rather than loosen the check, the state config lists that school’s ID as a known exception.

title: An Education Explorer for Public NCES Data
section: 6 A state is a config file
text:
6 A state is a config file
Nothing in the code is specific to Utah. The state is set by one file:
name: Utah
abbrev: UT
fips: "49"
bbox: [-114.06, 36.99, -109.04, 42.01]   # [W, S, E, N]
center: [-111.65, 39.32]
zoom: 6
site_title: "Utah Education Explorer"
Validation fails if a state name shows up as a literal anywhere in the outputs, which is what keeps that promise honest. The Colorado smoke run built the modern CCD, EDGE, IPEDS and PSS data with no schema or type drift once the fixes above were in.

title: An Education Explorer for Public NCES Data
text:
7 How it was built
I wrote the plan first, as a HANDOFF.md with the locked decisions (static hosting, no paid services, real NCES files rather than a third-party API, Utah as the target) and a phased plan, and built the project with Claude Code over a few days in October 2026. Every claim in the plan about URLs or columns was marked to be checked against the live source before use, and the first phase was nothing but spikes against real files. Several of the plan’s assumptions turned out wrong, the missing coordinates in the CCD directory among them, and those corrections are recorded in the repository’s SPIKES.md and docs/DECISIONS.md.

title: An Education Explorer for Public NCES Data
text:
8 Limits and what’s next

Not ingested: CCD 1986-87 to 1996-97 (fixed-width text only) and the 1997-98 district file. IPEDS tables before 2000 are in the table explorer but not on the map or in the charts.
Some data stay in the Data tab only: PSS items whose layout changed between surveys, and the 2016-2020 faculty salary files, which report only total outlays and are left blank rather than guessed.
Mobile layouts were tested in Chromium emulation only, and other browsers have not been tested.
Larger states were not a design target. They should work in principle, but file sizes and browser memory have only been tested for Utah. The next step is a full Colorado build, including the legacy CCD years, and a look at size and load time for a large state.

The code is on GitHub under the MIT license, and the README explains how to add a state. Education Explorer is archived on Zenodo with the DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23789925.

title: Borderline: A U.S. Geography Guessing Game
text:
I spend my days around maps of the U.S., which makes it a little embarrassing how often I cannot place a county. Borderline is the fix: you are given a place name, you click where you think it is on a black outline map, and you find out how close to “borderline” your geography really is.
It is a small game, but it turned out to be a good excuse to deal with some real cartography problems in plain JavaScript: which projection to draw a single state in, how to tell whether a click landed inside a county with a coastline full of islands, and how to keep an offline web app from serving stale code forever.

title: Borderline: A U.S. Geography Guessing Game
text:
1 Play


  
    Borderline
    Fullscreen
  
  
    
  



 Open app  GitHub

title: Borderline: A U.S. Geography Guessing Game
text:
2 The idea: no interior borders
Most map quizzes show you every state line and ask you to pick one. That turns the game into shape recognition with a lot of help: once you have found the neighbours, the answer is the only blank piece left. Borderline draws only the outer outline. In States mode you see the outline of the country and nothing inside it; in Counties mode you pick a state, the map zooms to that state’s outline, and again there are no county lines. You have to know roughly where Kansas is, not just what it looks like.

title: Borderline: A U.S. Geography Guessing Game
text:
3 How it plays

States mode: click inside the named state to score. Miss, and the correct state is highlighted in red and your click is marked, so you can see how far off you were.
Counties mode: you get county names, or the locally correct equivalent: parishes in Louisiana, boroughs and census areas in Alaska, and independent cities in Virginia, Maryland, Missouri and Nevada.
Easy or Hard: Easy keeps every answered shape on the map (green for a hit, red with a diagonal hatch for a miss) as a running record of the game; Hard clears it between guesses.
Untimed or Blitz: choose 10, 25 or all rounds, or race a 60-second clock. Counties mode hides round counts a state can’t fill: county totals run from 3 in Delaware to 254 in Texas, so Delaware only offers “All”.
Zoom and pan for fiddly shapes like tiny islands and thin coastal counties: scroll or pinch to zoom, drag to pan, or use the on-map buttons. The view resets every round.

The game remembers your best score per mode, round count, state and difficulty in localStorage, and across all your games it keeps a per-place miss rate. Once something has been asked at least twice and you keep getting it wrong, it shows up in a “you struggle most with” list on the start screen. At the end of a game, Retry these replays just what you missed, and Copy result puts a Wordle-style summary (score, a green and red grid of the rounds in order, and a link) on your clipboard.
The start screen’s settings are also mirrored into the URL, so the address bar is always a link to the current setup. For example, ?mode=counties&state=Texas&difficulty=hard&rounds=25&play=1 drops you straight into 25 rounds of Texas counties on Hard.

title: Borderline: A U.S. Geography Guessing Game
text:
4 Under the hood
Borderline is pure static HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules): no build step, no server, no CDN, built to live on GitHub Pages. The map is drawn on a <canvas>. Boundary data comes from the U.S. Census Bureau via us-atlas, which packages TIGER/Line boundaries as TopoJSON. The two libraries it needs, topojson-client and d3-geo, are bundled once with esbuild into small ES modules and committed to the repository, and the fonts (Space Grotesk and Space Mono) are self-hosted. Keeping it dependency-free means it loads fast and is easy for anyone to read and fork.
The code is split into small modules: game.js is the round and scoring state machine, mapData.js loads the topology and builds prompt lists and labels, geometry.js holds projections and hit-testing, renderer.js does the canvas drawing, and stats.js tracks the lifetime miss rates.

title: Borderline: A U.S. Geography Guessing Game
text:
5 The interesting parts

One projection for the country, another for each state
States mode uses us-atlas’s pre-projected Albers USA file, with Alaska and Hawaii already scaled into insets. That is the familiar look for a whole-country map, and since the coordinates are already in pixel space, d3.geoPath() can draw them with a null projection.
The first version of Counties mode reused the same Albers coordinates and simply zoomed into one state’s bounding box. It looked wrong. Albers is a conic projection whose meridians converge toward the pole; at continental scale you never notice, but zoomed into a single rectangular state like Utah, Wyoming or Colorado the whole state visibly tilts. The fix was to switch Counties mode to the unprojected (longitude and latitude) county file and fit a fresh Web Mercator projection to each state’s extent every time the canvas resizes. Utah and Wyoming came out as clean, upright rectangles.
Alaska then broke that fix. Its Aleutian chain crosses the 180° meridian, and a plain Mercator fit sees a feature spanning almost 360° of longitude, so the state shrinks to a speck. d3.geoBounds is spherical-aware and reports a crossing feature with its west edge greater than its east edge, so the fitting function checks for exactly that and rotates the projection to centre on the state’s own longitude before fitting:
const [[west], [east]] = geoBounds(feature);
const crossesAntimeridian = west > east;
const centerLon = crossesAntimeridian
  ? (((west + east + 360) / 2 + 180) % 360) - 180
  : (west + east) / 2;

return geoMercator().rotate([-centerLon, 0]).fitExtent([[x0, y0], [x1, y1]], feature);
A related bug from the very first day went the other way: the bounding-box helper used d3.geoBounds on the already-projected Albers coordinates, and since that function expects degrees, it silently returned the whole world. The rule I ended up with is planar bounds for projected data, spherical bounds for longitude and latitude.


Did the click land inside?
Hit-testing reuses the drawing code. The target feature is turned into a Path2D in the same pixel space the renderer draws in, and a tiny off-screen canvas answers isPointInPath(). Because the path comes from the same projection as the picture, the answer matches what you see, including holes and multi-part shapes. Zoom and pan sit on top as a separate view transform, which the click handler inverts before the per-mode inversion, so hit-testing stays correct at any zoom level. Pointer handling tells a tap from a drag or pinch with a movement threshold and a pointer count, so panning never registers as a guess.


County names are not in the data
The county name property has no suffix, so the game adds one. Louisiana gets “Parish”. Alaska’s units (boroughs, census areas, consolidated municipalities, and “City and Borough” units like Juneau and Sitka) come from a hand-written lookup table, because they can’t be derived from the data. For the states with independent cities, the FIPS code decides: codes of 500 and above are cities, so the game can tell “Baltimore County” from “Baltimore City” and “Richmond County” from “Richmond City”. As a safety net, any name that still collides within a state gets its FIPS code appended. Washington, D.C. is never prompted (it would be a single-pixel target), though its outline stays on the map.


Keeping a fast first load
The county file is about 840 KB, against about 80 KB for the states, so it is fetched only the first time you switch to Counties mode. A player who only plays States never downloads it.


The offline bug that hid a fix
Borderline is an installable progressive web app: a service worker precaches the app shell on first visit and serves it cache-first afterward, so the game works with no network. That design has a sharp edge, which I found the hard way. A fix for Blitz mode getting stuck in a background tab (the countdown relied on setInterval ticks, which browsers throttle in hidden tabs; it now checks a wall-clock deadline) was correct in the source but never reached anyone who had already visited, because the cache name had not changed since the service worker was added. Their browsers kept serving the first cached main.js. The fix was to bump the cache name, add a regression test that seeds a stale cache and checks it gets purged on activation, and write a note in the README: any commit that touches a precached file must bump the cache name.


Tests that look at pixels
The game itself has zero dependencies, but there is a dev-only Playwright suite. It checks the things that actually broke during development: hit-testing across all states and the trickiest county cases (Utah’s tilt, Alaska’s antimeridian, Hawaii’s scattered islands, Virginia’s name collisions), Easy and Hard history by reading rendered canvas pixels, pan and zoom correctness, offline loading with the network disabled, and Blitz timing with a mocked clock instead of a real 60-second wait. A few counties are so thin or scattered that a random click point can miss them, so those checks use a 60% floor; a real regression drops the hit rate to zero, which is what the suite is there to catch.
One feature didn’t survive: I added a typed-answer box so screen-reader users could play unaided, then removed it the same day. The prompt already names the place (“Find Kansas”), so typing the name back tested nothing about geography. The canvas does keep a live aria-label and announces each result through an aria-live region, and every control is a real button.

title: Borderline: A U.S. Geography Guessing Game
text:
6 What’s next
The data is a fixed vintage from us-atlas: Connecticut still has its eight traditional counties rather than the newer planning regions, and Puerto Rico is not in the Albers files the game uses. Swapping in newer Census data would mean updating that handling.
The code is on GitHub. It is still borderline playable, so bug reports are welcome.

title: basemapper: Vector Basemaps for R and Python, Rendered Headlessly
text:
Every static map I make has two halves: the data I care about, and the basemap underneath that tells the reader where they are. In R and Python I have great tools for the first half. For the second half, I had been putting up with blurry tiles for years.
This post introduces basemapper, an R and Python package (with a Rust core) that renders vector basemaps straight into ggplot2, tmap, matplotlib and plotnine figures. It is also the story of how a small annoyance on a work project turned into a software port of MapLibre GL JS’s rendering pipeline, checked pixel by pixel against the real thing.

title: basemapper: Vector Basemaps for R and Python, Rendered Headlessly
text:
1 The map that started it
In mid-2026 I was building the Opportunity Zones 2.0 info sheets at the Wasatch Front Regional Council: a Quarto pipeline that produces a PDF page for every eligible census tract in the region, each with a large map of the tract and its surroundings. These pages go to investors and local governments, so the maps had to read well in print.
The Utah Geospatial Resource Center (UGRC) publishes a lovely basemap called Lite, and it publishes it two ways: as pre-drawn raster tiles, and as a vector tile style meant for MapLibre in a web browser. The R and Python basemap tools I knew only speak raster tiles. So the maps got the raster version, and the result looked like this: soft contours, labels that were hard to read, and a place name half hidden under a label box.
The vector version of the same basemap exists, looks far better, and is free. I just had no way to put it under a ggplot.

title: basemapper: Vector Basemaps for R and Python, Rendered Headlessly
section: 2 The trouble with tiles in a static figure
text:
2 The trouble with tiles in a static figure
Raster tiles were designed for slippy web maps. Each tile is a 256 or 512 pixel image drawn for one whole zoom level, and a web map shows them at exactly that size. A static figure breaks both assumptions:

Your figure’s extent picks a fractional zoom. A tract that fits the panel at zoom 15.6 gets tiles drawn for zoom 15 or 16, resampled to fit. Labels end up too small or too large, and always a little soft.
Your figure has its own resolution. A 300 dpi PDF wants three times as many pixels as a screen. Raster tiles for screens get upscaled, and print shows it.
The design is baked in. You cannot turn off the points of interest, drop the labels, or keep only roads and water. You get the picture the tile server drew.

A vector style fixes all three, because the map is drawn on demand from geometry and a style sheet. The catch is that vector styles are drawn by MapLibre GL JS, which runs in a browser on a GPU. You can screenshot a browser canvas, but that gives you a screen-resolution image of a web page, not a print-quality figure, and it drags a headless browser into your R session.
Here is the difference on one view of downtown Salt Lake City, both panels at zoom 15.6 and 2× pixel ratio. The left panel is UGRC Lite as raster tiles from UGRC Discover; the right panel is the same basemap from its vector style, rendered by basemapper. The bottom row enlarges the outlined area around the Courthouse TRAX station.



UGRC Lite as raster tiles (left) and as a vector style rendered by basemapper (right), same view and output size.


What I wanted was MapLibre’s output, at any zoom and any resolution, without a browser, callable from R and Python.

title: basemapper: Vector Basemaps for R and Python, Rendered Headlessly
text:
3 A quick tour
basemapper’s central object is a map view: a style, a size, and either a centre and zoom or a bounding box. From there you can render it to a PNG, an array, a georeferenced raster or a true vector SVG.

RPython


library(basemapper)

m <- basemap("UGRC.Lite", 800, 600, center = c(-111.8887, 40.7556), zoom = 12.4,
             pixel_ratio = 2)

render_png(m, path = "slc.png")   # 1600 x 1200, drawn natively at zoom 12.4
render_svg(m, path = "slc.svg")   # true vector; labels stay editable text
r <- render_raster(m)             # a terra SpatRaster in EPSG:3857


import basemapper

m = basemapper.basemap("UGRC.Lite", 800, 600, center=(-111.8887, 40.7556),
                       zoom=12.4, pixel_ratio=2)

m.render_png(path="slc.png")
m.render_svg(path="slc.svg")
a = m.render_array()              # (1200, 1600, 4) uint8 array



"UGRC.Lite" is a name from basemapper’s catalogue, which uses the same provider names as leaflet ("OpenFreeMap.Positron", "CartoDB.Voyager", "Esri.WorldImagery" and so on). Some names stand for several services stacked together: UGRC Lite is really three styles, a hillshade, a base map and a labels layer, and basemapper draws them as one map. Anything that is not in the catalogue can be passed directly: a style URL, a tile URL template, a TileJSON, a PMTiles archive, an ArcGIS service, or a WMS or WMTS endpoint.

In a plot
Most of the time I don’t want a picture of a basemap, I want a basemap under my data. Each plotting library gets a layer that works out the extent, projection and pixel size from the plot itself:

RPython


library(ggplot2)
library(sf)
library(basemapper)

capitol <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-111.888, 40.777)), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(26912) |>
  st_buffer(800)

p <- ggplot(capitol) +
  geom_basemap("UGRC.Lite") +
  geom_sf(fill = NA, colour = "navy", linewidth = 1)

ggsave("capitol.png", p, width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 300)


import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from shapely.geometry import Point
from basemapper import add_basemap

capitol = gpd.GeoSeries([Point(-111.888, 40.777)], crs=4326).to_crs(26912).buffer(800)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
capitol.plot(ax=ax, facecolor="none", edgecolor="navy", linewidth=2)
add_basemap(ax, "UGRC.Lite", crs=capitol.crs)

fig.savefig("capitol.png", dpi=300)






The R example’s output: an 800 m buffer around the Utah State Capitol over UGRC Lite, saved with ggsave(dpi = 300).


The important detail is when the basemap is drawn. geom_basemap() renders when the plot is drawn on a device, at that device’s size and resolution, so ggsave(dpi = 300) gets a basemap drawn at 300 dpi rather than a screen image stretched to fit. The matplotlib layer does the same at savefig() time. tmap gets tm_basemap(), and plotnine gets its own geom_basemap(). The providers’ attribution goes in the corner by default, and get_attribution() returns it as text for a caption.


Only the parts you want
Because the map is drawn from a style, basemapper can leave things out. labels = FALSE drops the labels, labels = "only" keeps just the labels on a transparent background, and features keeps or drops whole parts of the map (water, parks, roads, buildings, terrain, points of interest and a few more). Those names work across the common vector tile schemas (OpenMapTiles, Protomaps, Shortbread) and Esri’s layer names, so you don’t need to learn each style’s layer ids. When you do want that control, layers takes layer ids with * wildcards, and list_layers() previews what a render will draw.
# Terrain, water, parks and roads only, no labels
basemap("UGRC.Lite", labels = FALSE,
        features = c("terrain", "water", "parks", "roads"), ...)

# Satellite imagery under UGRC Lite's labels
basemap(c("Esri.WorldImagery", basemap_provider("UGRC.Lite", labels = "only")), ...)






UGRC Lite with only terrain, water, parks and roads, and no labels.







Esri World Imagery with UGRC Lite’s labels drawn on top.





The left panel is the kind of quiet background I want under a choropleth. The right one builds a hybrid map out of two providers that were never designed to go together.

title: basemapper: Vector Basemaps for R and Python, Rendered Headlessly
text:
4 Under the hood
basemapper is three packages around one Rust crate. The crate, basemapper-core, does all the work: it reads the style, chooses tiles, fetches them (with a disk cache, so re-running a report doesn’t download everything again), and renders. The R package binds it with extendr, the Python package with PyO3 and maturin. Both are thin: they turn a plot or a bounding box into a request and hand the pixels back. That is also why the R, Python and Rust APIs have the same functions, argument names and defaults; there is only one implementation to describe.
Raster sources are the easy half: fetch the tiles that cover the view, then composite them. Vector styles are where all the time went.

title: basemapper: Vector Basemaps for R and Python, Rendered Headlessly
text:
5 The hard parts

First attempt: borrow a GPU renderer
The first working version, in June, rendered vector tiles with maplibre-rs, an experimental Rust port of MapLibre that draws with wgpu. It produced maps, but it was the wrong tool for this job:

It needed a GPU, or a software stand-in for one, and the platform graphics libraries to go with it. That is a lot to ask of an R package installed on a locked-down office laptop or a CI runner.
It rendered tile by tile, so roads and labels broke at tile edges. I worked around the seams by drawing the whole tile grid in one pass, but that was a fix on top of a fix.
It built from my own fork, and needed protoc (the Protocol Buffers compiler) installed just to compile.
Its output was similar to MapLibre’s. It was not MapLibre’s.

That last point mattered most. A basemap style is designed by someone looking at it in MapLibre. If my renderer interprets a line width, a halo or a label collision a little differently, the map stops looking like what its designer intended.


Second attempt: port MapLibre to the CPU
So in November I replaced it with a renderer of basemapper’s own: a software port of MapLibre GL JS’s rendering pipeline. Not a renderer inspired by MapLibre, but its behaviour ported from the TypeScript source and its shaders, one module at a time: vector tile decoding, the style expression language, line tessellation, fills, circles, and, the biggest piece, the symbol pipeline that shapes, places and collides labels.
The rule was to reproduce what MapLibre does on the GPU, including the parts that look like accidents:

Colours are blended premultiplied, in float32, and stored to 8 bits with round-half-to-even, as the GPU does. (0.3 × 255 is exactly 76.5 in float32, and it stores as 76, not 77.)
Each tile’s geometry is clipped to the tile square, as MapLibre’s stencil test does, so features repeated in neighbouring tiles’ buffers are never drawn twice.
Primitives are sampled at pixel centres with the GPU’s top-left rule, and edges get their softness from MapLibre’s own shader formulas rather than from a generic antialiasing pass.
Labels follow MapLibre’s line breaking, glyph rounding, anchor choice and collision grid, in MapLibre’s order. Right-to-left scripts are shaped as MapLibre’s RTL plugin shapes them, and CJK text can run vertically.

My favourite bug from this stretch: point-of-interest icons that were sometimes one pixel off. Their edges sat 0.0175 px from a pixel centre. The reference images come from MapLibre running on SwiftShader, a software GPU that snaps vertex positions to a 1/16 px grid before deciding which pixels a triangle covers. On that grid the edge landed on the other side of the pixel centre. Snapping vertices the same way fixed the icons, and across the whole test suite it cut the number of mismatched pixels by a fifth and the mean colour difference by two thirds.
Dropping the GPU engine also shrank the project: the dependency tree went from 468 crates to 243, and building it now needs nothing but a Rust toolchain. No GPU, no protoc, no system libraries, no fork.


Measuring instead of eyeballing
None of that is possible without a way to tell “the same” from “close”. basemapper’s test suite has well over a hundred golden-image cases. Each one is a fixture with a style and exactly the tiles, fonts and icons one view needs, plus a reference image of that view rendered by MapLibre GL JS itself in headless Chromium. The test renders the same fixture with basemapper and counts pixels that differ by more than 24/255 in any channel.
The cases cover CARTO’s Positron, Dark Matter and Voyager and the full UGRC Lite stack at every MapLibre zoom from 1 to 22 over Salt Lake City, plus fractional zooms, 2× pixel ratio, multi-source styles from OpenFreeMap and Versatiles, raster tiles, layer filtering and SVG output. Every case has a limit on how far it may differ, and the limits only ever go down. Most cases now differ from MapLibre in well under a tenth of a percent of pixels. When something regressed, a small viewer with side-by-side, swipe, blink and diff modes showed exactly where.
This changed how the work felt. Instead of “does this look right?” the question was always “why is this pixel different?”, and that question has an answer you can find in MapLibre’s source.


SVG that is actually vector
For print and for editing in Illustrator or Inkscape, a PNG is not enough, so basemapper also writes the same view as SVG: real paths for fills and lines, and labels as editable <text>, each glyph placed where MapLibre placed it, with the style’s fonts embedded. Matching MapLibre here meant translating its conventions into SVG’s: dash lengths in MapLibre’s units, round caps that SVG would otherwise extend past the dash, and lines thinner than a pixel stroked at the width that gives the same visual weight. The golden tests rasterise each SVG and score it against the same MapLibre reference; the full UGRC stack at zoom 12.4 comes out 0.23% of pixels off.


Windows, R and Rust
The least glamorous part was getting install.packages-style installs to work on Windows. R on Windows is built with the GNU toolchain, so the Rust code has to be too (the MSVC toolchain cannot import R.dll’s exported global variables). RTools45’s GCC 14 dropped a library that Rust’s GNU target still links against, so the package build now creates an empty stand-in for it. And for a while library(basemapper) crashed outright with an access violation, until the import library marked R’s handful of exported global variables as data rather than functions. None of this is visible to users now, which is the point.

title: basemapper: Vector Basemaps for R and Python, Rendered Headlessly
text:
6 Building it with Claude
I built basemapper with Claude as a pair programmer, and it is fair to say the project would not exist otherwise: porting a large part of a mature graphics library is far more code than I could write on evenings and weekends. Claude was very good at the mechanical bulk of that work, reading MapLibre’s TypeScript and shaders and porting them faithfully, and at writing the tests and tooling around them.
What made it work was the golden-image suite. An AI assistant will happily tell you a renderer looks right. A test that counts mismatched pixels against MapLibre does not care how confident anyone sounds, and a ratchet that never loosens means progress sticks. My job was mostly deciding what “correct” meant, choosing what to measure next, and reading diffs.

title: basemapper: Vector Basemaps for R and Python, Rendered Headlessly
section: 7 Back to the Opportunity Zones maps
text:
7 Back to the Opportunity Zones maps
The info sheets were basemapper’s first production use, and the reason it exists. Each tract map in the pipeline now draws UGRC Lite through geom_basemap(), rendered at the report’s 200 dpi when ggsave() runs, at the same zoom as the old raster maps. Here is the same tract map before and after the switch, as committed to the repository; the overlay layers are identical, and only the basemap changed.




Before: raster basemap tiles



After: UGRC Lite vector, rendered by basemapper



Peak names, contour lines and the Heritage State Park label are now readable, and the hillshade has the detail the raster tiles smeared away. More about that project is on its project page.

title: basemapper: Vector Basemaps for R and Python, Rendered Headlessly
text:
8 What it doesn’t do (yet)
basemapper renders basemaps. Style features meant for data visualisation or interactive 3D, such as heatmap layers, point clustering and 3D terrain, are skipped with a warning (and line gradients draw in a single colour); draw that kind of data with your plotting library on top instead. Output is always Web Mercator, which geom_basemap() and friends reproject for you.
It is also new: for now it installs from GitHub and compiles the Rust core, so you need a Rust toolchain (and, on Windows, RTools45 and the x86_64-pc-windows-gnu target):
pak::pak("ar-puuk/basemapper/r-basemapper")
pip install "basemapper @ git+https://github.com/ar-puuk/basemapper#subdirectory=py-basemapper"
CRAN, R-universe, PyPI and conda packages will follow after a longer testing period. Until then, the documentation has guides for R, Python and Rust, and every map in them is drawn by the code shown next to it. If you try it and a style renders differently from MapLibre, please open an issue: with the golden-image setup, a mismatch is a test case waiting to be written.

title: basemapper: Vector Basemaps for R and Python, Rendered Headlessly
text:
9 Cite it
basemapper is archived on Zenodo with the DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24457061, which always points to the latest release. The code is on GitHub under the MIT license.

title: Drut: Linting and Formatting for Cube Voyager Scripts
text:
WarningUnder active development



Drut is a work in progress. If you hit a bug, please open an issue.
Travel demand models are programs. In much of the U.S., the language they are written in is Cube Voyager’s control-statement script (.s and .block files), and the tooling for it is thin: usually no syntax highlighting, no error checking until the model actually runs, and no consistent formatting across a team. A missing ENDIF can cost you a full model run to find.
Drut is my attempt to give those scripts the tooling that every mainstream language takes for granted: a parser that understands the block structure, diagnostics as you type, a formatter you can trust with model code, and editor support in VS Code and anything else that speaks the Language Server Protocol. This post covers what it does and the parts that were harder than they looked.

title: Drut: Linting and Formatting for Cube Voyager Scripts
text:
1 Why Voyager scripts need tooling
A Voyager script is a sequence of RUN PGM=... steps, each with its own block of statements: IF/ENDIF, LOOP/ENDLOOP, PROCESS PHASE=... sections, matrix loops (JLOOP) and link loops. A regional model can have well over a hundred of these files. Without an editor that understands them, the structure lives only in the author’s indentation.
When a block is left open, you find out when the model run reaches it. What I wanted was the experience I have in R or Python: the editor underlines the mistake while I type it, and a formatter keeps the shape of the code honest.

title: Drut: Linting and Formatting for Cube Voyager Scripts
text:
2 A quick tour

In the editor
Install Drut for Cube Voyager from the VS Code Marketplace (or from Open VSX in Cursor, VSCodium and others), open a .s file, and you get:

Syntax highlighting from a static TextMate grammar, so it works even before the language server starts. Control words, function calls, keyword=value pairs, data references (MI, MW, DBA, ZONES) and user variables are each independently recolorable.
Structural diagnostics: unmatched IF/LOOP/RUN/PROCESS blocks, unclosed comments, a BREAK with no enclosing block, and similar real mistakes, flagged as you type.
Hints about @token@ substitutions: a token that is used but never defined, or assigned but never used.
Formatting on save, on paste or on demand.
Hover, autocomplete and “did you mean” spell-check for control words and keyword names, plus code folding for every block kind.

You don’t have to install the language server separately. On first activation the extension looks for drut on your PATH, then in its own storage, and otherwise downloads the right binary for your platform from the latest GitHub release and checks its SHA-256. If no prebuilt binary exists for your platform, it falls back to highlighting only.


On the command line
The same engine is a CLI for scripts and CI:
cargo install drut-cli

drut check model/scripts            # structural diagnostics; --format sarif for CI tools
drut format model/scripts --diff    # show what the formatter would change
drut format model/scripts --write   # apply it


Shared configuration
Formatting is opt-in, one setting at a time. Every option defaults to preserve, and a team writes down its own preferences in a drut.toml at the project root, which the CLI, the editor and the MCP server all read:
[format]
casing_control_words = "upper"   # RUN, ENDRUN, IF, ENDIF ...
indent_width = 4
operator_spacing = "fixed"       # one space each side of =
line_wrap = "auto"               # wrap long keyword=value lists
A formatter that rewrites model code also has to be easy to hold back, so a range can be excluded with markers. Everything between them is left exactly as written:
; FMT: OFF
  ... a hand-aligned section you want to keep as is ...
; FMT: ON

title: Drut: Linting and Formatting for Cube Voyager Scripts
text:
3 Three ways in, one engine







Surface
For




drut CLI
scripting and CI checks


VS Code / Open VSX extension
day-to-day editing (it is a Language Server Protocol server, so any LSP-capable editor can use it)


Model Context Protocol server
AI coding assistants



All three are built on one shared Rust engine, so the editor, the CI check and the assistant always agree on what is valid. The core crate, voyager-core, holds every grammar and parsing rule and has no runtime dependencies beyond Rust’s standard library. Its public contract is a tokenizer and a parser that work on text in memory and never panic: malformed input comes back as diagnostics, not crashes. The CLI, the language server (drut-lsp), the MCP server (drut-mcp) and the configuration loader (drut-config) are thin adapters around it. This rule is written into the project’s design principles, because the alternative, a second copy of the grammar inside the editor extension, would sooner or later disagree with the first.
The MCP server exposes four read-only tools: diagnose, format, query_structure (which block encloses a given line, and where it ends) and lookup_keyword. The point is that an assistant asked to edit a model script can check its work against the real parser instead of guessing from text.

title: Drut: Linting and Formatting for Cube Voyager Scripts
text:
4 The hard parts

A language without a public grammar
There is no published formal grammar for Voyager scripts. Drut’s grammar was written up rule by rule as functional requirements, and checked against two things: the vendor’s documentation and a corpus of real scripts. The project’s rules forbid copying the vendor’s wording anywhere: keyword lists, diagnostic messages and hover text are all in Drut’s own words.
Some of what the documentation describes is odd. RUN and PROCESS blocks can close implicitly, when the next block of the same family opens (and a RUN can be closed by a shell-escape line), as well as with an explicit ENDRUN or ENDPROCESS. The parser is a recursive-descent block matcher that handles these cases, along with a single-line short IF form and a disabled !RUN variant. Interestingly, a full scan of the real corpus found no implicit closes at all; the parser supports them because the documentation says they are valid.


The real corpus as the test oracle
Correctness is measured against real code. Nine representative files (about 5,200 lines) from a production regional travel demand model, checked first for paths, credentials and other sensitive content, are committed as fixtures, and the model’s full set of 161 scripts was used for validation passes: 161 of 161 parsed with zero diagnostics and zero panics.
The guiding rule is that a false alarm on working code is worse than a missed bug. An unflagged mistake is forgivable; a red squiggle on a script that runs fine teaches people to ignore the tool. That is why only a handful of block kinds produce diagnostics when left open, and why several of the newer checks are Hint-level, editor-only messages.
Running against real files found real bugs early:

An encoding surprise. One real script contained a single Windows-1252 byte that isn’t valid UTF-8, so the parser couldn’t even load it. The fix decodes UTF-8 first and falls back to Windows-1252 only for the bytes that fail, leaving valid UTF-8 elsewhere in the file untouched. Only a byte with no Windows-1252 meaning at all becomes a diagnostic.
Subscripted assignments. MW[1] = ... (over 6,000 occurrences in one file alone) was being classified as a control statement instead of an assignment. No diagnostic fired either way, so the “zero diagnostics” test couldn’t see it, but a formatter consuming that classification could have mangled real scripts. A dedicated test now checks statement kinds directly.
Quotes. A word = value shape inside a quoted string (scripts that PRINT other scripts do this) was read as a second keyword pair.

The corpus also supplies data. The autocomplete list of keyword=value names was built from a census of the real scripts (keywords appearing in at least three files), not copied from documentation, and the default indentation width of 4 matches what the corpus uses: 82.4% of 30,652 nested-line indents.
Sometimes the data settled a question by showing there was no right answer. I expected the formatter to offer a “canonical” keyword casing. But for IF, ELSE, LOOP and their closers, the real scripts are 81 to 95% lowercase while the vendor’s documentation is 71 to 94% uppercase. Any built-in house style would either rewrite most real code or contradict the manual. So Drut ships no preset: every casing option defaults to preserve, and casing is split into four independent categories (control words, keyword names, data references, function names) that each project sets for itself in drut.toml.


A formatter you can trust with model code
The formatter has hard rules: it is idempotent (format(format(x)) == format(x)), it never reorders statements, never changes which lines are continuations, and never alters program meaning. It changes whitespace and, if you ask, keyword casing. Every formatter change is checked against golden files from the fixture corpus.
The subtlest bug was about broken code. If a PROCESS block was left unclosed, the parser’s best guess made the following RUN block a child of it, and the formatter indented it accordingly. When the author then added the missing ENDPROCESS, the RUN block became top-level again, but its formatter-written indentation stayed, because Drut deliberately never rewrites top-level indentation by default. (Only 20.4% of real top-level statements sit at column 0, so forcing them there would touch nearly every file.) The existing idempotency tests all passed, because formatting the broken output again was a no-op. The fix was to stop guessing: the children of a block that has a diagnostic keep their original indentation, and a new set of tests formats, edits, and formats again.
Automatic line wrapping went in later and needed a carve-out in the formatter’s own rules, since inserting a line break into a long keyword=value list does change which lines are continuations. It is allowed only using the language’s own continuation syntax, and it is off by default.

title: Drut: Linting and Formatting for Cube Voyager Scripts
text:
5 How it was built
Drut was developed with GitHub’s spec-kit workflow: each feature got a written specification, a plan, a task list and a pre-implementation review before any code, and the commit history reads that way, from the first parser crate in August to the CLI, the language server and extension, the MCP server and the configuration file. The editor extension’s structure (language IDs, bracket and comment configuration, scope naming) follows Bill Hereth’s earlier Cube Voyager VS Code extension, with his permission and credit, rewritten in Drut’s own code.

title: Drut: Linting and Formatting for Cube Voyager Scripts
text:
6 What’s next
Drut checks structure today, not meaning. Two larger phases are on the roadmap as stretch goals: validating keywords against the specific program a RUN block calls, and semantic checks that look across all the files in a model rather than one script at a time. Closer in, the roadmap logs a possible fifth casing category for matrix assignment targets (MW[1] = ...), which real authors write differently from other data references, and the Marketplace listing still needs real screenshots of the extension at work.
The extension resolves a working drut language server automatically on first activation:

VS Code: Drut for Cube Voyager on the Marketplace.
Cursor, VSCodium and others: the same extension on Open VSX.
CLI only: cargo install drut-cli, or build from source with cargo build --release -p drut-cli and put the binary on your PATH.

title: Drut: Linting and Formatting for Cube Voyager Scripts
text:
7 Documentation
The full user guide covers install, getting started, the CLI, editor and MCP references, formatter behavior and a field-by-field drut.toml reference.


  
    Drut User Guide
    Fullscreen

title: A Zero-Cost Freight Flow Explorer for Utah
text:
The Freight Analysis Framework (FAF) is the go-to public source for how much freight moves between U.S. regions, by commodity and mode. It is also awkward to use: several releases with different zone systems, benchmark years and dollar bases, plus a forecast that skips 2025 to 2029. Answering “what moves in and out of Utah?” usually means downloading gigabytes and wrangling them yourself.
So I built an explorer that does the wrangling once and ships the result as a static site. Utah is the configured state; adding another is a one-file change. It is the second project in the same pattern as my Education Explorer, and it reused that project’s conventions: a config file per state, a schema-drift guard, deterministic Parquet, and DuckDB running in the browser.

title: A Zero-Cost Freight Flow Explorer for Utah
text:
1 Try it
The live app is embedded below. Click a mode, commodity, partner state or year and every chart and the map follow.


  
    FAF Freight Explorer
    Fullscreen
  
  
    
  



 Open app  Methodology  GitHub  DOI

title: A Zero-Cost Freight Flow Explorer for Utah
text:
2 Why FAF is awkward
FAF is published by the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS) and the Federal Highway Administration, with Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The files are national CSVs: the FAF5.7.1 regional file alone is 1.18 GB, and the first pipeline run downloads about 2.5 GB. Then the differences between releases start:

Two generations, two zone systems. FAF5.7.1 has 132 zones and a 2017 benchmark; FAF6.0 has 134 zones and a 2022 benchmark. Six zone IDs are shared by both but have different names.
Different measures. FAF5 has tons, value and ton-miles, and current-dollar value only for 2018 to 2024. FAF6.0 has tons and value for a single year, 2022, and no ton-miles at all.
Gaps. FAF5 has annual years to 2024 and then jumps to forecasts for 2030, 2035 and so on to 2050. Nothing exists for 2025 to 2029.
Wide files with explicit zeros. Each year is a column, and a row exists if any year is positive, so more than a third of the rows in FAF5 are zero for a given year.

The two generations do not agree, either. For Utah in 2022, FAF5.7.1 puts domestic freight touching the state at 217,325 thousand tons and FAF6.0 at 329,980, about 52% more. National domestic tons are nearly equal in the two releases, so this is not a general rescale. Whatever the cause, it means the two can never share an axis, and that became one of the app’s firm rules.

title: A Zero-Cost Freight Flow Explorer for Utah
text:
3 A quick tour

Origin-destination flows in tons, value and ton-miles for every record that touches the state, by commodity, mode and year. FAF5.7.1 (2017 to 2050) and FAF6.0 (2022) are kept apart, never combined on one axis.
Forecast scenarios: the mid-range forecast plus FAF5’s published High and Low scenarios, with forecast and preliminary years marked and the unpublished 2025 to 2029 shown as a gap.
A timeline that shows which years exist (benchmark, final, preliminary, forecast), hatches the missing years, and plays through published years only.
Linked charts instead of tables: direction, mode and commodity (treemap), the largest partner states, trends with the scenario band, a commodity-by-year heat map, a two-year comparison, and a two-model comparison that puts FAF5 and FAF6 side by side with their own scales. Clicking any element filters everything else.
The FAF5 truck network with modeled link volumes, a FAF5-reprocessed state history (1997, 2002, 2007 and 2012), and clearly labeled experimental county-level estimates for 2022.
Search and jump with Ctrl K, keyboard shortcuts, a table with CSV export, and light, dark and color-blind-safe palettes. The whole view lives in the URL, so a link reproduces it.







ImportantData and caveats only



The app does not rank places, score performance, or present modeled values as measured counts. FAF flows are modeled estimates, and the app says so wherever they appear.


The interface follows a short list of rules written down in the repository’s design notes. Three of them do most of the work: not published is never zero (a missing measure shows “n/a” and why, and a control with no data stays visible but disabled with a reason), a gap is data (2025 to 2029 is hatched, never interpolated), and models are never merged.

title: A Zero-Cost Freight Flow Explorer for Utah
text:
4 How it works
Nothing runs on a server. A local pipeline turns the raw federal files into Parquet, GeoJSON and PMTiles, GitHub Pages serves them, and the browser queries them with DuckDB-WASM.






flowchart LR
  A["BTS / FHWA / ORNL / Census files"] --> B["pipeline/<br>Python + DuckDB"]
  B -->|"validate"| C["Deterministic Parquet,<br>GeoJSON, PMTiles"]
  C --> D["GitHub Pages<br>docs/"]
  D --> E["Browser<br>DuckDB-WASM + MapLibre"]






The pipeline is a small command-line tool run with uv:
cd pipeline
1uv run python -m faf_pipeline update --state utah
2uv run python -m faf_pipeline fetch --state utah --check-only
3uv run python -m faf_pipeline validate --state utah
4uv run pytest

1

Fetch, build, zones, county estimates, network and validation in one go. It prints a changelog of what changed.

2

Report changed files and new FAF releases without downloading anything.

3

Run the checks that must pass before processed data is committed.

4

Unit tests run on tiny fixture files for a fictional state.


Three design choices made the rest easy:

Deterministic output. Re-running update on unchanged inputs produces byte-identical files, so a second run leaves no git diff and every data change is reviewable.
A schema guard. Every downloaded file’s columns are checked against a column map, so a new release that renames or drops a column fails loudly instead of quietly corrupting results. A year that appears in a file but has not been classified as base, final, preliminary or forecast also stops the build.
No state literals in the code. Utah appears only in config/states/utah.yml; validation fails if a state name, abbreviation or zone id shows up as a literal elsewhere.

title: A Zero-Cost Freight Flow Explorer for Utah
text:
5 The interesting problems

GitHub Pages and range requests
Education Explorer relies on DuckDB-WASM reading only the byte ranges of a Parquet file that a query needs. I expected the same here, and the first spike showed it does not happen. On GitHub Pages, DuckDB-WASM fetched each Parquet file with one plain request, and the response came back gzip-compressed. Pages compresses on the fly, and a ranged request that also accepts gzip gets a slice of the compressed stream, with a Content-Range measured in compressed bytes. I did not pin down why the earlier project’s positive result did not reproduce, so the safe conclusion was not to rely on Parquet range reads on Pages at all. PMTiles range requests, made by the browser for the network layer, worked correctly.
Utah’s data is small, so the fix was to design for whole-file reads:

Flows are partitioned into one small file per version, scenario and year (roughly 0.3 to 0.7 MB each).
The first view draws from a 60-flow headline JSON file while DuckDB-WASM starts up, then the real query replaces it. Measured on the live site, the first arcs appear in about half a second.
The roughly 11 MB of all-years data for FAF5.7.1 loads only when a Trends or Compare view needs it, and the timeline’s sparkline reads a small precomputed year_totals.json instead.



Where should an arc start?
A flow map needs one point per zone. The obvious choice, a point inside the zone polygon, put Utah’s Salt Lake zone in the Tooele County desert, west of the city, and every arc started there. The fix uses the Census 2020 county centers of population: each zone’s anchor is the population-weighted mean of the county centers inside it, falling back to the most populous county center, and then to a point on the polygon. The method used is stored for every zone. The Salt Lake zone now anchors in the Salt Lake Valley.


Checking FAF against itself
FAF publishes the same flows at more than one level, and that makes good tests. The state-level file turned out to be exactly the regional file aggregated to states, with zero mismatched rows for both FAF5.7.1 and FAF6.0, so validation reconciles the two for every year and scenario at a tolerance of one millionth. The High/Low scenario files repeat the mid-range columns, and the build checks that they equal the mid-range files already written.
The experimental county product was harder. It is tons only, uses five commodity groups instead of 42, and has a mode code, 11, that is not in FAF’s list. BTS pages refuse scripted requests, so I found the technical report through a Wayback Machine snapshot; it defines 11 as truck and air combined. With that, the state-touching rows of the county tables sum to exactly FAF5.7.1’s 2022 domestic tons for Utah, mode by mode, and validation fails if any mode drifts more than 1% apart. Import and export totals still differ slightly, for reasons I have not established, and the methodology page says so.


A truck network without tippecanoe
The FAF5 network has 487,394 links. The pipeline clips it to Utah plus a 25 km buffer (computed in a local projection centred on the state, so it would also work for Alaska or Hawaii) and writes PMTiles directly with DuckDB’s spatial extension, about 2.4 MB, with no tippecanoe or GDAL command-line tools. In the browser, link volumes from a Parquet file are joined to the tiles with MapLibre feature-state. One surprise: the busiest truck link near Utah in 2017 was a centroid connector, a virtual link that connects a zone to the network. Connectors stay in the data but are hidden on the map by default.


When the basemap does not load
Testing with the basemap host blocked showed the app silently stopped before starting its query engine, because map operations ran before any style existed. Now, if the style fails or takes longer than ten seconds, the map switches to a plain background and flows, zones and the network keep working. Two details took some finding: the deck.gl overlay must receive its first layers before the style loads (holding them back stalls the map), and MapLibre’s error event also fires for a single failed tile or glyph, so only a style that never loads triggers the fallback.
A related lesson: building the map and the methodology page in one multi-page Vite build changed the chunk layout enough that the MapLibre and deck.gl WebGL contexts were lost at load. The two pages are now built separately.


A second state
To test the “one config file” claim, I ran the same code once for Colorado in a scratch copy. It needed one fix: the literal check flagged Colorado’s FIPS code 08 because 08 is also a commodity code, so FIPS codes are now checked only in code files. The county estimates again matched FAF5.7.1’s 2022 domestic tons by mode exactly. Utah remains the only supported state.

text:
6 Stack



Layer
Tools




Pipeline
Python, DuckDB, uv, pytest


App
Vite, Svelte 5, TypeScript

MapLibre, deck.gl, flowmap.gl, PMTiles


Queries

Observable Plot



Basemaps come from OpenFreeMap, and a content-security policy restricts the page to its own files and OpenFreeMap. Fonts are bundled for the same reason.

title: A Zero-Cost Freight Flow Explorer for Utah
text:
7 How it was built
As with Education Explorer, I wrote the plan as a HANDOFF.md (locked decisions, data landscape, phased plan) and built the project with Claude Code. Every URL, column name and unit in the plan was marked to be verified against the real files, and the first phase was spikes only. The plan was wrong in a dozen places, from FAF6’s missing ton-miles to the range-request behaviour above, and the corrections are recorded in docs/SPIKES.md and docs/DECISIONS.md. A full interface redesign followed the first complete version, rebuilding the presentation around the map, linked charts and the timeline while leaving the data and pipeline untouched.

title: A Zero-Cost Freight Flow Explorer for Utah
text:
8 Limits and what’s next

FAF6.0 has a single year and no ton-miles; FAF5 has no 2025 to 2029; High and Low have tons and value only. When BTS adds FAF6 annual years or ton-miles, the schema already maps those columns and the app discovers them from the data.
The network flows are a FAF5.3-era model assignment, not traffic counts and not updated to FAF5.7.1 or FAF6.
The FAF6 constant-dollar year (2022) is taken from the release notes and was not independently verified. The eight foreign regions are drawn at schematic positions.
Testing so far is headless Chromium with automated accessibility checks. Firefox, Safari, a real GPU, real phones and a screen reader have not been tried.

The methodology page lists every source file, release and caveat. The code is on GitHub under the MIT license; issues and PRs are welcome. Freight Explorer is archived on Zenodo with the DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23789900.

3 Data Acquisition and Loading

Population Hexagon Data
The analysis utilizes high-resolution population data from Kontur, provided in H3 hexagonal grid format at 400-meter resolution. This dataset offers superior granularity compared to traditional administrative boundary-based population estimates.


H3 is a hierarchical hexagonal grid. Hexagons are used because every neighbour is the same distance from the centre, which makes density maps smoother than square cells.

4 Data Processing and Visualization Setup

Initial Data Exploration
A quick map (Figure 2) confirms the hexagons line up with the national boundary before any 3D work starts.

ggplot2::ggplot(nep_hex) +
  ggplot2::geom_sf(ggplot2::aes(fill = population), color = "gray66", linewidth = 0) +
  ggplot2::geom_sf(data = nepal_boundary, fill = NA, color = "black",
          linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal() +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Nepal Population Distribution",
       fill = "Population")







Figure 2: Population in each 400 m hexagon, with the national boundary dashed.







Raster Conversion and Matrix Preparation
The conversion from vector hexagon data to raster format is essential for rayshader’s 3D rendering capabilities. This process involves calculating optimal dimensions while preserving the geographic aspect ratio.

bbox <- sf::st_bbox(nepal_boundary)

1bottom_left <- sf::st_point(c(bbox[["xmin"]], bbox[["ymin"]])) |>
  sf::st_sfc(crs = project_crs)
bottom_right <- sf::st_point(c(bbox[["xmax"]], bbox[["ymin"]])) |>
  sf::st_sfc(crs = project_crs)
top_left <- sf::st_point(c(bbox[["xmin"]], bbox[["ymax"]])) |>
  sf::st_sfc(crs = project_crs)

2width <- sf::st_distance(bottom_left, bottom_right)
height <- sf::st_distance(bottom_left, top_left)

3if(width > height) {
  w_ratio <- 1
  h_ratio <- height / width
} else {
  h_ratio <- 1
  w_ratio <- width / height
}

4size <- 1000 * 2.5

5pop_raster <- stars::st_rasterize(nep_hex,
                          nx = floor(size * w_ratio),
                          ny = floor(size * h_ratio))

6pop_matrix <- matrix(pop_raster$population,
                    nrow = floor(size * w_ratio),
                    ncol = floor(size * h_ratio))


1

Three corners of the bounding box are enough to measure its width and height.

2

Distances come out in metres, because the CRS is projected.

3

Scale the longer side to 1 and the shorter side in proportion, so the map keeps its shape.

4

The longer side of the raster is 2,500 cells, a balance between detail and render time.

5

Burn the hexagons into a grid of cells, each holding that area’s population.

6

Rayshader works on a plain matrix of heights, so the population grid becomes the heightmap.

title: 3D Population Density Mapping of Nepal
text:
8 Technical Methodology

Spatial Data Processing Pipeline

Data Transformation: Vector hexagon data converted to standardized coordinate reference system (Nepal Nagarkot TM - ESRI:102306)
Rasterization: Optimal grid resolution calculated to balance detail with computational efficiency (Section 4.2)
Matrix Conversion: Raster data transformed into height matrix for 3D rendering
Texture Mapping: Population values mapped to color gradients using perceptually uniform color spaces



Rendering Specifications

Resolution: 1980×1080 pixels for high-definition output
Sampling: 300 samples for anti-aliasing and smooth gradients
Lighting: Dual-source lighting system (directional + ambient)
Z-Scale: Optimized vertical exaggeration (250/2.5) for clear population peaks

9 Results and Applications
This methodology produces publication-quality 3D population density visualizations suitable for:

Urban Planning: Identifying population clusters and growth patterns
Infrastructure Development: Targeting high-density areas for transportation networks
Emergency Response: Understanding population distribution for resource allocation
Academic Research: Visual communication of demographic data

title: 3D Population Density Mapping of Nepal
text:
10 Conclusion
This workflow demonstrates the power of combining modern R packages for geospatial analysis with advanced 3D visualization techniques. The resulting maps provide intuitive understanding of Nepal’s population distribution patterns, highlighting the concentration of people in the Terai region and major urban centers while showcasing the relatively sparse population in mountainous areas.
The methodology is transferable to other geographic contexts and can be adapted for various demographic or infrastructure planning applications in transportation and urban development projects.

Want to contribute or suggest improvements? Visit the project repository at: https://github.com/ar-puuk/Population-Density-Maps

title: Overture Maps Data Download
text:
Overture Maps Foundation provides a collaborative, open-source initiative to create the world’s most comprehensive and interoperable geospatial dataset. As transportation planners and data analysts, we often need access to high-quality geospatial data for buildings, transportation networks, places, and administrative boundaries. This post demonstrates how to efficiently download Overture Maps data using both R and Python with DuckDB’s powerful spatial capabilities.

Overture Maps is an open-source mapping initiative that provides global-scale geospatial data across four main themes:


Buildings: Footprints and building parts

Transportation: Road segments and connectors

Places: Points of interest and place data

Admins: Administrative boundaries and localities

Base: Infrastructure, land use, land cover, and water features

The data is stored in cloud-optimized Parquet format on AWS S3, making it ideal for efficient querying and analysis.

Before diving into the code, ensure you have the following dependencies installed:


 R
 Python




# Install required packages
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "sf", "mapview", "DBI", "duckdb", "arrow"))




# Install required packages
pip install duckdb matplotlib geopandas pandas shapely folium pathlib fastparquet





First, we need to load our libraries and configure the environment for spatial data processing.


 R
 Python




# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(mapview)
library(DBI)
library(duckdb)
library(arrow)




import duckdb
import geopandas as gpd
import pandas as pd
import shapely.wkb
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import folium
import os
from pathlib import Path





Overture data is organized by themes, and we need to map specific data types to their corresponding themes for proper S3 path construction.


 R
 Python




# Define the theme map
map_themes <- list(
  "locality" = "admins",
  "locality_area" = "admins",
  "administrative_boundary" = "admins",
  "building" = "buildings",
  "building_part" = "buildings",
  "place" = "places",
  "segment" = "transportation",
  "connector" = "transportation",
  "infrastructure" = "base",
  "land" = "base",
  "land_use" = "base",
  "water" = "base"
