title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
text:
Population demographics are fundamental to transportation planning and urban analysis. Understanding age distributions helps inform infrastructure decisions, transit planning and resource allocation. A population pyramid is the quickest way to see an age distribution, and a map is the quickest way to see where it changes. I wanted both on one screen.
The Population Pyramid Explorer is a Shiny app that does that for every U.S. county. It uses the {mapgl} package’s story map layout: you scroll from a national overview to a state, where a tract-level map of median age sits behind a population pyramid for the county you pick. This post covers what it does, how the story map and the pyramid are built, and ideas for what comes next.

title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
text:
1 A quick tour
The app has two sections, and scrolling moves between them.



The first section: pick a year and a state over a globe view of the United States.


The first section is the overview. You choose a year (2015 to 2023) and a state, over a globe-projected map of the country with state outlines, navigation controls and a small globe minimap in the corner.
Scroll down and the map flies to the chosen state, filters the outlines to it, and fills its census tracts by median age. A county picker and the population pyramid appear in the panel on the left. Hovering over a tract highlights it, and clicking it opens a popup with the county name and the tract’s median age. Scrolling back up returns to the national view.



The second section: a population pyramid for Autauga County, Alabama, in 2023, over a map of Alabama’s census tracts colored by median age.

title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
section: 2 Two Census products in one view
text:
2 Two Census products in one view
The two halves of the screen come from two different Census Bureau products, both requested through tidycensus:

American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the map: median age (B01002_001) for every tract in the state, with geometry.
The Population Estimates Program for the pyramid: county population by sex and five-year age group, from the characteristics product.

The tract layer gives spatial context, and the county estimates give the detail. Both follow the year selector, so the map and the pyramid always describe the same year.

title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
text:
3 Key dependencies and setup
The application uses a small set of R packages for data processing, spatial analysis and visualization:
# Custom function to load packages, installing them first if not already installed
load_pkg <- function(pkg) {
  if (!require(pkg, character.only = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg)
  }
  library(pkg, character.only = TRUE)
}

# Data manipulation and visualization
load_pkg("dplyr")
load_pkg("tidyr")
load_pkg("ggplot2")
load_pkg("scales")

# Spatial data and mapping
load_pkg("sf")
load_pkg("mapgl")
load_pkg("tigris")

# Census data integration
load_pkg("tidycensus")

# UI framework
load_pkg("shiny")
The load_pkg() helper installs any missing package before loading it, so the app runs on a fresh machine with one command. You do need a Census API key, installed once with tidycensus::census_api_key().

title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
text:
4 The story map

User interface design
The UI is a single call to {mapgl}’s story_maplibre(), which places a full-screen map behind a column of scrolling sections:
mapgl::story_maplibre(
  map_id = "map",
  font_family = "Poppins",
  sections = list(
    "intro" = mapgl::story_section(...),
    "state_detail" = mapgl::story_section(...)
  )
)
Each section holds ordinary Shiny inputs and outputs: the year and state dropdowns in intro, and the county picker and pyramid plot in state_detail.


Drawing the map once
The map itself is rendered only once. Every change after that goes through a maplibre_proxy(), which updates layers on the existing map instead of rebuilding it:
mapgl::maplibre(
  mapgl::carto_style("voyager"),
  center = c(-98.5, 39.5),
  zoom = 3,
  scrollZoom = FALSE
) |>
mapgl::set_projection(projection = "globe")
The base map uses Carto’s Voyager style for clean, readable cartography. Turning off scroll zoom matters in a story map: the page scroll is how you move between sections, and the map would otherwise swallow it.
State boundaries are loaded once at startup:
states_sf <- tigris::states(cb = TRUE) |>
  sf::st_transform(crs = 3857) |>
  sf::st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM")
Cartographic boundary files (cb = TRUE) are simplified, so they draw quickly at the national scale. The geometries are projected to Web Mercator and any Z or M dimensions are dropped before they are handed to the map.


Reacting to sections
{mapgl}’s on_section() runs code when a section scrolls into view, and that is where the map changes happen. Entering the overview clears the tract layer and the legend, removes the state filter, and flies back to the whole country:
mapgl::fly_to(
  center = c(-98.5, 39.5),
  zoom = 3,
  bearing = 0,
  pitch = 0,
  duration = 1500
)
Entering the state section adds the tract fill layer and its legend, filters the state outlines to the chosen state, and fits the map to that state’s bounds. The tract colors interpolate between five stops from 20 to 60 years, using ColorBrewer’s spectral palette, from young (orange-red) to old (purple). Tracts without an estimate are drawn in light grey.

title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
text:
5 Building the pyramid

Shaping the data
A population pyramid is a horizontal bar chart with males to the left of zero and females to the right. The Population Estimates data needs a few steps to get there. The request returns several kinds of age groups (five-year bands, broader groups, all ages), so the code keeps only the rows whose label starts with “Age” and drops the “Both sexes” totals. Then:
dplyr::mutate(
  value = ifelse(SEX == "Male", -value, value),
  age_min = ifelse(
    stringr::str_detect(AGEGROUP, "under"), 0,
    as.numeric(stringr::str_extract(AGEGROUP, "\\d+"))
  )
)
Male counts become negative so their bars point left, and the first number in each age label becomes a sort key. The age groups are then turned into a factor in that order, so “5 to 9” comes after “0 to 4” rather than after “45 to 49” as it would alphabetically.


Chart design
The pyramid is a ggplot2 chart rendered with renderPlot():

Two colors: navy for males, dark red for females.
Labels on the bars: each bar shows its count, using the absolute value so male counts do not print as negative numbers. The same trick formats the x-axis.
Minimal grid lines, so the shape of the distribution carries the chart.

The age labels from the Census API are wordy (“Age 0 to 4 years”), so the axis strips the repeated words:
scale_y_discrete(labels = ~ stringr::str_remove_all(.x, "Age\\s|\\syears"))

title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
text:
6 Details that took some fiddling
Two ways of naming a tract. The ACS returns each tract’s name as one string with the tract, county and state in it. The app splits that string into three columns to get the county name for the popup, and the split uses a regular expression that accepts either a comma or a semicolon as the separator, so it handles both forms the Census API returns.
State and county names to FIPS codes. The inputs hold names, but the API calls want FIPS codes. The app converts them with tidycensus’s own validate_state() and validate_county(). Those are internal functions, reached with tidycensus:::, which works but could break if the package changes them.
A fast county picker. The county list comes from tidycensus::fips_codes for the chosen state and is loaded into a selectizeInput() on the server side (server = TRUE), with type-to-search. The first county is selected by default, so the pyramid appears as soon as you scroll down.
Caching. options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE) keeps boundary files on disk between sessions, and shiny::req() holds back every request until the state and county inputs exist.

title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
text:
7 Rough edges
Looking at the code and the screenshots again, there are a few things I would fix:

The caption names the wrong source. The pyramid’s caption reads “Data: US Census Bureau ACS”, but the pyramid data comes from the Population Estimates Program. Only the map uses the ACS.
The axis double counts thousands. The x-axis title says “Population (thousands)”, and the tick labels are also scaled with a “k” suffix, so a tick of “2k” reads as two thousand thousand.
The selected county is not highlighted. A county outline layer is written but commented out, so the map shows the whole state’s tracts without marking the county in the pyramid.
The legend sits under the panel. The median-age legend is placed bottom-left, where the story panel covers most of it.
The chart font is local. The plot asks for Futura Md BT, which is installed on my machine but will fall back to a default font almost anywhere else.
The tract layer is a live download. Every new state or year requests all of that state’s tracts, with geometry, from the Census API while you wait. Preparing those layers ahead of time would make the state section open faster.

title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
text:
7 Ideas for later
Possible extensions include:

Multi-county comparison, with two pyramids side by side
Time series, showing how a county’s pyramid changes over the years
Additional demographic variables (income, education, housing)
Export functionality for the chart and the data
Integration with transportation metrics for planning analysis
Highlighting the selected county on the state map
Pre-built tract layers, so the state view opens without waiting for a live Census download

title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
text:
8 Try it locally
The app is a single app.R. Clone the repository, install the packages, set your Census API key, and run it:
tidycensus::census_api_key("YOUR_KEY_HERE", install = TRUE)
shiny::runApp("app.R")
A free key is available from the Census Bureau. The code is under the MIT license, and suggestions and pull requests are welcome.

title: Mirror: a Robocopy Command Builder
text:
Robocopy is the best file-copying tool built into Windows, and one of the hardest to remember: dozens of switches, several of which can delete files at the destination. Mirror lets you build the command visually instead. It covers every option in robocopy /? (97 settings), explains what each one does, and warns before anything can delete files. It runs entirely in your browser; nothing is uploaded.
Mirror began as a single-page Robocopy GUI in 2025 and was redesigned as part of Conduit, a pair of command builders that share one design system. Its sister app is Fetch, the Wget builder. This post covers why I wanted it, what it does, and how the two apps are built from one source.

title: Mirror: a Robocopy Command Builder
text:
1 Try it


  
    Mirror
    Fullscreen
  
  
    
  



 Open app  GitHub

title: Mirror: a Robocopy Command Builder
text:
2 The problem with Robocopy
Robocopy can do almost anything with files: copy only what changed, keep permissions and timestamps, retry over a flaky network, copy with many threads at once, log everything, and run on a schedule. All of that is switches on one command line, and the switches are terse. /MIR, /PURGE, /MOV and /MOVE look harmless and can each remove files, either from the destination or from the source. A typical backup line ends up looking like this:
robocopy "D:\Projects" "\\server\share\backup" /E /XO /MT:16 /R:3 /W:5 /Z /FFT /NP /LOG:backup.log
If you write one of these a year, you look every switch up again each time, and you hope you did not mix up /MOV and /MOVE. I wanted a form that writes the command for me, says in plain words what each part does, and makes the dangerous parts impossible to miss.

title: Mirror: a Robocopy Command Builder
text:
3 A quick tour

Pick a starting point. Choose a preset (Daily backup, Exact mirror, Archive with permissions, Fast LAN copy, or Move and clean up) or start from scratch.
Fill in the tabs. Locations, What to do, Filters, Preserve, Performance, Automation, Logging and Advanced. Rarely used options stay hidden until you turn on Show advanced.
Watch the command. It updates as you choose, with every flag explained.
Add to queue. Build several jobs, reorder them, then download one .bat or .ps1 script. Stop on first failure is on by default.







CautionSome options delete files



The /MIR (mirror), move and purge options can remove files from the destination. The app shows a clear notice for each of them before anything can be deleted, so read it before you run the script.


Every command gets one of three labels: “No destructive options”, “Review before you run”, or “This can delete files”. Unless the label is the first one, and while Preview only (/L) is off, the warning comes with a Turn on preview only button, so the first run just lists what would happen. Mirror also points out combinations that do not do what you might expect: copy threads cannot be combined with a packet pause, telling Mirror to leave extra files alone means it will not delete them, and adding /PURGE to /MIR changes nothing because mirror already purges.

Other ways in

Find an option. Type a name or a flag, such as retry or /MT, to search every tab at once.
Paste a command. Paste an existing robocopy command and the form fills in. Flags the builder does not recognise are kept under Advanced.
Command palette. Ctrl+K jumps to any option, preset or page, and Ctrl+Enter adds the current command to the queue.
Profiles. Save a full set of options and load it later. Profiles, the queue and the form are remembered in your browser.

title: Mirror: a Robocopy Command Builder
text:
4 How it works

One list of options drives everything
Each Robocopy option is written once, as a small declarative entry: its flag, a label, a one-line explanation, which tab it belongs to, whether it is advanced, and, for the risky ones, a risk level and the warning to show. For example, the “What to do” choice lists Copy, Mirror (/MIR, “Deletes in destination”), Move and Move files only. The form, the colored command, the per-flag explanations, the search, the command palette and the risk label are all generated from that one list, so adding an option in one place makes it show up everywhere.


Reading a command back in
Pasting a command runs the same list in reverse. The parser splits the text into tokens while keeping quoted paths together, joins lines that were continued with ^, and drops a leading robocopy or robocopy.exe. Robocopy’s switches are case-insensitive, so it matches them in upper case, and it understands both bare switches (/E) and switches with values (/MT:16, /LOG:backup.log). Switches that take a list, such as /XD for skipped folders, consume the following words until the next switch. Whatever is left is positional: the first two are the source and destination, and anything after them becomes the file patterns. Anything it does not recognise is not thrown away but kept in the Extra flags field under Advanced, so a pasted command never silently loses part of itself.


Scripts that stop at the right time
Robocopy does not use exit codes the way most programs do. Codes 0 to 7 all mean success (they report whether files were copied, skipped or found extra at the destination), and only 8 and above mean that something failed. A script that treats any non-zero code as an error would stop after every successful copy. So when stop on first failure is on, the .bat export checks if errorlevel 8 goto :failed after each Robocopy job, and the PowerShell export checks $LASTEXITCODE -ge 8. Both exports are written with Windows line endings, and the .ps1 file is saved as UTF-8 with a byte order mark.


Two apps, one source
Mirror and Fetch share one source file, design/shell.html, which contains both tools plus a page documenting the design system. A small Node script, design/build.js, turns it into two self-contained index.html files: it keeps one tool’s definitions, swaps in that app’s name, accent color, defaults and navigation, replaces sample paths with ones under %USERPROFILE%, and adds saving to browser storage. Every replacement checks that its target text exists and the build stops with an error if not, so a change to the shared source cannot quietly produce a half-built app. A jsdom smoke test then loads each built page and clicks through it: tabs, search, the command palette, adding to the queue, downloading both script formats, and saving a profile.
The result has no build step to run and no backend, so it is light and works from GitHub Pages. Icons are from Lucide and the fonts are Bricolage Grotesque, Instrument Sans and JetBrains Mono. The code lives in the source repository.

title: Mirror: a Robocopy Command Builder
text:
5 How it got here
The first version, in June 2025, was a single HTML page generated with Gemini 2.5 Pro and then updated with Claude Sonnet 4. It grouped options into a few sections and could add commands to a batch and download them as one .bat file. In December 2025 I gave it a Fluent-style redesign with Gemini Pro, and the same month built a Wget counterpart in the same style.
In November 2026 I rebuilt both as Conduit, with Claude as a pair programmer. That redesign added the tabs, the risk labels, search, the command palette, paste-to-fill, profiles, PowerShell export and coverage of every option in robocopy /?. The hand-drawn icons were replaced with unmodified Lucide icons, inlined so the app is still one file.

title: Mirror: a Robocopy Command Builder
text:
6 Who it is for

System administrators managing file synchronization
IT professionals setting up backup routines
Anyone copying large directory structures with specific parameters
Learning Robocopy syntax by seeing what each option does


Want to contribute or suggest improvements? Visit the project repository at: https://github.com/ar-puuk/robocopy-gui

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
Most of my day-to-day GIS work happens in R or Python: load a shapefile, write a few spatial queries, make a quick map to sanity-check the result. That is fast when you are already in a scripting environment, and annoying when you just want to look at a file, or hand someone a tool without asking them to install anything.
I wanted something simpler: open a file, write a SQL query, see the answer on a map. No server, no accounts, no desktop GIS. That itch became Spatial Explorer. It started in February as a single-page app inspired by Kyle Walker’s Spatial SQL Explorer, and it has since been rebuilt into a web app and a VS Code extension that share one engine. This post is about what it does now and why it is built the way it is.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
1 Try it
Use Try sample data for US counties, or drop in your own file. Everything runs in your tab.


  
    Spatial Explorer
    Fullscreen
  
  
    
  



 Open app  GitHub

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
2 What it does
The scope is deliberately small: look at a file, query it, style the result, export it.

LookQueryStyleAnalyzeExport and print



Formats: GeoJSON, GeoPackage (several layers), SQLite/SpatiaLite (Cube 7 networks, for example), FlatGeobuf, Shapefile, GeoParquet, Parquet, GML, CSV, PMTiles and Excel. File Geodatabases (experimental) and GTFS transit feeds open too, and a zip opens like the file inside it.
A map and an attribute table kept in sync, any source CRS, and 129 basemaps from 26 providers with real previews, plus a globe view.
One search box for layer values, coordinates and places.
Map tools: measure distances and areas, draw shapes to select or filter rows (or to use as a SQL table called drawn), and turn on terrain with hillshade and elevation. These are scratch geometry only; your data is never edited.



DuckDB spatial SQL runs against the file by its own name, with autocomplete and inline errors. Results replace the map and the table.
1SELECT * FROM us_counties
2SELECT * FROM layer
3SELECT * FROM us_boundaries.counties
4SELECT * FROM ST_Read('data/links.shp')

1

The open file us-counties.parquet is available under its cleaned-up name.

2

…and always as layer, whatever it is called.

3

A multi-layer file such as a GeoPackage exposes its layers as views in a schema named after the file.

4

Other files can be read in the same query: by workspace-relative path in VS Code, or files you have added in the web app.


There are also 24 ready-made snippets that fill in the open layer’s own table and column names, and a word search (ranked, with stemming) beside the plain text search.


Single, categorized, graduated (by a column or a SQL expression), continuous, as-is, bivariate, rule-based, heatmap and cluster styles, with ramps previewed on the map. Under Vary by attribute, several properties can each follow their own column (size, width, outline, shape, pattern, opacity, rotation), so one map can show roads colored by level of service and widened by traffic. Labels, layer opacity and 3D polygon extrusion are there too, and styles are saved as a QGIS .qml sidecar.



Grid cells: bin any layer into H3 hexagons or A5 equal-area pentagons, counted or averaged per cell, with a live preview and the SQL it writes.
Dot density: one dot stands for an amount you choose, placed at random inside its polygons, with up to six columns in their own colors.
A time slider that filters the map and table by a date column and plays across time, and arrows that show the direction of lines.



Export all, filtered or selected rows to GeoParquet, GeoPackage, GeoJSON, newline-delimited GeoJSON, FlatGeobuf, Shapefile, KML, CSV, Parquet, Excel or JSON, in any EPSG CRS. Print lays the map out as a page (paper size, title, legend, scale bar, north arrow, a table and chart of the rows, even an atlas with a page per feature) and saves PNG, PDF or SVG with editable text.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
3 One codebase, two shells
The first version was a single page of JavaScript with module-level state, and it showed. It worked, but sharing a link or restoring a session meant threading state through everything. When I wanted a VS Code extension, I rebuilt it so the engine and the interface don’t know which shell they are in.






flowchart TD
  W["apps/web<br>browser shell"] --> UI
  X["apps/vscode-ext<br>custom editor + webview"] --> UI
  UI["packages/ui<br>map, table, panels"] --> CORE
  CORE["packages/core<br>sources, queries, styles, export"] --> DB["DuckDB-WASM"]






packages/core and packages/ui are forbidden (by a lint rule) from importing vscode, touching the File API or using IndexedDB. Anything platform-specific goes through one interface, the HostAdapter: pick the theme, open files, read a file as bytes or a URL for range reads, save a file, persist state, set a status. The web app implements it with the browser; the extension implements it with the VS Code API. Each custom-editor webview gets its own DuckDB instance.
The stack is Svelte 5, Vite and strict TypeScript, MapLibre GL JS for the map, CodeMirror 6 for the SQL editor, Terra Draw for drawing, and DuckDB-WASM underneath.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
4 Running DuckDB in a webview
DuckDB-WASM is the heart of it: a WebAssembly build of the DuckDB analytical engine, including the spatial extension that provides ST_Within, ST_Intersects, ST_Transform and friends.
In the first version I leaned on multi-threading, which needs SharedArrayBuffer, which needs special response headers that GitHub Pages cannot set. A service worker (coi-serviceworker) papered over that. VS Code webviews can’t use that trick, so the rebuild uses the single-threaded DuckDB-WASM bundle in both shells. One engine configuration to test is worth more than the speed-up.
A few decisions followed from taking the engine seriously:

The engine is not bundled. DuckDB-WASM, its extensions (spatial, parquet, json, and the optional full-text search, H3 and A5) and sql.js are downloaded once from pinned URLs and checked against SHA-256 hashes recorded in the repo, then cached locally (Cache Storage on the web, extension storage in VS Code), so later starts work offline.
There is a known ceiling. The engine’s memory limit is about 3.1 GiB in both shells, which I measured rather than assumed, and the design works around it.
Reads are ranged where possible, so the whole file is not copied into the webview.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
section: 5 Big data without re-querying on every pan
text:
5 Big data without re-querying on every pan
Drawing a million features as GeoJSON would freeze any tab, and re-running a query on every pan is slow. The rule is a size threshold:

Results under 100,000 rows (and files under 100 MiB) are converted to GeoJSON once and drawn from memory.
Larger ones are drawn from vector tiles that DuckDB builds per tile with ST_AsMVT, served to MapLibre through a custom protocol handler. A “Load all” link is there if you really want everything.

That is how files with millions of rows and several gigabytes stay pannable.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
6 The query is the product
Several features that look like dialogs are really generators of SQL, and show you the SQL.
Grid cells bin a layer into H3 or A5 cells with a live preview. The SQL it writes is the same SQL a power user would write, so you can copy it, change it, and run it as a normal query. The result gets the same styling and export as any other.
Dot density is the best example. DuckDB has no point-in-polygon generator (ST_GeneratePoints takes a bounding box), so the query samples each polygon’s box with a deterministic hash(feature, column, k) and keeps the first n points that are ST_Within the polygon. Because the hash is deterministic, the map looks the same every time instead of reshuffling the dots on each redraw.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
7 Formats that fight back
File Geodatabases are the format I most wanted and the hardest to read.






ImportantWhat the engine cannot do



DuckDB-WASM’s GDAL build has the OpenFileGDB driver turned off for WebAssembly, so the SQL engine cannot open a .gdb at all, and it cannot read inside a zip either.








TipThe workaround



gdal3.js (GDAL 3.8.4 compiled to WebAssembly) is downloaded only the first time you open a geodatabase, and converts the chosen layer so DuckDB can query it. In a spike on an 818 MB geodatabase it listed layers in 87 ms and converted 4 million parcels to FlatGeobuf in 34 seconds.








CautionStill unreadable



Compressed (CDF/SDC) geodatabases remain unreadable by any open-source reader, so that format stays marked experimental.


GTFS feeds are detected by what is inside the zip (stops, routes, trips, stop times and their columns), never by file name, so GTFS.zip, google_transit.zip and data.zip all work. A feed opens as two layers drawn together, routes (lines, in each route’s own color) and stops (points), each its own table.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
8 Styles that travel
Styles are saved as a QGIS .qml sidecar, so a styled file looks right in QGIS too, and the app imports and exports QML, SLD and Mapbox GL style JSON. Labels are drawn with system fonts (nothing is downloaded), saved with the style, and included when you export the map image.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
9 What I’d say about scope
The project has an explicit list of things it will not do: feature editing, georeferencing, a processing toolbox, notebooks, plugins, raster analysis, stacked basemaps, multiple map layers. One layer is on the map at a time; multi-file work is done in SQL. Every exception (a globe projection, polygon extrusion, terrain) was a recorded decision. For a tool whose point is “never open QGIS for basic work”, staying a quick-look tool matters more than any one feature.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
10 Privacy and network use
Your data stays on your machine. The network is used for the engine’s code (downloaded once, then cached), for basemap tiles, and for an opt-out place search that sends only the text you type.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
11 Wrapping up
The code is MIT-licensed on GitHub, and the changelog has the details of every release. The project owes a lot to GeoLibre and Qiusheng Wu, a constant reference for the style panel, basemap picker and data-loading design, and to Kyle Walker’s original Spatial SQL Explorer for the idea. If you work with spatial data and want a scratchpad that doesn’t need a server, give it a try. Issues and PRs welcome.

title: Restyling Utah’s Vector Basemap for MapLibre
text:
Utah’s UGRC publishes a very good free vector basemap, the “Lite” basemap, as three Esri vector-tile services: VectorHillshade, LiteBase and LiteLabels. It has one look. If your app is dark, or you want something warmer, you are rewriting hundreds of layer styles by hand.
ugrc-styles is my answer to that. It is two things in one repository: a small Python tool that generates alternate themes from the live UGRC services, and a visual editor in the browser for tweaking, comparing and downloading any of them without touching JSON. This post covers why it exists, how a theme gets generated, the bugs that taught me the most, and what the editor does.

title: Restyling Utah’s Vector Basemap for MapLibre
text:
1 Try the editor
Pick a built-in theme (or drop in your own style), click a layer to edit its colors, opacity, filters or zoom range, and use Compare against to swipe your edit against another theme or UGRC’s own live basemap.


  
    UGRC Style Editor
    Fullscreen
  
  
    
  



 Open app  GitHub

title: Restyling Utah’s Vector Basemap for MapLibre
section: 2 Why restyling a basemap is harder than it sounds
text:
2 Why restyling a basemap is harder than it sounds
A MapLibre style is a JSON file: a list of layers, each saying which part of the vector tiles to draw and how (“draw this road class in this color, this wide, from this zoom”). Changing the look of a basemap means changing those paint values. For UGRC’s Lite basemap that is a lot of layers, and they are not organised the way you would hope. ArcGIS Pro’s vector tile publisher writes a separate layer for each zoom band, so a single road class can appear as a dozen or more near-identical copies, each with its own color.
Two other things make a hand edit fragile. The style lives on UGRC’s servers and changes when they update it, so a copy edited by hand goes stale. And the highway shields and point icons are raster images in sprite sheets, which no paint property can recolor.
So rather than editing a style, I wanted to describe a theme as a set of rules and regenerate it from UGRC’s current style whenever I like.

title: Restyling Utah’s Vector Basemap for MapLibre
text:
3 How a theme is generated
The project started as a dark version of Lite, built with one-off R and Python scripts. On 23 September 2026 I rebuilt it as a proper Python package managed with uv, and the following day restructured it so the repository could hold several themes side by side.
Each build does the same few steps:

Fetch UGRC’s three styles live. UGRC’s style definitions are never copied into the repository. Every run pulls them fresh from the ArcGIS endpoints listed in config/services.json.
Fetch the theme’s palette live too. A theme names a palette source. The first dark theme read its colors from Protomaps’ dark flavor; sol, a warm light theme, reads them straight out of CARTO’s public Voyager style JSON. A small palette_extra.json adds the few tokens that source has no equivalent for, with a rule that nothing in it may duplicate a value the live source already provides.
Apply the theme’s rules. Each service has a rules file. A rule matches layers by source layer, type or id (all regular expressions) and sets paint values, usually by palette token:
{ "note": "contours",
  "match": { "source_layer": "^Contours" },
  "paint": { "line-color": "@contour", "line-opacity": 0.3 } }
Fall back for everything else. Any color no rule touched gets a generic treatment from fallback.json: fills, lines and circles keep their hue but have their lightness squeezed into a band (high and pastel for sol) and their saturation reduced, while label text gets a muted tint. That way a layer UGRC adds next month still comes out looking like part of the theme.
Rework the sprites. For a dark theme, the generator inverts every icon’s lightness in HLS space, which keeps a red shield red instead of turning it cyan the way an RGB invert would. Sol goes another way: it swaps in UGRC’s colorful Vector_Overlay icon set (built for their Hybrid basemap) in place of Lite’s muted grayscale icons, using a map from Lite’s icon names to Vector_Overlay’s, and pastes back the few icons that have no equivalent there, such as trailheads and the railroad tie marks.

Only the generated styles and sprites are committed, so anyone can use them without running the code. Regenerating is uv run ugrc-styles, and adding a theme means adding a directory under config/themes/; nothing in the code or the web page changes.

title: Restyling Utah’s Vector Basemap for MapLibre
text:
4 Bugs that taught me something
A few problems from the first week shaped how the project works now.
Layer order is not alphabetical. The config loader originally read each theme’s three services in alphabetical order. That put VectorHillshade last, and since later layers draw on top, the hillshade covered every fill and label underneath it. Services now load in the order services.json declares them: hillshade, base, labels, bottom to top.
A renderer bug that looked like missing data. With MapLibre GL JS 4.7.1, LiteBase tiles failed to decode (“Unimplemented type: 3”) whenever another source was on the map, leaving rectangular holes with no roads or water. LiteBase alone rendered fine. I reproduced it in isolation at the failing coordinates and confirmed it went away on 5.24.0, the last release that still shipped a UMD bundle, and moved the page to that version.
Respect the original’s precision. UGRC tunes each trail layer’s dash pattern against its line width, so every width and zoom tier ends up with the same effective dash length (around 2.7 px). My first attempt at Voyager-style trails replaced those dashes with one new ratio, and neighbouring tiers fell out of phase into a messy line. The fix was to let a rule scale Esri’s own values instead of replacing them, which keeps their alignment and lengthens the dash.
Keep the output Esri-shaped. UGRC planned to host the generated dark styles on ArcGIS Online, not only use them in MapLibre. So the build keeps Esri’s own url reference to the vector tile server rather than rewriting it into a MapLibre tiles array, and the generated files differ from UGRC’s only in paint and sprites. The price is the one gotcha described below.
The attribution was “me”. UGRC’s hosted tile server sets its source’s attribution text to the literal string "me", apparently left over from a template. The editor strips it when rendering and credits UGRC and MapLibre itself.

title: Restyling Utah’s Vector Basemap for MapLibre
text:
5 The themes now

sol: the warm light restyling on CARTO’s Voyager colors, with UGRC’s colorful Vector_Overlay icons.
Dark: UGRC’s official dark basemap, loaded live from their three ArcGIS items. For a while the repository generated its own dark theme, called shadow. In November 2026 its paint and layout were identical to UGRC’s official dark basemap, so I removed my copy and load theirs directly instead.
Lite: UGRC’s original, also loaded live, for comparison.

title: Restyling Utah’s Vector Basemap for MapLibre
Restyling Utah’s Vector Basemap for MapLibre
Restyling Utah’s Vector Basemap for MapLibre
text:
8 What’s next
The repository keeps a short backlog of editor ideas in PIPELINE.md. The ones I find most useful are a button that exports the current swipe comparison as one image, a shareable link that encodes only the properties you changed, and MapLibre’s label collision boxes as a debug overlay, which would answer the recurring “why is this label not showing at this zoom?” question directly. New themes are a directory of rules away.
I built the generator and the editor with Claude as a pair programmer. The code is on GitHub under the MIT license, and the basemap data and tiles are UGRC’s.

title: Analyzing the Utah Bikeways data
text:
This analysis examines the distribution of roadway and bikeway infrastructure across Utah municipalities. The primary objectives are to:

Calculate total road lane miles for each municipality
Calculate bikeway lane miles by facility type for each municipality
Compare roadway and bikeway infrastructure across municipalities

All spatial data is sourced from the Utah Geospatial Resource Center (UGRC) (Utah Geospatial Resource Center 2025) and processed using the R spatial ecosystem. The diagram shows how the pieces fit together.

text:
2.3 Environment Variables
We use EPSG:3566 (NAD83(HARN) / Utah North) projection, which uses US survey feet as the base unit. This projection is appropriate for statewide analysis in Utah and ensures accurate distance calculations.

1PROJECT_CRS = "EPSG:3566"

2tmap::tmap_mode("view")


1

Every layer is reprojected to this CRS, so lengths come out in US survey feet.

2

tmap draws interactive maps in the web version of this post.

title: Analyzing the Utah Bikeways data
text:
3.1 Utah City Boundaries
Municipal boundaries are used to aggregate roadway and bikeway data by city. These boundaries represent the legal limits of incorporated municipalities in Utah.

1path_ut_cities <- file.path(dir_data, "UtahMunicipalBoundaries.gpkg")

2if (!fs::file_exists(path_ut_cities)) {
3  sf_ut_cities <- arc_read_retry(
    "https://services1.arcgis.com/99lidPhWCzftIe9K/ArcGIS/rest/services/UtahMunicipalBoundaries/FeatureServer/0",
    crs = PROJECT_CRS
  ) |> janitor::clean_names()
  sf_ut_cities |>
4    sf::st_write(path_ut_cities, layer = "UtahMunicipalBoundaries", append = FALSE)
}

5sf_ut_cities <- sf::st_read(path_ut_cities, quiet = TRUE) |>
  sf::st_transform(PROJECT_CRS)


1

Where this layer is cached.

2

Download only if there is no local copy yet.

3

Read the feature service with the retry wrapper from Listing 1.

4

Write it to a GeoPackage for next time.

5

Always read from the local copy, so the geometry column is the same whether the file was just downloaded or already existed.




The same download-once pattern repeats for the county, roads and bikeways layers below.

title: Analyzing the Utah Bikeways data
text:
3.2 Utah County Boundaries
County boundaries are used to aggregate roadway and bikeway data for unincorporated areas in Utah.

# Define paths
path_ut_counties <- file.path(dir_data, "UtahCountyBoundaries.gpkg")

# Download if not exists
if (!fs::file_exists(path_ut_counties)) {
  # Read data using arcgis package
  sf_ut_counties <- arc_read_retry(
    "https://services1.arcgis.com/99lidPhWCzftIe9K/ArcGIS/rest/services/UtahCountyBoundaries/FeatureServer/0",
    crs = PROJECT_CRS
  ) |> janitor::clean_names()
  # Write to a GeoDatabase
  sf_ut_counties |>
    sf::st_write(path_ut_counties, layer = "UtahCountyBoundaries", append = FALSE)
}

# Always read from the local copy, so the geometry column is the same
# whether the file was just downloaded or already existed
sf_ut_counties <- sf::st_read(path_ut_counties, quiet = TRUE) |>
  sf::st_transform(PROJECT_CRS)


tmap::qtm(sf_ut_cities)

}

title: Analyzing the Utah Bikeways data
text:
4.2 Calculate Lane Miles
Road lane miles are calculated by multiplying the length of each road segment by the number of through lanes.






WarningMissing lane counts are assumed to be one lane



Where a road segment’s through-lane count is missing (NA), the calculation assumes 1 lane as a conservative estimate. Fixing this in the source data is still a to-do.


The calculation converts the geometry length from US survey feet to miles using the units package, which properly handles unit conversions and maintains unit awareness throughout the analysis.

sf_ut_roads <- sf_ut_roads |>
    dplyr::mutate(
1        dot_thrulanes = dplyr::if_else(is.na(dot_thrulanes), 1, dot_thrulanes),
2        miles = units::set_units(sf::st_length(`geom`), "mile"),
3        lane_miles = units::set_units(dot_thrulanes * miles, "mile")
    )

sf_ut_roads |>
  dplyr::select(dot_thrulanes, miles, lane_miles) |>
  head(20)


1

A missing through-lane count is treated as one lane (to do: fix this in the source data).

2

Segment length, converted from US survey feet to miles.

3

Lane miles are the length times the number of through lanes.

title: Analyzing the Utah Bikeways data
text:
4.3 Aggregate by Municipality
Using spatial join, we associate each road segment with its municipality and sum the lane miles. Roads that fall outside municipal boundaries will have NA for city_name.

# Calculate total lane miles by municipality
road_miles_by_city <- sf_ut_roads |>
1    sf::st_join(
      sf_ut_municipal,
      join = sf::st_intersects
    ) |>
2    dplyr::group_by(Name) |>
    dplyr::summarize(
      total_lane_miles = sum(lane_miles, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
3    sf::st_drop_geometry()

road_miles_by_city |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(total_lane_miles))


1

Spatial join: attach each road segment to the city or unincorporated area it falls within.

2

Group by municipality and add up the lane miles.

3

Keep a plain table; the geometry is no longer needed.

title: Analyzing the Utah Bikeways data
text:
5.1 Reclassify Bikeway Types to Categories
We use forcats package to respect the hierarchy of the bicycle facilities.

1facility_class_order <- c(
  "Paved Path",
  "Protected Bike Lane",
  "Bike Lane",
  "Marked Route",
  "Unmarked Route",
  "Other"
)

sf_ut_bikeways <- sf_ut_bikeways |>
  dplyr::mutate(
2    facility1_class = dplyr::case_when(
      facility1 == "Trail or Pathway" ~ "Paved Path",
      facility1 %in% c(
        "Cycle track, at-grade, protected with parking (1A)",
        "Cycle track, protected with barrier (1B)",
        "Cycle track, raised and curb separated (1C)"
      ) ~ "Protected Bike Lane",
      facility1 %in% c(
        "Buffered bike lane (2A)",
        "Bike lane (2B)"
      ) ~ "Bike Lane",
      facility1 %in% c(
        "Marked shared roadway (3B)",
        "Signed shared roadway (3C)"
      ) ~ "Marked Route",
      facility1 == "Shoulder bikeway (3A)" ~ "Unmarked Route",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    facility2_class = dplyr::case_when(
      facility2 == "Trail or Pathway" ~ "Paved Path",
      facility2 %in% c(
        "Cycle track, at-grade, protected with parking (1A)",
        "Cycle track, protected with barrier (1B)",
        "Cycle track, raised and curb separated (1C)"
      ) ~ "Protected Bike Lane",
      facility2 %in% c(
        "Buffered bike lane (2A)",
        "Bike lane (2B)"
      ) ~ "Bike Lane",
      facility2 %in% c(
        "Marked shared roadway (3B)",
        "Signed shared roadway (3C)"
      ) ~ "Marked Route",
      facility2 == "Shoulder bikeway (3A)" ~ "Unmarked Route",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
3    facility1_class = factor(facility1_class, levels = facility_class_order),
    facility2_class = factor(facility2_class, levels = facility_class_order)
  )


1

The classes, from the most protected facility to the least, in the order forcats will respect.

2

Collapse UGRC’s detailed facility names into five broader classes; the same recoding is applied to facility2 below.

3

Turn both columns into ordered factors, so tables and plots keep this order.

Bridging transportation modeling with economic quantification


Good morning! I’m Pukar Bhandari, and I’m excited to discuss how economic impact analysis can enhance WFRC’s already strong transportation planning capabilities.
I completed my graduate education here at the University of Utah in Transportation Planning, and over the past three years, I’ve specialized in developing methods that bridge transportation modeling with economic quantification. Most relevant to this role, I’ve had direct experience working on Utah’s transportation planning context - I led economic assessments for Utah’s Unified Transportation Plan 2023-2050.
What really excites me about WFRC is the opportunity to support investment prioritization in one of the nation’s fastest-growing regions, contribute to 2034 Olympic legacy planning, and be part of your transition to activity-based modeling. My technical background in travel demand modeling with Cube and TransCAD, combined with economic impact tools like IMPLAN, positions me to contribute from day one.

WFRC has built a sophisticated foundation - you have strong travel demand modeling capabilities, you’re transitioning to activity-based modeling, and you’re dealing with complex investment decisions in a rapidly growing region.
Where I see an opportunity to add value is moving from asking “How does the system perform?” to “What does this investment do for our region’s economy?”
Traditional analysis focuses on travel time savings, VMT reduction, crash reduction, and emissions benefits. Enhanced analysis that I can bring adds regional job creation, economic multiplier effects, business attraction potential, and return on investment metrics.
This enhanced perspective doesn’t replace what you’re already doing well - it helps justify investments to stakeholders and supports competitive grant applications, which is increasingly important in today’s funding environment.

title: Quantifying Economic Effects of Transportation Investments
text:
Economic Impact Framework I’ve Applied







flowchart TB
    A["<b>Transportation Investment</b>"] --> B("Direct Construction<br>Stimulus") & C("User Cost Savings<br>Time • Crashes • Fuel") & D("Market Access Improvements<br>Larger Labor/Supplier Pool") & E("Business Attraction<br>Enhanced Site Competitiveness")
    B --> F(["<b>Regional Economic Impacts</b>"])
    C --> F
    D --> F
    E --> F
    F --> G["Jobs Created"] & H["Household Income"] & I["Business Output"] & J["GDP Growth"]

    style A fill:#005577,color:#ffffff
    style F fill:#e8f5e8
    style B fill:#fff3e0
    style C fill:#e1f5fe
    style D fill:#f3e5f5
    style E fill:#fce4ec









Key insight from my experience: Not all transportation benefits create wider economic impacts. Understanding this distinction helps prioritize projects that maximize both mobility and economic returns.



Here’s the systematic framework I’ve developed through my work. Transportation investments create economic impacts through four main pathways:
First, direct construction stimulus - the immediate jobs and spending from building infrastructure. Second, user cost savings - when people save time, reduce crashes, and spend less on fuel, that money gets reinvested in the economy. Third, market access improvements - better transportation expands labor pools and supplier networks for businesses. And fourth, business attraction - enhanced infrastructure makes locations more competitive for new investment.
All of these feed into broader regional economic impacts: jobs created, household income growth, business output increases, and GDP growth.
The key insight from my experience is that not all transportation benefits create wider economic impacts. Understanding this distinction helps prioritize projects that maximize both mobility and economic returns.

Let me show you how this works in practice with Utah’s $88+ billion transportation plan.
My methodology integrated travel demand model outputs with benefit-cost analysis frameworks and economic impact analysis. This workflow produces clear, reproducible, data-driven impact reports that can directly support WFRC’s future RTP development, Olympic planning, and federal grant applications.

title: Commute Flow Explorer
text:
NoteDeveloped at the Wasatch Front Regional Council (WFRC)



The application and its repository belong to WFRC; this page only summarizes my work.

title: Commute Flow Explorer
text:
Why a second commute tool
WFRC already had a commute flow map: Commute Patterns, which answers questions about named places. Where do Salt Lake City’s residents work? Where do Davis County’s workers live? That works well when the question follows a city, county or district boundary.
Many planning questions don’t. A transit station, a new employment center or a corridor doesn’t have a boundary in the Census data, and the people asking about it want to know how many commuters move between that spot and a few others. The underlying data, the Census Bureau’s LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics (LODES), is published for Census blocks, so the detail is there. What was missing was a way to draw your own areas and compare them.
The repository puts the difference plainly: use Commute Patterns when your question is about a named jurisdiction, and use Commute Flow Explorer when you want to draw your own catchment areas and compare them.

title: Commute Flow Explorer
text:
What it does
The app opens on an overview flow map of every commute flow across the eight-county Wasatch Front region. Zoomed out, nearby flows are clustered into a readable picture of the region; zooming in breaks them back apart.
Pressing Select Points switches to analysis mode. Click anywhere on the map to place 2 to 10 analysis points. Each point captures a ring of H3 hexagons (about 0.1 km² cells) around the click, and the ring size can be set for all points at once or for one point on its own. Then:

Flow lines connect every pair of points, in both directions, scaled and coloured by the number of commuters. Hovering a line shows the total with wage and industry breakdowns, and a click pins that tooltip in place.
An OD matrix lists every origin-destination pair in a colour-coded table, with the same wage and industry detail.
Point cards in the sidebar show each point’s name (editable), county, colour, and outbound and inbound totals. Points can be dragged to reorder them.
A year selector covers LODES data from 2002 to 2023. Selecting 2020 or 2021 shows a badge warning that those years were disrupted by COVID.

Everything runs in the browser: LODES data is queried with DuckDB-WASM, with light and dark themes, and there is no server or API key behind it.

title: Commute Flow Explorer
text:
How it’s built

The data pipeline
A set of Python scripts, run with uv, prepares the data once. They download the LODES origin-destination files and the workplace area files for the configured counties, and use the Census geography crosswalk to assign every block to the H3 resolution 9 cell that contains it. Flows are then summed from block pairs to hexagon pairs and written as one Parquet file per year: total commuters, three wage bands, and three industry groups. The industry counts come from the workplace files, joined at the work block before aggregation so that they describe the jobs at the destination. A small metadata file lists every populated cell with its centre and county, and is loaded once when the app starts.
The list of counties lives in a single YAML file. Adding or removing a county, even one in another state for a cross-state metro, means editing that file and rerunning the scripts; the app code doesn’t change.


The app
The front end is React with Vite. MapLibre draws the map, h3-js turns a click into a ring of cells, and Flowmap.gl on deck.gl draws the flows. When the points, the year or a ring size change, the app sends DuckDB-WASM a query for the flows between the selected cells and rebuilds the flow lines and the matrix from the result.

title: Commute Flow Explorer
text:
Interesting problems
Running DuckDB on GitHub Pages. The multi-threaded builds of DuckDB-WASM need cross-origin isolation headers that GitHub Pages doesn’t set. The app uses the single-threaded bundle, which needs neither those headers nor a server, and reads each year’s Parquet file over HTTP.
Keeping the overview fast. Drawing every hexagon pair in the region at once made Flowmap.gl’s clustering slow. The overview query instead aggregates flows to a 0.1-degree grid inside DuckDB before they reach the map, which leaves a few hundred cells for the flow layer to cluster and keeps panning responsive.
Overlapping catchments. Two points placed close together can share cells. The app detects this, names the overlapping pair in a warning, and highlights the shared cells. A flow from a shared cell is counted for both points, which is stated in the warning rather than hidden. Shrinking the ring of one point, or of all of them, clears the overlap.
Naming a county for an empty cell. Each point card shows its county, looked up from the cell metadata. Cells in sparse areas, such as the Tooele salt flats or mountain wilderness, have no blocks with people or jobs and so no metadata. For those, the lookup falls back to the cell’s much larger resolution 5 parent cell (about 250 km²) and takes the county from there.
A basemap that wouldn’t render. UGRC’s vector basemap is an option alongside the default Carto basemap. Its tiles, served by ArcGIS, encode some data in an older Protocol Buffers form that MapLibre’s tile parser doesn’t accept, leaving holes in the map. A small service worker intercepts those tile requests and rewrites the affected fields into the standard encoding before MapLibre sees them.
Clicks that meant two things. Clicking a flow line to pin its tooltip also counted as a click on the map, which placed a stray analysis point underneath it. The flow layer now marks the click as handled, so the map’s click handler skips it.

title: Commute Flow Explorer
text:
How the work was organized
I built it spec-first. Before any app code, the repository held a set of principles (no server, data fidelity, geography from config, accessibility among them), a specification with user stories and requirements, a research note on each library choice, the data model and an ordered task list. The first full implementation followed those documents, and the commits after it are refinement: the overview mode, the dockable tooltips, the WFRC theme, resizable panels and per-point ring control.

title: Commute Flow Explorer
text:
What I worked on
The full application: the data pipeline that builds the hexagon flow files, a React and Vite front end, MapLibre with flowmap.gl and deck.gl for the flow layer, and the Parquet data that DuckDB-WASM queries.
My role: developer. I authored all the commits in the repository.

title: GTFS vs. TDM Transit Network Comparison
text:
NoteDeveloped at the Wasatch Front Regional Council (WFRC)



The tool and its repository belong to WFRC; this page only summarizes my work.

title: GTFS vs. TDM Transit Network Comparison
text:
Why compare the two
The regional travel demand model (TDM) represents transit service, meaning routes, stops and the line-haul network, for a defined base year. The model’s transit results depend on that network, so the base year should match the service that was actually running. GTFS feeds, which transit agencies publish for trip planners and apps, describe the same service as it was actually operated. Putting the two side by side is the most direct way to check the model’s network.
Before this tool, that check was a manual QGIS project: convert a GTFS feed to GIS layers, load the model’s transit lines, and compare. The conversion lost information along the way, including each route’s own colour, its route type and the separate shapes of its variants. This tool puts both on one map so the two can be checked against each other, with any feed.
It is deliberately a visual validation tool: there is no automated route matching or coverage-gap scoring. A person looks at the alignment and decides.

title: GTFS vs. TDM Transit Network Comparison
text:
What it does

Overlay or swipe: draw both networks on one map, or compare them side by side with a swipe control.
Flexible GTFS sources: a saved snapshot, a feed URL, a calendar date resolved to the historical UTA snapshot closest to it, or an uploaded GTFS zip.
TDM options: the base year or forecast scenarios, and line types (rail, BRT, core, express, local), each shown as lines, stops or both.
Details on demand: hovering a line names it, and clicking a route or stop opens a panel. For GTFS that includes the agency, the number of trips and stops served, the route’s website, and for stops the stop code and wheelchair boarding information.
Validity dates: the map shows the date range the loaded feed covers, read from the feed itself.
Basemaps that follow light and dark mode.

The base year is the default, since comparing a forecast scenario with present-day GTFS isn’t meaningful, but the forecast networks stay available for anyone who wants to see them.

title: GTFS vs. TDM Transit Network Comparison
text:
How it’s built
The tool exists in two forms, sharing the same data and the same logic.
An R Shiny app came first. It uses tidytransit to read GTFS, sf to read the model network, and mapgl for the MapLibre map and the swipe view. Both datasets are processed live from their original files: the GTFS zips as downloaded, and the model’s network as exported, a zipped file geodatabase read in place through GDAL’s virtual file system. There is no processed copy of either to keep in sync, and the pipeline discovers the model’s transit groups from the geodatabase itself, so it keeps working as new groups are added. The app’s colours, fonts and logos come from WFRC’s brand repository, included as a git submodule.
A static web app, the one linked below, is a port to Svelte and TypeScript built with Vite, so it can run on GitHub Pages with no R server behind it. The model network is converted to GeoJSON ahead of time with GDAL and committed. GTFS is parsed in the browser.

title: GTFS vs. TDM Transit Network Comparison
text:
Interesting problems
Making the model’s lines the right colour. The comparison reads best when a model route is drawn in the same colour as the real route it represents, so a mismatch stands out. The model doesn’t store route colours, so they have to be inferred. Rail is matched by named line (the TRAX lines, the S-Line and FrontRunner). For buses, the model’s route name almost always contains the real route number once the agency prefix and leading zeros are stripped (S513 becomes 513), and flex routes map to their F-prefixed names. That name crosswalk gives 71 of the 75 base-year bus routes their exact colour from the GTFS feed. The rest fall back to a rule based on mode and headway: the base-year network doesn’t tag frequent “core” routes, so a local route with a best headway of 15 minutes or less is coloured as core. A spatial check against the live network found that this rule, with the per-line rail colours, raised the colour match from 77% to 89%, and the crosswalk caught a route the rule had wrong. The crosswalk is limited to the base year, because some forecast-only project codes happened to end in digits that matched unrelated present-day routes.
Parsing GTFS in a browser. There was no maintained JavaScript library that turns a GTFS zip into route shapes and stops in the browser; the purpose-built packages I found were Node-only. So the static app has its own port of the R pipeline, using unzipit and papaparse, and was checked against the R app on the same feed: the known route colours and the feed’s validity range match exactly. The parsing runs in a Web Worker so the page stays responsive. Before parsing, the app reads the uncompressed size of the largest files straight from the zip’s index and warns about feeds large enough to strain the browser. Setting that limit took measurement rather than a guess: UTA’s feed is about 4 MB as a zip but over 25 MB uncompressed, because the stop times compress so well, so a first guess of 10 MB would have rejected the very feed the tool is for.
Historical feeds without a backend. The “by date” source asks the Mobility Database, which archives past GTFS feeds, for the UTA snapshot that was in service closest to a chosen date. Its API requires a personal token. A server could hold a shared one, but the static app deliberately has no server, and anything shipped in a public JavaScript bundle can be read by anyone. So each visitor supplies their own free token, which is stored only in their own browser. The same constraint shows up with the feed URL source: most transit agencies’ servers don’t allow cross-origin requests from a browser, so when that fails the app says why and suggests downloading the zip and uploading it instead. A set of dated UTA snapshots committed to the repository covers the common case with no setup at all.
Swipe mode and clustering. In the R app’s overlay view, GTFS stops cluster at low zoom. In its swipe view they don’t, because mapgl’s compare widget drops the clustering options when it builds each side’s map; that is a limit of the package rather than of this app.

title: GTFS vs. TDM Transit Network Comparison
text:
What I worked on
The comparison app and the pipeline that turns GTFS feeds into route shapes and stops, including colors derived from each route’s own color. That covers both versions: the R Shiny app and the static Svelte port, along with the colour matching for the model network and the Mobility Database lookup.
My role: developer. I authored all the commits in the repository.

title: Opportunity Zones 2.0 Tract Info Sheets
text:
NoteDeveloped at the Wasatch Front Regional Council (WFRC), with Mountainland Association of Governments (MAG)



The reports and repository belong to WFRC; this page only summarizes my work.

title: Opportunity Zones 2.0 Tract Info Sheets
text:
Why tract-level info sheets
Opportunity Zones offer federal tax incentives for investment in designated census tracts. With the second round of the program (OZ 2.0), Utah has a long list of eligible tracts, and the people weighing them, from local governments to investors, need to compare tracts on the things that make investment work: land that can be developed, access to jobs, transit, planned housing and expected growth.
That information exists, but it is spread across a dozen regional datasets maintained by different teams: Wasatch Choice centers, station area plans, the Access to Opportunities index, small-area growth forecasts, census demographics and the housing unit inventory. The info sheets bring it together into one consistent page per tract, and a one-page table per county to compare tracts side by side.

title: Opportunity Zones 2.0 Tract Info Sheets
text:
What’s on a page
Each detail page is built to be read in under a minute:

The header names the tract (with a descriptive name, such as “SLC - U of U Main Campus”), its acreage, and the Urban Institute’s investment likelihood rating.
Four key measures across the top: how much of the tract lies in a metropolitan, urban or city center; a 0 to 100 Access to Opportunities index combining driving and transit access to jobs and households; planned housing density from station area plans; and projected growth from 2027 to 2037 in equivalent residential units (ERU) per developable acre.
The map shows the tract with Wasatch Choice centers, station area plan buffers, rail and BRT stops and freeway exits.
Six panels give the detail behind the headline numbers: the tract profile, center and district coverage, housing and demographics, transit, auto access and projected growth.

The county summary puts every tract in a county on one page with the same measures, and an Excel workbook carries all of it with live formulas, plus a PDF version that prints the workbook as Excel would.

title: Opportunity Zones 2.0 Tract Info Sheets
text:
How it’s built
The pipeline is a Quarto project in R, in four stages:

Load. GIS layers are pulled from ArcGIS services and local sources and cached as GeoPackages, then read with sf using SQL and spatial filters so only the needed features come in.
Calculate. Per-tract metrics: center and station-area overlaps, housing joins, Access to Opportunities scores weighted by developable acres, and growth forecasts area-proportioned from traffic analysis zones.
Map. A ggplot per tract, saved at 200 dpi and cached so the summary and detail documents share them.
Render. Parameterized Quarto documents render each county’s summary and detail PDFs with Typst, which gives precise control over a dense, fixed landscape layout.

The page design came from a visual mock-up, and the Typst templates reproduce it to the point (literally: the mock’s pixel sizes convert directly to points). Fonts ship with the repository, and R packages are pinned with renv, so anyone can regenerate the full set when the eligible list or the underlying data changes.

Sharper maps with basemapper
The first version of the maps used raster basemap tiles, and in print they looked soft: blurry contours, and labels that were hard to read. UGRC publishes the same basemap as a vector style, but no R tool could draw one under a ggplot. So I wrote basemapper, an R and Python package that renders vector basemaps at the figure’s own zoom and resolution, and switched the maps to it.




Before: raster basemap tiles



After: UGRC Lite vector, rendered by basemapper

title: Opportunity Zones 2.0 Tract Info Sheets
text:
What I worked on
The whole pipeline: caching and joining the GIS sources, computing the per-tract metrics, generating the maps, designing and building the Typst layouts, and producing the Excel workbook. I authored all the commits in the repository, and wrote basemapper along the way.
The current release covers 108 eligible tracts across Box Elder, Weber, Davis, Salt Lake, Tooele and Utah counties.

title: SE 2025 Urban Form D Variables (H3)
text:
NoteDeveloped at the Wasatch Front Regional Council (WFRC)



The data, tool and repository belong to WFRC; this page only summarizes my work.

title: SE 2025 Urban Form D Variables (H3)
text:
Why the D variables
The “D variables” are a standard framework for describing the parts of the built environment most strongly tied to how people travel: whether they drive, take transit or walk, and how far (Cervero and Kockelman, 1997; Ewing and Cervero, 2010). Measuring them consistently across a region gives planners and modelers a common way to compare places.
WFRC’s SE 2025 socioeconomic data (households, population, residential units and jobs by sector, from the parcel-level Real Estate Market Model) is the natural starting point. This project turns it, together with census, transit and amenity data, into a set of D variables on a uniform grid of H3 hexagons at resolutions 9 and 8, and an explorer for browsing them.
The project began as a smaller job, smoothing the SE data across neighboring hexagons, and grew into a full D-variable pipeline with the smoothing built into each variable.

title: SE 2025 Urban Form D Variables (H3)
text:
What it calculates







Variable
What it measures




Density
Residential units plus jobs (converted to household equivalents) per square mile


Diversity
Balance of households and jobs: 1 when they are in balance, near 0 for a purely residential or purely employment area


Design
Street-network connectivity, with 4-way intersections scored 1 and T-intersections 0.5


Destinations
Overlap with Wasatch Choice centers (60%) plus the presence of six everyday amenities (40%): healthcare, high school, grocery, city hall, park and EMS, each also kept as its own column


Demographics
Median household income and an Income Diversity Index


Distance to transit
Distance to the nearest frequent stop: a weekday median headway of 15 minutes or less, or commuter or heavy rail



A supplementary Rental Housing Attainability Index, developed by Cascadia Partners with WFRC and UTA, is included alongside them. It averages the multifamily share of housing units with the share of renters paying less than 30% of income on rent, on a 0 to 100 scale. The raw SE counts are carried through too, so population, households and jobs by sector can be explored in the same map.

title: SE 2025 Urban Form D Variables (H3)
section: Smoothing: what a place is like, not what is inside a hexagon
text:
Smoothing: what a place is like, not what is inside a hexagon
A level-9 hexagon covers only about 0.04 square miles. A park one block away matters just as much to a resident whether or not it falls inside the same hexagon, and raw per-hexagon values produce sharp edges at cell boundaries that nobody actually experiences.
So each variable is smoothed across up to three rings of neighbors, roughly a half-mile radius. The cell itself keeps 40% of the weight and the rings get 30%, 20% and 10%, so a hexagon’s own character still dominates. The detail that matters is that smoothing is applied to the inputs of each formula, not its output. Smoothed density is still people and jobs per square mile, computed from smoothed counts, rather than an average of neighboring density scores. For ratios like diversity or the attainability index, the counts are smoothed first and then divided.
At the edge of the study area, missing neighbors contribute nothing and their weight is not handed to the neighbors that are present, so a boundary cell is not dominated by the few cells around it. Every variable is also stored unsmoothed, and the explorer’s swipe control puts the two side by side.
Level 8 follows two rules. Raw counts are a plain sum of each cell’s seven level-9 children, so regional totals match exactly at both resolutions. The D variables are recomputed on the level-8 grid with their own smoothing, so each score means the same thing at its own scale.

title: SE 2025 Urban Form D Variables (H3)
text:
Choices worth explaining
Income diversity took three tries. The first version used one minus the Gini coefficient of household income. The second switched to Shannon entropy, so that a mixed-income area scored well regardless of how wealthy it was, but entropy values clustered near the top and were hard to read. The current index splits the region’s households into three income tiers, with the breakpoints drawn from the regional distribution so each tier holds about a third of households, and scores each hexagon as the smallest tier share divided by the largest. A score of 1 means all three tiers are equally present; 0 means at least one is missing entirely. A wealthy area where everyone earns about the same scores low, not because incomes are high but because there is no mix. The same rework fixed a bug that had cut the income brackets off at $75,000.
Filling in counties outside the model. The SE 2025 data covers only the core travel-model area. For Box Elder, Tooele, Morgan, Cache, Summit and Wasatch counties, the grid is extended using the Utah Statewide Travel Model’s own SE 2025 data, spread from traffic analysis zones onto hexagons by area. New hexagons are created only inside cities, towns and census-designated places, since covering whole counties would add a large number of hexagons over empty land.
A buffer or the grid? Cascadia Partners computed the multifamily share with a quarter-mile buffer. I recomputed it in the pipeline as a point-in-hexagon count with the standard ring smoothing. A check script reproduced Cascadia’s buffer values almost exactly, so the reason for the switch is consistency with the rest of the pipeline, not a correction, and the documentation says so.
Small data bugs with large effects. Point layers from the state’s ArcGIS services were at first cached with every coordinate at (0, 0) until the request named a coordinate system explicitly. GDAL’s File Geodatabase writer can produce a corrupt spatial index that makes features vanish when zoomed in, so the pipeline deletes that index before zipping and also writes a GeoPackage copy.

title: SE 2025 Urban Form D Variables (H3)
text:
The explorer
The explorer is a Vite, React and TypeScript app on MapLibre GL, deployed to GitHub Pages. Choosing a variable shows a swipe map, smoothed on the left and raw on the right; for plain counts that have no smoothed version, it becomes a single full-width map. A hover panel lists every variable for the focused hexagon, and a histogram legend shows the distribution.
The map switches from level 8 to level 9 at zoom 11. The hexagons were first served as GeoJSON and are now PMTiles written straight from R, so the browser loads only the tiles in view. Both levels load together and their opacities crossfade over a zoom range, computed on the GPU, which removed a flash of bare basemap during the switch. Thinning features at low zoom and rounding stored values cut the level-9 tiles by more than half. Color classes are Fisher natural breaks computed in R, pooled across smoothed and raw values so both sides of the swipe share a scale.

title: SE 2025 Urban Form D Variables (H3)
text:
Outputs
The pipeline is a single R script with documented, editable parameters at the top: smoothing weights, the jobs-to-household ratio, Wasatch Choice center weights and the income-tier mode. Remote layers are cached locally in full, and filters are applied when they are read, so a filter can change without downloading again. It writes a File Geodatabase and a GeoPackage with level-9 and level-8 layers, the PMTiles and break metadata for the app, and a methodology document that describes each formula.

What I worked on
The R pipeline that computes and smooths the variables, the extension to counties outside the model area, the integration of the Rental Housing Attainability Index, and the interactive explorer.
My role: developer. I authored all the commits in the repository. The Rental Housing Attainability Index method is Cascadia Partners’ work with WFRC and UTA.
